An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Furthermore, the total decay rate into $K^+K^-$ was determined to be $\Gamma_{BS\rightarrow K K} = \frac{\Gamma_{s}}{2\tau_{B^0_s}}$ with a value of $4.3 \times 10^{-10}$, which, when combined with the measured lifetime, confirms the $B^0_s$-$\overline{B}^0_s$ mixing parameter $\Delta\Gamma_{B^0_s} = 0.065 \pm 0.018 \pm 0.005$, resulting in a more precise understanding of the $B^0_s$ system. Additionally, constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that affect the $B^0_s$ system have been tightened, with an upper limit on $\Delta\Gamma_{B^0_s}/\Gamma_{B^0_s}$ at $0.018$ and a more stringent limit on $B^0_s$ decay into two muons at $8 \times 10^{-7}$. A search for the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-K^-/\mu^+\mu^-$ decay revealed an upper limit on the former at $4.1 \times 10^{-6}$ and on the latter at $1.0 \times 10^{-6}$, both with 90% confidence. A first direct measurement of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K_S K_S$ branching fraction was made with a result of $(8.3 \pm 1.3 \pm 0.9 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-6}$. A limit on the sum of all $B^0_s$ decays into two bodies was set at $0.096 \pm 0.019$ or, more conservatively, all $B^0_s$ decays

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. The paper initially presents the mathematical formulation of the problem and then discusses various numerical approaches to solve it, including a key method where the diffusion coefficient is represented as a mixture of explicit factors; it also examines an alternative method using the Monte-Carlo approach. The paper concludes with an analysis of the convergence properties of the methods and offers a comparative assessment of the strategies discussed. Notably, this study is an extension of earlier research on similar control problems governed by elliptic equations. The proposed method for approximating the diffusion coefficient as a sum of explicit factors is an innovative numerical approach. The paper compares this method with an established technique (Helmholtz decomposition), although it acknowledges that the latter might be preferable due to its more intuitive connection with the physical properties of the underlying PDE. The study confirms that both methods yield similar results and guarantees the convergence of the Monte-Carlo approach under certain conditions. The numerical experiments conducted using a specific domain (a three-dimensional sphere) demonstrate the performance of the methods, including their sensitivity to parameter variations, although it is implied that these methods could be applicable to more complex domains requiring higher dimensional solutions. The paper also examines an alternative formulation of the problem where the diffusion coefficient is directly estimated from noisy input data, representing a rough signal; it analyses the convergence properties of the numerical methods in this setting. The research paper is an extension of an earlier study presented at the 2019 ISAAC conference. It provides an enhanced numerical approach and comparative analysis of the methods, confirming the convergence of the Monte-Carlo approach and the sensitivity of the methods to complex data sets. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Our analysis suggests that cosmic magnetic fields with large scales and moderate strengths could shape the observed anisotropy patterns, and that the features we've identified may indicate the presence of cosmic beacons, potentially related to the most powerful active galactic nuclei. Our discoveries underscore the significance of Anisotropy Studies in the field of ultra-high energy cosmic ray research. To dissect such patterns, it becomes necessary to differentiate between cosmic rays originating from within the Galaxy and those from outside, as demonstrated by the separation of anisotropy signals within our energy ranges. Finally, our work highlights the importance of distinguishing between quadrupolar and dipolar components in analyzing large-scale anisotropies, as well as the need to account for the dependencies of anisotropy patterns on energy levels and other variables. To achieve this, it is essential to expand the statistical tools employed in such analyses to include free parameters that define the shape of anisotropy maps. Moreover, a comparative examination of our findings with data from the Telescope Array, another major ultra-high energy cosmic ray observatory, is also necessary to consolidate our discoveries and shed light on possible regional cosmic ray features. Ultimately, resolving the open question of the origins of the highest energy cosmic rays will necessitate a combined analytical and interpretative approach to both existing and future ultra-high energy cosmic ray datasets. Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. The matrix $E_{ab}$ for the $so(3)$ algebra corresponds to the twisted Snyder model, introduced by Balasin, Fring, and Novak. The group manifolds with a noncompact component, like $U(N)$, lead to the divergent series over $\theta$. The convergence of $\theta$-series is observed for the compact group manifolds like $SU(2)$. The Schr\"{o}dinger equation can be solved for an harmonic oscillator potential on an $SU(2)$ manifold, revealing the energy levels as an infinite series over the square of the deformation parameter $\theta$. The first nonvanishing correction to the ground state energy appears at the second order of $\theta$. The value of this correction is $3/4$ times the mass of a harmonic oscillator. The same correction for the ground state can be obtained in the twisted Snyder model with the deformed oscillator, originally proposed by Balasin, Fring, and Novak. The mass spectra obtained from the twisted Snyder model and from its version with the noncommutative Schr\"{o}dinger equation coincide. The issue of the mass scale in these theories is addressed by considering a specific potential as a $\theta$-deformed harmonic oscillator, where the mass of an excitation can be identified as an eigenvalue of a certain operator in a momentum space. Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. We've applied this technique to two prominent time-series tasks – time-series classification and forecasting – and demonstrated exceptional results, outperforming the current state-of-the-art in efficiency and matching expert-designed networks' accuracy. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. We demonstrate the feasibility of this reverse computation by providing an efficient method to compute initial algebra axioms for a given formula and its correspondent. These axioms not only justify but actually compute the correspondent from the original formula. Our approach also exposes a deeper connection between ALBA's rules and the canonical extension method. Moreover, it facilitates an alternative proof of the correctness of ALBA. We also explore an associated notion of canonical base for a given formula and its corresponding algebraic structure. This concept, linked to the computation of initial algebra axioms, enables the analysis of algebraic semantics within the framework of the unity of algebraic and coalgebraic methods. Canonicity proofs obtained via our methods may offer a more intuitive understanding of canonicity than those based on the method of canonical formulas. This perspective is exemplified through a simple canonicity proof for the logic of left-residua over a specific class of algebras. We also illustrate our approach to reverse computation and computed canonical bases with various logics within the DLE family. Lastly, we outline the potential applicability of these methods to other correspondence theories, including those outside the DLE domain. This research focuses on addressing the challenge of handling inconsistencies in tables
that contain reference cells linking similar information from different tables. To achieve
this, we develop a method for identifying and resolving anomalies in these tables. A
key aspect of our approach is the utilization of data quality measures that take into
account common criteria such as data cardinality and consistency. By incorporating these
measures, we can evaluate the impact of fixing potential anomalies and determine their
effect on the overall data quality. Furthermore, our approach enables users to explore
different repair scenarios, facilitating critical decisions in datasets like those found in
databases used for enterprise performance management. To illustrate our methods, we examine
specific examples in detail. Additionally, we examine the computational complexity of our
algorithms and discuss possible enhancements to our technique. Lastly, we discuss other
possible applications of our repair framework and explore connections with related areas
like data exchange and satisfiability problems. By addressing the challenge of handling
inconsistencies in tables, we also identify key open research questions. Our approach
can also be used to handle repairs in the absence of reference cells and may incorporate
additional data quality measures. We demonstrate this by analyzing a set of criteria
common in academic evaluations. Lastly, we discuss possible extensions to our repair
framework and its connections to other areas like data exchange and satisfiability problems. 

This research is an extension of my PhD thesis [1], and I have incorporated additional
ideas and examples for clarity. In particular, I have included more detailed scenarios
and explored repair scenarios in datasets like those found in enterprise performance management
databases, also highlighting the computational complexity of my previous methods and
considering possible improvements. Moreover, I have added possible applications to my repair
framework and identified open research questions. 

[1] M. F. Goodrich. Repairing Inconsistent Tables with References. PhD thesis, University of
Maryland, College Park, 2018. Available at https://drum.lib.umd.edu/bitstream/1902.1/UX6J_Y7FZ.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our research includes both a time-varying and a traditional fixed-parameter specification for comparison. Our findings from the empirical studies suggest that the TV-PARX model offers superior forecasting accuracy than its fixed-parameter counterpart and a notable improvement in predicting default probabilities shortly after default events. Our research has been conducted using R and the relevant program code is available upon request. Our research has resultant publications presented at the 2022 European Meeting of the European Economic Association and the 2022 annual meeting of the Southern Economic Association. Lastly, our work is accompanied by an R package named "tvparx" featuring the TV-PARX model and accessible on the CRAN website. This package includes numerous functionalities such as maximum likelihood estimation, forecast generation, and posterior estimation using Bayesian methods. The "tvparx" package also encompasses various functions for visualizing and analyzing model outcomes, forest plots for default probabilities, and shifting parameter plots for a deeper understanding of time-varying coefficients. Moreover, our package enables users to conduct multiple robustness checks such as sensitivity analysis, robustness analysis, and cross-validation. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 8 categories for 3D objects
from the YCB dataset. Notably, our method naturally incorporates
SE(3)-equivariance, a crucial property for object manipulation. In experiments,
we successfully retrieve objects, imitate expert demonstrations, and adapt task
policies to novel instances and configurations. The code is available at
https://github.com/tingyf/ndf_object_manipulation. Our findings highlight the
potential of Neural Descriptor Fields as a primitive object representation for
revisiting and adapting action plans in 3D, category-level scenarios.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was probably the result of smaller low-mass Asymptotic Giant Branch stars. A radial velocity mean of -178.6 km/s and minimal velocity dispersion of 2.99 km/s was discovered for the cluster, indicative of typical globular cluster features, including an eccentric orbit. The lack of straggling stars as well as the absence of horizontal branch phases other than RHB support Tononzintla 2's aging of over ten billion years. The absence of straggling stars in Tononzintla 2's stellar stream system suggests that it may have originated from a small, bound core. The findings provided initial insights into Tononzintla 2's formation and chemical evolution as well as the cluster's place within the larger LMC context. Next steps include expanded membership studies, orbit paths, and a more in-depth analysis of the cluster's chemistry. Ultimately, a comprehensive analysis of Tononzintla 2 and similar LMC globular clusters will contribute to a deeper understanding of the chemistry and physics of second-generation stellar populations within the Large Magellanic Cloud.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs exhibits characteristics of a scale-free network, with a small group of prominent authors contributing the majority of content, and the distribution of proof lengths following a normal curve. However, further analysis is required to confirm these findings and to investigate other aspects of the archive, such as the longevity of users and the relationships between them. To facilitate future research, I plan to establish a publicly accessible database within the Isabelle system, allowing users to easily contribute and browse through the archive's contents, and to explore various measures of user and document properties. Ultimately, my goal is to conduct in-depth statistical analysis of the Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs with the aim of gaining insights into the development and use of the archive, as well as the broader theorem proving community. To accomplish this, I plan to integrate the archive with an appropriate database within the Isabelle system, and to establish a framework for defining queries and computing relevant statistical measures. As a result, I hope to facilitate future research in the same area by providing a set of tools and methods for working with the archive. Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science,  
constitute an intricate field, involving electromagnetic systems characterized by  
thin, expansive, and minutely featured particles that can also vary spatially,  
temporally, and linearly.  To tackle this intricacy, researchers need to employ a  
unified approach, integrating theoretical design and analysis methods, supported  
by an established framework.  Recent breakthroughs, facilitated by Generalized  
Sheet Transition Conditions in combination with surface susceptibilities,  
now enable designers to develop intricate metasurfaces, addressing longstanding  
challenges.  This paper delves into computational modeling of these complex  
structures through GSTC-susceptibility methodology and underscores its critical  
importance in the holistic design of metasurfaces, reviewing the evolution of  
recent frequency and time-domain computational methods.  Key considerations  
affecting accurate numerical modeling are also examined, including surface  
approximations, boundary treatments, and computational domain size, along with  
their influence on desired electromagnetic properties and behavior.  Various  
numerical methods are compared, contrased, and critiqued in this context,  
emphasizing the significance of their numerical conservation properties for  
accurate metasurface modeling.  This review is further expanded to include time-  
domain computational methods, considering recent Generalized Finite Difference  
and Nyström methods, and discusses their potential applications and challenges.  
The paper also discusses potential research directions in this area, including  
the development of robust, verified, and easy-to-use numerical methods for metasurface analysis, the exploration of novel computational methods, and the investigation of boundary conditions in metasurfaces, all of which are crucial for the continued design and development of these complex structures.  This review is intended as a starting point for a broader discussion among researchers and can contribute to the establishment of a unified computational framework for metasurface modeling, addressing both frequency and time-domain domains.  This review is part of a larger initiative aiming to provide a comprehensive overview of the field, encompassing theoretical design, analysis, and application of metasurfaces, and is available as a free online book "Metasurfaces: A Computational Electronics and Photonics Perspective". This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. To
demonstrate its effectiveness, we trained and tested the eCPNN framework on a diverse
set of 26 two-valence-electron atoms spanning the 10th to 45th rows of the periodic
table, employing a range of methods including ab initio benchmarks and observations
of correlation between predicted and actual energies. Notably, the eCPNN's level of
accuracy varies significantly depending on the atom in question – for example, it
achieves a high degree of precision (better than 0.35 eV) on the difficult carbon atom,
while also demonstrating the counterintuitive phenomenon of sometimes obtaining more
accurate results when the training process is constrained than when it is optimized for
minimum error. Additionally, we found that the eCPNN's level of accuracy is directly
correlated with the energy gap between the two main energy levels in these atoms. To
better understand the underlying causes of the eCPNN's success, we also compared its
predictions to those of another cutting-edge approach, the highly acclaimed Neural
Network Electronic Structure, and found that these two methods face challenges in a
similar set of three-electron atoms. Lastly, we used the eCPNN to design potential
functions that could potentially lead to new methods of solving the many-electron
problem, and made its code publicly available on the GitHub platform.  This approach
represents a novel, groundbreaking way of addressing one of the fundamental challenges
associated with the development of new ab initio methods for complex atomic and molecular
systems, and could serve as a valuable starting point for various related deep learning
projects.  In addition, we include a comprehensive glossary explaining key terms and
acronyms used in the text for the benefit of those not familiar with deep learning jargon.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and the STARS telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to refine the method and determine the precision of this approach. After removing data taken under poor viewing conditions and with optical malfunctions, we were left with over 4500 data sets from the Pierre Auger Observatory and 1100 data sets from the Cherenkov Telescope Array site. We calibrated the data and estimated the aerosol depth, then assessed the precision by comparing the results from different fields of view and individual exposures within a given field. We found a precision of 0.02 for the current generation of telescopes, which is in line with previous research, and also discovered that the precision varies between 0.01 and 0.04, depending on the specific telescope and viewing conditions. To reach the desired precision of 0.01 for aerosol depth measurements, we developed a modified version of the method, which includes the rejection of additional poor-quality data and employs an alternative calibration approach. As a result, we were able to achieve a precision of 0.01 with all available data. This refined method has important implications for the calibration of optical astrophysics systems, particularly in wide-field telescopes with simple, low-cost calibration systems. Such systems will be essential for future ground-based experiments aimed at detecting dark matter, which often involve wide-field optical components. In these experiments, the focus on dark matter detection may lead to the aerosol depth being overlooked as an important calibration tool. However, our research shows that with proper data analysis, the precision required for dark matter research can be achieved with a precision of 0.01 for aerosol depth measurements. Consequently, we believe that the approach presented here should become the new standard for wide-field optical astrophysics systems. In particular, it is now publicly available as a Python package called pyaerosol, which incorporates the modified method and can be applied to various types of telescopes and optical systems. This code can be used to monitor the precision of aerosol depth measurements, provide detailed calibration of the data, and even automate the calibration process itself

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/yunison/Refine-Pose-Pipeline.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and intuitive connection to real-world physics. This paper delves into the aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a thorough examination of the theory and its numerical representations. Various bond-based PD integral kernels have been presented along with their distinguishing characteristics, leading to discussions on their implications and common traits such as the representation of force as an area integral. A closer examination was conducted on the impact of non-locality on force calculation and the potential for further research into structure-based peridynamics. Finally, the limitations of bond-based PD in modeling materials with diverse microstructure are highlighted, suggesting that the exploration of more sophisticated PD models like structure-based PD is warranted. This study is intended to facilitate a deeper comprehension of bond-based PD and its underlying mechanics, ultimately aiming to contribute to the development of more advanced PD models that can effectively capture the intricate mechanisms within complex materials and systems. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. Our approach is particularly useful for analyzing citation networks, where the centrality value of a paper or a node represents its importance or betweenness. Notably, our team leveraged this method to analyze a high-impact citation network, specifically the set of highly cited papers following the Higgs discovery, and identified key factors that contribute to a paper's importance. Furthermore, our approach enables the ranking of papers, nodes, and layers based on their centrality values, and can identify the most influential authors and the most important research areas within these networks. Like standard eigenvector centrality, our approach is robust and unaffected by the presence of redundant or intermediate nodes. In our research, we also explore the concept of multi-layered centralities, including flow and closeness centrality, and our results have implications for the analysis of citation networks and other multi-layered networks. Our software, along with guidelines and examples, is freely available for download at https://github/MultiLayerEigCentrality. In our research, we use R and the ARPACK library for solving the characteristic equation. Our hybrid algorithm combines an iterative Newton-Raphson method with a score relaxation process to solve the multi-layer eigenvector centrality equation. The accuracy of our approach is validated through a set of synthetic and real-world networks, and we compare our method's performance to current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks. Our study on citation networks, specifically the set of highly cited papers following the Higgs discovery, is also presented as a key contribution. The code for this research is freely available for download at https://github/MultiLayerEigCentrality. In our analysis, we use R and the ARPACK library for solving the characteristic equation. We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking for noisy raw images by introducing a unified approach that handles these problems in two dimensions. Our proposed ADMM algorithm combines demosaicking and deblurring steps, with each being represented by anisotropic tensor operators that account for color information and the raw image mapping. Sitter spacetime.

Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software components behaving correctly to prevent harm. 

This behavior can be ensured through a trusted execution environment (TEE), which safeguards sensitive operations and protects user data. 

However, implementing secure communication channels and secure storage within TEEs proves difficult and costly for consumers, forcing manufacturers to take a hardware-centric approach that limits flexibility in software.

Our study presents a flexible, multi-domain hardware design for consumer devices, dividing hardware components into secure and nonsecure sections, with overlapping functions to maximize efficiency and minimize costly hardware expenditures.

We center our design on an example application - a secure payment system - and show that our approach allows for low-cost development of secure software, with payment transactions processed entirely within the TEE, protecting users' financial information.

Our payment transaction protocol demonstrates that our approach can prevent attacks from nonsecure software, ensuring the security and integrity of transactions, including funds transfer and balance inquiries.

Our evaluation indicates that our design yields exceptionally low overhead, with transaction processing speeds comparable to mainstream payment processors and minimal additional hardware costs.

Furthermore, our design minimally disrupts existing payment processing infrastructure, enabling seamless integration with existing payment networks, including the ability to transfer value directly to any bank account, without requiring additional hardware or software modifications.

We have collaborated with industry partners to successfully test our payment transaction protocol on actual consumer devices, with transaction processing speeds of less than one second.  Our design and protocol implementation are openly available for broad adoption and to spur further research in this area.  Ultimately, our research aims to encourage industry-wide adoption of secure payment systems, facilitating the development of other security-critical applications, and informing the broader design of multi-domain hardware systems. We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. Interestingly, we discovered that the natural policy gradient method can be robust when the corruption is bounded and is capable of finding an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal policy. We developed a Filtered Policy Gradient (FPG) algorithm, capable of tolerating unbounded reward corruption, and achieved an $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$-optimal policy. The FPG algorithm represents a pioneering solution to robust reinforcement learning in scenarios with significant adversarial interference. Moreover, we verified the effectiveness of an FPG implementation utilizing a neural network on MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks. The results showed that FPG outperforms safe convergent policies in challenging tasks and obtains performance comparable to that of an optimal policy with moderate corruption levels ($\epsilon \geq 0.2$). We also introduced the concept of robust policy mirroring, enabling an FPG agent to benefit from feedback from an optimal policy learner over time. Ultimately, we established that FPG can find an $O(\sqrt{\epsilon}/\sqrt{t})$-optimal policy after an exponential number of iterations, underscoring the methods' general applicability to robust reinforcement learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/yash-soni-19/filtered-policy-gradient.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions. Furthermore, our results show that the associated molecular and atomic orbital distributions contribute to cubanite's insulating nature and lack of spectral weight at the Fermi level, both consistent with experimental findings. In addition, our analysis indicates that the spin state of cubanite's iron ions is intermediate, in line with experimental indications, and that this state is stabilized by both on-site and adjacent atomic interactions, with significant contributions from superexchange mechanisms. Notably, our results also predict that increasing pressure will strengthen these interactions, causing the iron spin state to transition to a more stable high-spin state, which could potentially lead to an electrical conductivity switch from insulating to metallic. This predicted transition offers a promising explanation for the experimentally observed increase in conductivity with pressure in cubanite. Our study provides a theoretical framework to enhance our understanding of cubanite's electronic structure and also offers predictions amenable to experimental verification in the laboratory. In addition, its orbital-selective behavior makes cubanite a valuable comparative subject with other 3d transition metal compounds, facilitating the further development of theoretical models aiming to describe the physics governing these substances. We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface. Lastly, we discuss the potential experimental signatures of the described phenomena using STM, spectroscopy, and charge dynamics techniques.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in real-time is essential to capture the associated uncertainties. We incorporated an ensemble-based iterative method called LM-EnRML, a computationally efficient form of the Levenberg Marquardt method within our formation evaluation framework. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Several synthetic scenarios with diverse logs confirmed that this method can yield accurate parameter estimations. The comparison of computational times indicated that LM-EnRML possesses at least 10 to 125 times faster CPU times relative to conventional methods such as Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo, while the ensemble-based approach allows for concurrent processing on multiple CPUs. The successful testing of the proposed method in a simulated case mimicking real field data demonstrated precise formation evaluations, demonstrating that LM-EnRML is an efficient and reliable method to calculate petrophysical formation properties, layer boundaries, and related uncertainties making it suitable for real-time geosteering. Moreover, this method can handle dense ensembles, thereby enabling the storage of multiple earlier formation evaluations, which is crucial for geosteering applications. Ultimately, we successfully demonstrated the capability of LM-EnRML to handle complex well logs, including boundary crossings and thick layers, and it has the potential to be an extremely fast method, potentially suitable for on-board drilling platforms with limited computational capabilities. Nevertheless, we believe that this method has greater potential to be run on more sophisticated computing systems, enabling the simultaneous analysis of large ensembles, thereby fully leveraging its ensemble-based form. This could allow the storage of multiple earlier formation evaluations, enabling geosteering to benefit from this level of detail. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Moreover, to address the lack of corpus-level information in NER, this study introduces features based on corpus statistics, including Point-wise Mutual Information, to enhance model performance and adaptability from sentence-level to corpus-level. Our experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks and showcase significant improvement in domain adaptation through the proposed holistic modeling. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/Consecutive-Parser. Meanwhile, the adapted NER models and data are hosted on https://github.com/ghrua/Zero-Shot-NER for zero-shot classification tasks. The adapted models have achieved over 89% EMA metric on RCV1/TEST after being trained from scratch without additional fine-tuning. Notably, our domain adaptation technique has a crucial implication for applying NER to new domains with limited annotations, thanks to the adaptability of pre-trained models. However, labeling entities in large-scale corpora remains a significant bottleneck for this approach. Another potential solution, NER for low-resource languages, also benefits from our work, as demonstrated by our experiments on Arabic NER. Despite achieving a high accuracy of over 90% on standard Arabic NER dataset Zht10, our method still relies on extensive human annotation and manual labeling to train and adapt NER models. Therefore, developing automatic or efficient data collection methods for NER is a pressing research direction. One such direction is extracting entities from text based on their definitions, which is explored in our work on zero-shot NER. This study involves adapting NER models to classify definitions as either entity-defining text or not, which is achievable with just a few annotations. By doing so, we were able to successfully test our domain adaptation technique, which is typically more challenging than zero-shot classification. Consequently, our work on zero-shot NER offers a unique opportunity to evaluate and improve domain adaptation for NER. We extend the use of tropical methods to counting in arithmetic problems, such as enumerating objects in higher-dimensional spaces using values from specific algebraic structures, over fields that have been modified to have special values, such as plane quartics with specific tangent properties as a reference. We look at curves defined by equations that are smooth, or at least have smooth properties in certain situations, over such modified fields. We express obstacles to counting these curves and their associated tangencies by altering the structure of these curves and their starting properties, focusing on edges and how they are affected. We show that by understanding how these curves and their starting properties change when modified, we can calculate the relative importance of these curves when counting them using these specific algebraic structures, or "GW-multiplicity". This allows us to verify a previously proposed mathematical relationship involving these curves and their counts. This verification relies on a deeper understanding of how the algebraic structures of these fields are related, especially when these fields are modified to have special values, or "residue fields". We also explore connections between these curves and their starting properties, and geometric objects with the same properties, but defined over different fields, or "minimal models". We use these relationships, and a deeper understanding of how these curves and their starting properties change when modified, to calculate their relative importance when counting them using these specific algebraic structures, or "algebraic multiplicity". This allows us to relate these relative importances to the geometric objects with the same properties, but defined over different fields, or "minimal models". We also show that these relative importances are equivalent to another way of counting these curves, especially when the fields are modified to have special values, or "GW-A^1". This verification relies on a deeper understanding of how these curves and their starting properties change when modified, or "differentiation of GW-multiplicity". Research into the location detection of mobile nodes within wireless sensor networks is currently ongoing. We develop and test an innovative RSSI-based location finding method suitable for 802.15.4 (ZigBee) networks. To counteract interference between different technologies operating in the same frequency range, we design and execute a new method for calculating the distance between nodes. The aim of this approach is to minimize the average error in location estimation, and when compared to ideal, interference-free results, we have achieved a level of accuracy of less than half a metre using actual hardware. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of using multiple base station nodes on location accuracy and observe significant improvements of around 70% when using four nodes instead of one. Ultimately, with our proposed method and a network of four nodes, we are able to locate mobile nodes to an accuracy of less than 0.5 metres. This suggests that reliable location detection of mobile nodes can be achieved over short to medium distances within domestic and industrial environments using ZigBee technology. However, larger scale location detection may require more sophisticated methods. The code developed for this research is freely available online. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. Although English-Hindi code-mixing materials are scarce, we leverage existing datasets to develop two simple models. One of these models demonstrates improved performance when applied to two tasks: identifying hate speech and determining the sentiment of movie reviews. Our findings suggest combining monolingual word embeddings from both languages can yield better results in sentiment analysis than employing only the Hindi monolingual embedding. Similarly, using a monolingual English model and transferring knowledge to the Hindi code-mixed domain yields better performance than utilizing a multilingual Hindi model. All code and data employed in this research are made publicly accessible. As a result, this study represents a preliminary exploration into English-Hindi code-mixing with potential applications to other language combinations. Nevertheless, significant advancements are necessary before it can be utilized in the mentioned critical scenarios. Ultimately, we hope this research sparks interest in NLP developments for multilingual communities and encourages more comprehensive, annotated datasets that can facilitate greater progress. Additionally, we propose potential lines of inquiry for researchers to explore in this field. These potential lines of inquiry involve developing more effective models for addressing societal challenges in multilingual communities and creating larger, more thoroughly annotated datasets for these tasks. Moreover, establishing specialized datasets, along with specialized datasets, models, and resources with clear ethical implications, can facilitate NLP applications that promote greater societal good. As an example, we outline a potential dataset for addressing English-Hindi code-mixing in healthcare but with implications for other language combinations. This potential dataset could include annotated text related to medical crises, healthcare information dissemination, and health-related fake news, along with associated models and constraints. Consequently, this research offers a foundation for further exploration into NLP developments for multilingual communities and potential applications in healthcare and other critical areas. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, we might utilize datasets labeled by non-expert visually impaired users for coarse-grained assessment, which could provide insight into whether a system is generating safe or factually accurate descriptions. Furthermore, we propose utilizing datasets labeled by experts for fine-grained assessment, which involves evaluating generated captions on a visual impairment proxy, such as risk-level classification. To demonstrate this concept, I present results using the recent large language models, Barzel et al.'s risk classification metric on the COCO dataset, and a smaller-scale qualitative study among visually impaired individuals. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's performance at the particle level, researchers typically model Ta$_2$O$_5$ using the Bethe-Salpeter equation within many-body theory. However, this approach is computationally intensive and usually relies on the linear response formulation of time-dependent density functional theory. To make Ta$_2$O$_5$ calculations more feasible for large systems, we develop a tight-binding model that accounts for local correlations and can be applied to bulk, Ta$_2$O$_4$, and Ta$_2$O$_5$ structures. This model demonstrates comparable dielectric values to ab initio results and includes the fundamental band gap of Ta$_2$O$_5$. It also highlights the significance of oxygen spinors in the valence band and indicates that Ta$_2$O$_5$ may be a suitable material for hadron therapy applications due to its ability to absorb protons and heavy ions, as well as its ability to maintain its crystalline structure after impact. To further investigate this, we simulate the interaction of protons with Ta$_2$O$_5$ using the tight-binding model and consider various factors including the incident proton energy, crystal orientation, and temperature. Our results show that protons can create damage trails up to 5-6 nm in length, and that heavier ions like gold may generate even longer damage trails, potentially affecting multiple Ta$_2$O$_5$ unit cells. These findings suggest that Ta$_2$O$_5$ may require a level of electron relaxation that is more akin to that of biological tissues in order to prevent enhanced radiotherapy effects. To validate our approach, we compare our results to existing research utilizing the Bethe-Salpeter equation and time-dependent density functional theory. Our study provides a computational framework for investigating the interaction between Ta$_2$O$_5$ and ions of varying masses and electric charges. This could lead to a better understanding of the underlying physics and may help identify other materials with similar properties suitable for hadron therapy applications. Notably, our results also highlight the potential for Ta$_2$O$_5$ to host multiple electronic states, including localized and delocalized electrons, offering a potential starting point for the theoretical investigation of other materials

Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. However, we also discovered that users in places with large cultural differences tended to seek out and share distinct, often false, news more frequently, indicating a form of "information tribalism." We explored the implications of these findings for strategies to combat the spread of misinformation. In conclusion, the large cultural divides in America are fueling the circulation of false information, and therefore any effective misinformation mitigation techniques must consider these demographic factors. We suggest adapting established interventions from the fields of health, education, and consumer behavior to tackle the root causes of misinformation dissemination. Ultimately, combating the spread of misinformation requires a multifaceted approach that takes into account the cultural nuances in each region and population. We propose that organizations working to combat misinformation also consider collaborating with entities that can provide reliable information to traditionally disadvantaged populations, promoting greater cultural inclusion in the information circulation network. We believe that, in doing so, we may reduce the efficacy of tactics like deepfakes and improve public knowledge of factual information. In the long term, this strategy could contribute to enhanced social cohesion and a more unified cultural identity in America. In the process, we also developed a theoretical framework that can be applied to study the dissemination of misinformation in other regional and global contexts. Our study provides initial insights into the factors influencing the spread of misinformation and suggests that further, more in-depth research is needed to fully comprehend this complex phenomenon. In the short term, we propose that organizations working to combat misinformation prioritize adapting established interventions from the fields of health, education, and consumer behavior to tackle the root causes of misinformation dissemination. Ultimately, our study highlights the value of considering cultural nuances in each region and population when developing strategies to mitigate the spread of false information. We introduce a groundbreaking, efficient, and user-friendly detection algorithm called HALFADO. HALFADO uses a limited number of human judgments to effectively identify anomalies in real-time, high-frequency data streams. Implementing a precise detection system is crucial for empowering human teams across the digital world by providing reliable decision support. As these systems have profound societal implications, transparency into how they operate is a fundamental human right.

Conceptually, our method builds upon a well-established machine learning technique, leveraging its established theoretical benefits, but takes a semi-supervised approach, combining the strengths of human intuition and computational capabilities. In practice, HALFADO improves upon traditional expert systems by integrating their capabilities into a single comprehensive system.

We showcase the algorithm's performance in two complex scenarios: (1) detecting derogatory language on a social media platform and (2) detecting financial fraud in real-time transaction data. HALFADO's development challenges the misconception that advanced machine learning methods are only achievable with significant computational resources and extensive human annotation. The code and dataset for both applications are openly available, providing a valuable resource for researchers and companies seeking to empower human teams across the digital world. However, we do not consider our work fully viable due to several limitations, and we welcome feedback and contributions to further improve the algorithm. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Furthermore, our results indicate that supervised learning approaches can excel in distinguishing speech content related to task elements as opposed to background conversations. These findings provide important insights into how to design more effective speech recognition systems and learning algorithms in conjunction with robotic demonstrations and natural speech input. Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the algorithm in Monte Carlo simulations and prove that it can be utilized to calculate the exact number of unique ordered trees for a given degree. Lastly, we show how the algorithm may be modified to accommodate delayed sampling for specific tree structures. This delayed sampling approach could be particularly useful in scenarios where only a small subset of the total number of unique trees is required. We validate the effectiveness of the algorithm by comparing it to alternative methods. Furthermore, we examine the underlying structure of the proposed algorithm using the algorithmic Shannon entropy as a metric. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies. A notable discussion involves differential regularization strategies, solving the integro-differential equation for Fubini-Study state complexity, and further exploring the underlying geometric properties. Moreover, our discussion is complemented by newly developed numerical algorithms for nonlinear Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential generalizations. A notable feature of our study is the explicit demonstration of both state and Fubini-Study state complexity in the context of the SU(2) Wess-Zumino-Witten model. A key implication of our analysis is that complexity theory will likely exhibit distinct behaviors at low and high energies. Notably, the latter corresponds to the thermodynamic limit, where the overall state or operator complexity is dominated by its low-lying, non-universal sector. Consequently, refining our understanding of these fundamental theories, particularly in the low-energy limit, is critical to the development of a comprehensive and theoretically sound complexity theory. A key aspect of this is studying the interplay between the non-universal sector and the universal, conformal field theory properties that drive state or operator complexity optimization. This research is an essential step towards a theoretically grounded complexity theory, with a proposed pathway involving the study of both general and specific 1+1 dimensional CFTs. A key future direction is investigating both global and local bulk properties of these theories, driven by their unique fundamental aspects, to better comprehend the underlying state or operator complexity dynamics. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals, albeit often with limited user bases due to the complexity of deployment. To simplify the process, automated tools can streamline the setup, refinement, and testing of these systems, including conversational agents. Nonetheless, creating suitable testing data for these agents poses significant challenges, including ensuring that the generated text mimics natural language usage. To address this issue, we developed a method to craft high-quality data for testing conversational agents in isolated scenarios. Our approach combines automated techniques with human input to produce relevant and coherent data, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by successfully testing an advanced commercial system. The approach we took is designed to be adaptable to different domains and scenarios, and we also explored alternative methods for generating text, including the use of style transfer techniques, although these approaches proved less effective in our tests. Nonetheless, we believe that our method offers a valuable contribution to the development of conversational agents and can facilitate the creation of more advanced testing data, leading to greater system reliability and usability. Additionally, we made our code and data available for others to examine and utilize in their own work.

Using a sophisticated mathematical model known as the Fisher information matrix, it's possible to estimate the measurement uncertainties $\sigma_M$ associated with detecting a hypothetical "Planet X" by analyzing its impact on the gravitational field of the known planets. Based on existing measurements from the Juno, Cassini, and Mars-orbiting spacecraft, a  statistical model forecasts a typical measurement uncertainty of $\sigma_M=0.22M_\oplus (d_x/400\,\textrm{AU})^3.$  Under ideal conditions, a  Planet X with mass five times that of the Earth at a distance of 400 AU can potentially be confirmed with certainty across the entire sky, whereas a  Planet X of the same size but located at 800 AU can be confirmed with the same level of certainty only over about 5% of the sky. The gravitational effect of an undiscovered Earth or Mars-mass object should be detectable for more than 90% of the sky up to 260 and 120 AU, respectively. Upcoming Mars ranging missions may provide slightly improved detection limits. The influence of measurement errors, specifically the uncertainty in gravitational potential maps, can hinder the ability to detect a small, heavy Planet X and raises the threshold for its existence from 1.25 to 1.5 times the mass of Mars at 10 AU. The limitations of the model are addressed, including the assumption that the existence of Planet X can be captured by a single monopole term. According to the model, the most promising locations to search for a Planet X include around 400 AU in the direction of Ophiuchus and between 800 and 1200 AU in the direction of Sculptor. The model also suggests conducting a search for a Planet X in the plane of the sky aligned with the orbit of the Galactic Center. The gravitational effect of an undiscovered super-symmetric dark matter object could potentially be detected in the near future, but the model indicates that it would require an improvement in ranging accuracy by several orders of magnitude. The model can be utilized to estimate how variations in the solar system's velocity vector along the line of sight towards the Galactic Center may influence the gravitational effect of dark matter and make it more detectable in the near future. The model further indicates that an improvement in ranging accuracy by several orders of magnitude will be necessary to detect the gravitational effect of an undiscovered super-symmetric dark matter object in the near future. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghrua/xl-tm.

Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies resembling low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later removed, and upon re-examination, we found no statistically significant evidence supporting the existence of low-variance circles or Hawking points. Our analysis does indicate the presence of local non-Gaussian fluctuations in the CMB, suggesting that the real sky may differ from theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we discovered a significant correlation between our findings and the locations of modern black hole mergers, as identified by gravitational wave detectors. While our discovery does not offer conclusive proof for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, it does highlight the potential for non-european ground-based gravitational wave detectors to influence the CMB. In the context of the CC model, this could provide insight into the relationship between black hole physics and the CMB. Ultimately, with more precise data from future experiments, we may be able to confirm or refute the existence of low-variance circles and Hawking points. In the process, we will gain a deeper understanding of the fundamental connections between black hole physics, the CMB, and the large-scale structure of the universe. In the short term, we propose upgrading HawkingNet to analyze upcoming CMB experiments such as the Simbol-South Pole Telescope and the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment. In the long term, we suggest integrating gravitational wave signals with CMB analysis, which will become increasingly feasible with more precise data from both fields. In this scenario, we may uncover new evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model, potentially leading to a greater comprehension of black hole physics and the fundamental characteristics of the universe. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011). Moreover, an outstanding reduction of over 50% in the number of required episodes can be achieved while maintaining similar performance.
