Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The inherent flexibility of MSDCR also permits easy integration of new domains with no requirement for additional training, making it highly practical for real-world applications. In summary, we contribute a groundbreaking multi-target CDR framework called MSDCR, a pioneering attempt in this field, with our comprehensive study offering both a novel model and substantial insights into addressing the ubiquitous data sparsity in cross-domain recommendation scenarios. The source code of MSDCR is publicly available at https://github.com/hongzheng1995/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Further, the generated formulations exhibit desirable analytical properties offering better insights for the underlying application at hand. Hypatia is now an available open-source package on GitHub. Its capabilities can be particularly beneficial for large-scale optimization applications, providing both faster solutions and more compact expressions that are easier to interpret. Moreover, the code has better memory performance, especially in cases where the original problem description occupies a substantial amount of memory. Hypatia now serves as one of the primary solvers for large-scale convex optimization within the JuMP framework. It has already been put to use to solve several large-scale optimization problems in various scientific disciplines. In one such example, it helped in finding solutions to an optimization problem with over 500,000 variables and 200 million constraints within a manageable time frame for scientists studying the Abraham-Lorentz damping model. Similarly, another large-scale optimization problem in the field of plasma physics with over 10 million variables and over 700 million constraints was solved efficiently using Hypatia. The success of these projects relies heavily on the interior-point solver's ability to handle large-scale problems by handling exotic cones and providing simple equivalent formulations for complex optimization problems. Hypatia continues to evolve with enhanced functionality, better performance, and more exotic cones. Its code has been thoroughly overhauled for better clarity and is now entirely Julia. It maintains its tight integration with JuMP, the standard modeling language for mathematical optimization in Python, via the MathProgBase interface. Additionally, Hypatia now features an interactive Python interface via the Pyparsec interface, enabling it to leverage the powerful data exploration capabilities of Pandas and the efficient numerical computation of NumPy and SciPy. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This study's findings provide valuable insights and guidelines for designing and implementing automated quality control strategies for MRI data, emphasizing the importance of considering specific challenges posed by each research project. Additionally, our results highlight the benefits of tailored quality control approaches over one-size-fits-all solutions in complex, multi-center MRI analysis projects. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings suggest that this strange attractor underlies the foundation of the Epsilon Delta problem discussed in the paper 'The Hard Problem of the Dynamics of Networks'. The developed model also provides a theoretical basis for understanding how autonomous agents, driven by local bifurcations, can give rise to a higher-level dynamic process exhibiting a strange attractor behavior characteristic of a chaotic phenomenon. In addition, this framework enables us to present a model that addresses one of the main concerns raised in the paper 'The Hard Problem of the Dynamics of Networks'. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, our results from density functional theory reproduce the A2u Raman active mode around 80-100 cm-1 and propose additional Raman active modes at approximately 175 cm-1 in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series. These findings provide a theoretical foundation for further experimental investigation of these materials. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The bilepton model forecasts that when produced, biletons and heavy quarks will decay into visible particles within seconds, providing researchers with an opportunity to study the bilepton model by analyzing decay products of heavy quarks and biletons as well as the production of heavy quarks and biletons themselves. The paper outlines how to distinguish the bilepton model from the standard model in this way. The predicted characteristics of the model can be tested with existing LHC data and the upcoming LHC runs, particularly when the energy and luminosity are increased in its final stage. The study finds that with optimized searches, the Fermi-LHC complex has a reasonable potential to find evidence for the bilepton model or confirm that it is incorrect. The paper also examines how adding a simple supersymmetry element to the bilepton model affects its predictions. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our findings give new insights into the structure of ordered generating sequences and their connection to the standard Coxeter presentation, which may lead to a deeper understanding of the fundamental properties of finite Coxeter groups. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, control over the formation of T centers in different locations within the device layer is shown, allowing for the creation of multi-layer quantum networks with distinct communication paths and varying levels of spectral diffusion. This capability enables more flexible design of quantum communication systems. A description of the fabrication process and the measurement techniques employed is included. A proposed setup for a multi-layer quantum network is presented as well as the concept of spectral diffusion-gate teleportation to improve the fidelity of quantum information transfer. Successful creation of high T center densities within the device layer has been verified through optical characterization using the method described in ref. [1]. However, the exact T center density is yet to be determined through atomic-scale imaging such as HAADF-STEM. The developed process and concepts have potential applications not limited to quantum communication systems. The ability to consistently create high T center densities in the 220nm device layer of SOI wafers makes this technology suitable for the production of reliable and efficient photon-spin interfaces in quantum devices. The ability to control the formation of T centers across different layers within the device layer provides the capability to design complex quantum systems with distinct communication paths and levels of spectral diffusion. This capability enables more flexible design of quantum communication systems. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This new approach to line list construction is an important step in the ongoing effort to develop more accurate techniques for finding exoplanets, particularly around low-mass stars. Nevertheless, further research is still needed to achieve optimal results in highly active stellar environments. 

Keywords: M dwarfs, stellar activity, least-squares deconvolution, line list construction, exoplanet detection.

For our task that considers context, a suitable object detector is needed.
Different object detectors exploit scene context for recognition in varying ways.
This study categorizes object detectors into 3 groups based on context usage:
one that doesn't use context by isolating the input, another that uses partial
context by isolating part of the feature map, and one that uses full context
without isolation.
Our evaluation method assesses the effect of context for each deep detector
category systematically. A specially designed dataset is created to test the
effect of context for deep detectors. The impact of removing the background
context and foreground objects on the MS COCO is also examined.
It is shown that both two-stage and single-stage object detectors can make use
of the context due to their extensive receptive field.
Thus, selecting the best object detector for a particular application depends
on the specific context in question. Some object detectors are better suited
for certain situations than others. For instance, RetinaNet performs better
in low-context situations, whereas FCOS performs better in high-context
situations. The effect of context is visible across all evaluated datasets
including the large one, but it also strongly depends on the dataset.
Therefore, it is not possible to determine the best object detector once
and for all. The effect of context also varies across different methods of
evaluation. It is present in both the easy and hard categories, but it is
more visible in the hard category.
Finally, to improve the effect of context, the backbone network and the
object detector itself should be optimized together, not separately.
Some object detectors like Bi-FCN, VIBE, and Bi-FEN address this issue by
jointly optimizing the backbone and the object detector network.
These methods outperform the conventional two-stage methods, but they
still have a limited number of category instances available during training.
Thus, they might not be suitable for large-scale datasets like the MS COCO
with over 20k categories.
Therefore, three strategies are proposed to use the effect of context in such
situations: using all classes as background, using foreground objects instead
of the background context, and transferring the context from related categories.
The proposed strategies are evaluated on the entire MS COCO dataset using
all three approaches mentioned above.
The code for the evaluation method and the context effect experiments can be
found here: <https://github.com/developer cisco/Eval-Context-Object-Detectors>.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. These results are accomplished via the introduction of an $R$-analytic regime, derived from overconvergent $R$-analytic tilting, allowing us to induce comparisons from locally analytic to crystalline cohomologies. The case where $X$ is affine and smooth is established through a strategy involving the use of Fontaine-Liu's formal patching technique. The general case is then proved through a method employing inductive descent. Finally, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying these comparisons to achieve results on motivic Serre duality and the motivic Tate conjecture for smooth projective varieties over $R$. The latter is established in collaboration with Christian Jensen and Pierre Laudemont. Moreover, we derive from these comparisons a general approach to proving the weak motivic monodromy conjecture for smooth projective varieties over $R$. This part of the research is accomplished in partnership with Shun-Wen Zhang. Lastly, we include an initial exploration of Fontaine-Messing theory extended to base rings of the form $S$, consisting of power series over the Witt vectors of a perfect field of characteristic greater than two. Notably, we establish the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes over $S$. This comparison is shown to follow from an induced comparison from locally analytic to crystalline cohomologies, with the underlying reason being the perfectness of the base field $k$. Consequently, this enables us to prove the weak motivic monodromy conjecture for smooth projective varieties over $S$. This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we demonstrate that this asymmetry is highly sensitive to the dihadron fragmentation function's "diagonal" part, which cannot be studied in exclusive reactions like dihadron electroproduction. Consequently, studying the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS represents a vital complementary approach to investigating the dihadron fragmentation function in a more comprehensive manner.

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. This research also explored the arrangement of these conjugacy classes within the group's structure and identified various subsets, including those centered around the identity element and the group's central congregation. A comprehensive arrangement of conjugacy classes and their resultant hierarchies has been detailed in the research. This work ultimately showcases the sophisticated framework governing the structure of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group. This translation is now made available as the 24th work in our series of historical document translations.

A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we outline the potential for applying realistic models, which could be useful in guiding clinical decision-making, and ultimately helping more patients receive life-saving kidney transplants. We also examine the potential for applying MDP models to other organ transplants, such as liver and heart transplants, although the issues surrounding these transplants differ significantly from those in kidney transplants. Lastly, we discuss the challenges associated with estimating the parameters required for these models, using data from actual transplant situations, which is also referred to as the identification problem. Several techniques that could be employed to address this problem are also discussed. Ultimately, we believe that a multidisciplinary approach, involving experts from both medicine and mathematics, is the key to successfully addressing these complex issues. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this, we propose a simple yet effective method to extract a subset of the most semantically meaningful word2vec components. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms baseline methods across multiple tasks, encompassing both company name disambiguation and sentiment analysis on financial news headlines. Our analysis and methods are universally applicable to all embedding-based NLP projects. We make our code and dataset available for replication purposes.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDET systems as alternatives to our previously proposed optimal wideband waveforming strategy in [1].
Fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimisation problems are defined and formulated.
By leveraging an algorithm that utilizes fixed points, we derive the optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput values for SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM systems. 
Numerical examples demonstrate the efficacy of these strategies. 
Additionally, we find that SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM outperform our previously proposed wideband waveforming strategies. 
Generally, MISO-OFDM yields greater performance than SISO-OFDM. 
Yet, when the number of transmit antennas is sufficiently high, the difference in performance between SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM becomes negligible. 
This implies that for such cases, SISO-OFDM's simplified design may be preferred. 
A summary of our main conclusions is provided. 
This research is an early step towards addressing waveforming challenges in wideband IDET systems. 
Further investigation is needed to explore additional techniques and scenarios.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Notably, this approach allows for robust treatment of moving and re-entering boundaries, proving particularly valuable for studying ice sheet dynamics. To further improve solution accuracy, we've implemented a second-order time-stepping method with a precursor phase. Furthermore, we've established a fully heterogeneous multi-scale framework to enhance the efficiency of large-scale simulations. This involves utilizing a highly resolved interface model for local domain refinement and has been demonstrated in an ice sheet application. Despite this, all models can be run using the same efficient solver, with no need for adaptive time-stepping or unstable oscillations. This, along with other benefits, facilitates seamless use of this method in our new code, IceBA. Developed using the CLAWPACK toolkit and built on top of the FlexFlow framework, IceBA showcases the powerful capabilities of this numerical strategy and outperforms industry standards in terms of efficiency. Additionally, we present preliminary results for melting boundary cases, including both stationary and moving boundaries, and provide insights into the potential of IceBA to tackle the complex problems surrounding ice sheet dynamics. Ongoing developments include integrating this method into the larger community through the FEMBA package for finite-element methods. This approach has been successfully applied to model the Larsen B ice shelf collapse and is currently being used to study Antarctic ice velocities and Greenland outlet glaciers. Along with other applications, IceBA is now part of the larger-scale research initiative led by the CMIP6 Ice Sheet Model Intercomparison Project. Current versions of the Lambek Calculus used in computational linguistics are expanded upon using unary modalities to govern structural rules affecting sentence order and phrasing. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To enable the compositional interpretation of the extended calculus, a compact category has been proposed; however, these proposals neglect the modalities' control aspect, limiting them to purely syntactic roles. To remedy this, our approach elevates modalities to first-class entities within the vectorial interpretation, drawing from the directional density matrix semantics. By introducing an extra spin density matrix space to the type system's interpretation, our method results in the expression of multiple co-existing interpretations for ambiguous sentences through their tensoring with orthogonal spin states. Moreover, our results demonstrate that learning a rationalizable action profile can be achieved with significantly improved sample efficiency when compared to equilibria learning, with significantly reduced dependence on action sampling. This is particularly relevant in large-scale multiagent systems where rationalizable behavior is more relevant and actionable. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we have developed an open-source framework that utilizes Python and PyTHIA tools to automate the conversion of leading-order parton-level calculations to usable PDF candidates, enabling the inclusion of such processes in PDF fitting programs like NHXPDF. As an illustration of this framework's capabilities, we show examples of evolving PDF candidates with DGLAP equations using different kernels and discuss plans to expand its features to accommodate next-to-leading-order processes. Since this framework is fully open-source and publicly available on the GitHub platform, we invite the community to contribute to and utilize it in various phenomenological studies and PDF fitting initiatives. As an aside, we have discovered anomalies in the x-dependence of scaled distributions for dijet production in deep-infrared limit processes. As a result, we have identified potential soft factors that could be associated with the splitting of partons within the DGLAP framework. However, further NLA calculations are necessary to confirm this finding. As an additional aspect of this project, we have developed an experimental approach to constrain the gluon distribution function in the medium-x region through the measurement of dijet transitions in deep-infrared limit processes. To facilitate the understanding and replication of our methods, we have provided comprehensive code reviews and detailed explanations within the code comments. As an open-source community, we welcome feedback, suggestions, and potential collaborations with research groups working on PDF-related initiatives. To get involved, please feel free to reach out to us directly or contribute to the code repository on GitHub. As the field of PDF research continues to evolve, we are committed to upholding the principles of openness, collaboration, and transparency within this project and beyond. In the future, we plan to expand the code's capabilities to address outstanding challenges in PDF fitting and related phenomenological studies, as well as explore new perspectives on DGLAP evolution equations and PDF-related factors such as conformal PDFs

However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their differing levels of relevance. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Moreover, the proposed method's variance-reducing variant outperforms existing replay methods beyond the target distribution's equilibrium. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation in a certain thickness range. These results demonstrate the presence of a universal spin-lattice relaxation mechanism in LaNiO$_3$ that is independent of the LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness and is observable in thinner films, contradicting earlier claims that LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness must exceed 4 unit cells to support a finite mean-field-like relaxation component. Instead, our findings indicate that the mean-field-like relaxation component is an intrinsic property of LaNiO$_3$. Furthermore, we have investigated the electronic structure of LaNiO$_3$ using density functional theory and found that the mean-field-like relaxation component is associated with electrons located at the base of the conduction band, with an orbital composition dominated by $t_{2g}$ Ni states in thinner films and a more equal composition of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ Ni states in thicker films. Our results provide clear insights into the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ and offer a framework for comparing it to other transition metal oxides. Additionally, they underscore the value of NMR in conjunction with theory for understanding the intricate electronic structures of these materials. Lastly, our work highlights the capacity of LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices to serve as a reliable testing ground for fundamental concepts in condensed matter physics. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. Furthermore, the positive energy condition is ensured by the nonlocal gravity theory in the context of weak fields. The proposed approach also leads to the conclusion that cosmic strings cannot exist in this framework. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. The framework also decreases the difficulty of designing new CRDTs significantly. The RWF project is openly available for public use on GitHub at https://github.com/AlibabaCloud/flight-berlin.

Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. For example, from being the 20,000th most influential to the 5th most influential, for a specific variant associated with Crohn's disease, by considering the effect of variants on local chromatin structure. Additionally, by examining the gene regulatory potential of variants, we have gained insights into the molecular basis of several traits and have identified key target genes such as IRF5 in rheumatoid arthritis, MAST4 in fat mass and IL12B in Crohn's disease. By applying this approach to available GWAS data and the upcoming phase III exome data, we plan to further analyze the genetic basis of various human traits and diseases. We have made our approach and results publicly available at http://www.broadinstitute.org/dnase/associated_sites with full details included in the supplementary materials. We have also presented our method for ranking associations in GWAS by considering the effect of variants on local chromatin structure as an R package available at http://bioinformatics.org/user/subini/. We believe that this approach will not only provide new insights into the molecular basis of various human traits and diseases but also raise the confidence level of associated SNPs in a significant number of cases. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Therefore, the existence of a large population of stellar mass black holes in the galaxy's center is unlikely. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest correlation with human judgments to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 9% improvement in NLI diversity. When evaluated in actual conversations, this method was found to increase user satisfaction by 7%. The code and data utilized in this research are openly accessible at this link.

Automated driving systems depend on predictive modules to assess risks and avoid accidents, however, their current implementation is hindered by expensive and complex technologies. A novel artificial intelligence approach has been developed for classifying high-risk maneuvers from a single camera, using pre-trained image processing algorithms to improve performance and efficiency. This advanced system utilizes deep learning and temporal sequence analysis to recognize patterns of behavior from a dataset with annotated risk indicators, and was optimized using various feature extractors for maximum effectiveness, ultimately achieving a 0.937 AUC score. Testing the system on an private dataset showed comparable performance, with a 0.917 AUC score, indicating its potential to contribute to proactive automated driving systems. In addition, an exploration of relevant ethical considerations highlighted potential risks and concerns associated with predictive technology, emphasizing the need for clear communication between humans and machines to avoid misunderstandings, as well as the importance of transparent data collection and processing practices. Furthermore, possible pathways to further improve the system were identified, including the exploration of multi-sensor setups and more advanced algorithms, as well as the integration of additional safety protocols. In conclusion, this study demonstrates the capability of deep learning to recognize and predict risky behavior from a single camera, and paves the way for its potential use in future automated driving systems. Additionally, it emphasizes the importance of clear communication, transparency in data collection and processing, and the need for rigorous testing and validation to ensure trustworthiness and safety in such systems. As such, it offers a valuable contribution to the development of predictive automated driving systems, and serves as a foundation for further exploration into this exciting and rapidly evolving field. Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. This study investigates whether the same level of computationally efficient determination exists for the specific case of bipartite graphs when no nodes need to be split, i.e., when edge-free representations exist without node fragmentation. Contrary to expectations, it was found that this question does not have a reliable, verifiable solution that can be calculated in a finite amount of time for all instances of this case. In response to this discovery, new problems are being defined with similar objectives in mind, especially one focused on minimizing node splits compared to a proposed metric. A particularly relevant problem is identifying the minimum number of node splits necessary to convert a bipartite graph into an edge-free representation. Although this question seems straightforward, different approaches still yield dissimilar estimates for certain instances, highlighting the need for further research to obtain a definitive answer even in relatively uncomplicated cases, such as small, free-floating subgraphs. A notable characteristic of the proposed approach to determining whether an edge-free representation exists without node fragmentation is its excessive computational efficiency compared to existing methods. This study also introduces an alternative solution strategy for the previously mentioned problem of determining the minimum number of node splits required to convert a bipartite graph into an edge-free representation, but it is purely theoretical and would take an impractically long time to actually compute it in real-life scenarios. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. The code for the experiments is openly accessible on the GitHub platform. Additionally, the dataset generators implemented during this research are now available under the Open Source license. Consequently, this work provides a foundational framework that lays the groundwork for further investigations into the complexities of real-world visual learning environments. It also raises crucial questions regarding the efficient incorporation of past experiences and the management of example memories in the presence of ever-growing datasets. Ultimately, this research underlines the potential benefits of score calibration in counteracting the challenges of imbalanced incremental learning. It is reasonable to hypothesize that its applications will extend beyond visual classification tasks, making it a relevant topic for ongoing research in the field of machine learning. In the future, we intend to explore additional aspects of this topic, especially the complex scenario in which the learning process is affected not only by a growing dataset but also by the continuous evolution of the class distribution and the presence of noisy examples. A precise LHCb method for determining the CKM angle gamma from decays at the tree level is explained. LHCb can generate up to 16 separate measurements, using different decay modes of various beauty and charm mesons, but they do not have the same level of sensitivity to gamma. By combining all available results, a highly accurate value can be obtained. These proceedings provide a detailed overview of several independent determinations used for this combined result and report the most recent outcome available as of Summer 2018. Additionally, a new determination based on data from 2015 to 2018 is presented for the first time in these proceedings. With an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse femtobarns, this result significantly improves the precision of gamma and strengthens the case for further precision measurements at the LHC in the future. As of Summer 2018, the combined value for gamma is determined to be 17.6 degrees +/- 1.8 degrees, where the total uncertainty includes both statistical and systematic components. This result is expected to benefit from enhanced data sets and more sophisticated analyses in the coming years.

Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices. However, our analysis also reveals that, under certain conditions, the parallel strategy can result in decreased performance. This phenomenon is attributed to increased memory usage and contention in parallel implementations, leading to suboptimal performance in certain scenarios. To verify these findings, a comprehensive experiment was conducted, involving matrices of varying sizes up to 1024x1024 in both theoretical and practical applications. Furthermore, our investigation explored how matrix data distribution among processing elements (PEs) influences performance. Our study demonstrates that, although parallel processing initially outperforms sequential computation in terms of speed, with smaller matrices (256x256 and below) exhibiting comparable or slightly inferior performance, significant performance gains are achieved with larger matrices (512x512 and above), with speeds exceeding sequential computation by 2-3 times. Nonetheless, with extremely large matrices (1024x1024), memory constraints prevent further acceleration. This research provides matrix-based problem designers with insights to optimize matrix multiplication performance in computational applications. It is now possible for practitioners to design matrix-based problems that take into account the complexities of matrix multiplication, ultimately leading to more effective and efficient solutions. This study is the first of its kind, addressing a long-standing issue and featuring an innovative comparison of sequential and parallel matrix multiplication approaches. It is an original contribution that is both comprehensive and far-reaching, with relevance across multiple disciplines and areas of science and engineering. It is our hope that this comparison will inspire further research, new applications, and more innovative solutions to matrix-based problems. It is also our intention that future works will build upon these comparisons, taking the discussion to the next level. Ultimately, we believe that this comparison represents a significant milestone in the ongoing quest to solve matrix-based problems. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Notably, our results show that our method not only achieves comparable accuracy under certain conditions but also outperforms RFF in several scenarios, especially when data points are sparse. Furthermore, this method enables efficient large-scale learning by reducing storage requirements from linear to quadratic, thereby enabling kernel-based learning on devices with limited memory on machines with limited memory capacity. Our results also demonstrate that this method facilitates efficient active learning by simplifying the computation of remaining data importance, allowing for a 5 times performance improvement in relevance determination. Lastly, we successfully apply this method to deep kernel methods on large datasets, obtaining better performance while cutting training time in half. All of our code is openly accessible online. Optimally timing pulmonary valve replacement surgery in Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) patients primarily relies on heart volume and function as per existing medical guidelines. The best indicators for these factors are found through 3D image analysis of the heart obtained from magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging. Recent research involving a type of neural network called U-Net has yielded impressive outcomes when tested against certain heart imaging data sets, although real-world medical imaging presents unique challenges due to variations in image quality stemming from the specific medical imaging technology used and individual differences in heart conditions. Furthermore, there is a shortage of high-quality, specially tailored data sets for training models on rare conditions such as TOF.

For this research, we first evaluated how accurate models become when they generalize beyond the data they were trained on. Then, we fine-tuned one of these models using a relatively small data set of CMR images from TOF patients. The model was tested against the task of predicting volume and function indicators from the sacuboidal center of the heart, as well as against the more complex task of predicting volume and function indicators in its entirety. The models' performance was compared to that of healthcare professionals who manually calculated the indicators through 3D image analysis. We also assessed how well the models performed under different scenarios that mimic the decision-making process of surgeons. Finally, we analyzed how reliable the models are when they are applied to individual cases and how the models' performance could be improved with more and better-quality training data. 

The research revealed that, although the models perform reasonably well when tested against the data they were trained on, their performance significantly declines when they are applied to new cases. Furthermore, when they are applied to the complex task of predicting volume and function indicators in the heart as a whole, their accuracy is lower than that of healthcare professionals who manually calculated the indicators through 3D image analysis. However, when the models are fine-tuned with a relatively small data set of CMR images from TOF patients, their performance improves substantially. The models' performance was also found to be reliable in certain scenarios that mimic the decision-making process of surgeons. However, the models' reliability declines when they are applied to individual cases. Lastly, the research found that the models' performance improves with more and better-quality training data, especially when the complex task of predicting volume and function indicators in the heart as a whole is considered. 

In conclusion, deep learning models such as U-Net can be an effective tool for analyzing CMR images from TOF patients

Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within the context of detection systems and sheds light on its success through an optimization lens. It identifies that incorporating FPN results in distorted backpropagation pathways, limiting each backbone network level to focus on specific scale ranges. Consequently, two practical approaches are presented to empower each backbone level to consider all objects within the detection framework. Firstly, introducing auxiliary objectives facilitates direct propagation signals during training. Secondly, constructing the feature pyramid more reasonably can circumvent irrational backpropagation paths. Comprehensive experiments validate the analysis and demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods on the COCO benchmark, resulting in substantial improvements of over 2% across one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors. Moreover, the models pretrained with these methods achieve competitive performance on the PASCAL-12 benchmark with only fine-tuning. The model code has been made available at https://github.com/CYH8888/FPN-for-Object-Detection.

Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. These models still lag behind humans, but they exhibit a marked enhancement in understanding and sequencing unordered multimodal instructions. In particular, they exhibit improved capabilities when handling difficult procedures, instructions that include exceptions to the normal order of events, and visual aids that provide valuable but secondary information. In conclusion, our research provides an evaluation of machine learning models' ability to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions, which is an essential skill required for complex tasks and tasks that involve communicating with humans. Additionally, we have made the datasets and code for this research available to the community in an effort to spur further advancement in this area. The datasets we created can also be of use in any other task that involves sequential understanding from a visual and textual combined perspective. The code we developed, which incorporates a variety of sequential-aware pretraining techniques, can also be of use in any other task that involves understanding text that is separated and not in linear order. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. Notably, even with an increasingly large chain size, the average reduction in peak precision remains consistently near one percent. Furthermore, this robustness comes at minimal expense of execution time and state fidelity. In fact, our experiment on three ions demonstrates that this frequency robustness feature incorporates a minor increase in duration, however, numerical simulations on larger chains indicate this duration increment to be negligible. In total, this self-balancing design appears poised to play a crucial role in the development of reliable quantum gates for extensive trapped ion systems.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used CFW and AFLW2000-3D datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Our code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghoul007/SADRNet.

This regime facilitates the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs). Our calculations were carried out within a spatially flat gauge with a non-zero fluctuation in the inflaton field and its impact on the background gravitational field. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues, but it may also result from a lack of consideration given to the economic incentives underlying storage unit operation. In order to investigate this further, we developed an agent-based model in which risk-averse and risk-neutral storage units respond to varying price environments. Our analysis of this model revealed that risk-averse storage units tend to follow a risk-minimizing strategy, sticking with established operating practices and thus failing to fully participate in periods of extreme prices. Conversely, risk-neutral units are more likely to engage in arbitrage opportunities, despite sometimes incurring losses. It is essential to account for the economic incentives of storage units in grid management strategies, rather than solely focusing on their technical capabilities. Our results also suggest that utility-based pricing mechanisms and capacity remuneration mechanisms may encourage storage units to participate in grid services, but their effectiveness is curbed when there is significant price volatility. Full-scale simulations of these storage units within a mock grid, along with real-world price data, are also presented in order to validate our findings. In conclusion, the failure of storage units to fully engage with high-price signals during periods of low energy supply appears to be an inescapable aspect of their operation, and therefore this issue should be addressed by reforming pricing mechanisms in future low-carbon grid designs. Full-scale simulations of these storage units within a mock grid, along with real-world price data, are also provided in order to validate our findings. Consequently, this study's findings should be considered in grid management strategies, and pricing mechanisms like utility-based pricing and capacity remuneration mechanisms should be employed to encourage full-scale participation of storage units. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Despite numerous theories, there has not been a clear understanding of the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors, particularly in their mixed-state Hall resistivity. This study involved an in-depth examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, to confirm a previously suggested theory proposing that the Hall anomaly arises from vacancies moving within pinned fragments of the vortex lattice. This proposed mechanism is validated by analyzing the vortex states near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in the vortex crystal and by comparing the measured activation energies to the calculated creation energy of the vortex-anti-vortex pair and the vacancy energy in the flux-line lattice. No adjustments were required in the calculations, providing a comprehensive theoretical foundation and prerequisites for the vacancy model. Furthermore, our analysis highlights that vacancy activation energies are significantly lower than those of isolated vortex lines, offering a framework that may also inform other research on activated transport processes in type-II superconductors. This study's findings are relevant to the ongoing debate on the vortex core order parameter and its relationship with vacancy creation in these materials. By developing this concept, this work lays the groundwork for a more in-depth examination of the vortex state, particularly by considering the effects of vacancy populations through variations in the flux-line lattice periodicity and by exploring the implications of the vacancy model for the understanding of the mixed-state transport phenomena in type-II superconductors. This study's findings also raise intriguing questions regarding the root cause of the AT transition in the vortex state and its possible connection to the vacancy creation in flux-line lattices, which merit further investigation through numerical simulations of the Ginzburg-Landau model, incorporating the effects of vacancy populations by considering the lattice periodicity. Ultimately, this study's findings provide a theoretical foundation for a new perspective on the vortex state, one that views the vortex lattice as a collective phenomenon arising from the interaction of vacancies within this lattice, rather than isolated vortex lines. This new understanding of the vortex state may lead to the identification of additional collective phenomena that have yet to be discovered. This study's findings also raise the possibility that the Hall anomaly observed in type-II superconductors is an intrinsic property of these materials, resulting from the motion of vacancies within the vortex lattice rather than pinned vacancies, as also confirmed through an additional examination of the magnetotransport measurements conducted on BSCCO thin films, as presented in Zhao et al.'s 2019 paper, with no adjustments required in the calculations. A characterization of strongly faithful, unitary, natural isomorphisms for such subfactors is derived, leading to an extension of Borcherd's monodromy theorem. Additionally, monoidal categories constructed from subfactors or C*-algebras possess an intrinsic symmetries property. A characterization of strongly faithful, unitary natural isomorphisms for such categories leads to an application in recovering the underlying subfactor or C*-algebras, with this recovery being highly non-unique. A connection to the classification of strongly faithful unitary natural isomorphisms arises from the strong convergence of matrix coefficients of representations of such isomorphisms, resulting in an irreducible representation of the fundamental group of the category's representation space. A similar analysis applies to strongly faithful unitary natural isomorphisms for commutative subfactors or C*-algebras, with an additional rotation symmetry. A further investigation into this symmetry leads to the discovery of new examples of large unitary fusion categories in positive characteristic. A final investigation extends the underlying principles to the context of braided or spherical categories. A related paper expands upon these findings with more extensive examples. A final section discusses potential directions for future research. A appendix is included for closure conditions and their application to strongly faithful unitary natural isomorphisms. In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. The code for this project can be found at the provided link. As traditional neural network training relies on ordinary differential equations, it is surprising that this basic approach has not been proposed as a meta-learning framework before. We believe this concept holds even broader potential and would appreciate feedback and suggestions for further exploration.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the reliable model performed better than both a standard baseline model and a model with extensive cleaning efforts but significantly less time and effort. The code for the proposed system is now available on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can acquire the code and the data used in the experiments by visiting the following link: https://github.com/awashik/safety-augmentation. The paper this code is based on has been accepted into the proceedings of Association for the Advancing of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI), 2022.

In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Additionally, we establish the relationship between $J_n^T$ and the colored Melvin-Kashaoui invariant, and explore its properties. Lastly, we propose that $J_n^T$ extends the property of volume conjecture to biperiodic links. To achieve this, we introduce a new construction of $J_n^T$, based on the Melvin-Kashaoui invariant, and demonstrate its connection to the colored Kauffman polynomial. This implies that $J_n^T$ is capable of detecting the volume conjecture for biperiodic links. To do so, we need to verify that $J_n^T$ is strong, i.e., it is able to distinguish between links. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Moreover, an evaluation of different knowledge augmentation approaches reveals that the direct utilization of definitions with a certain sense score proves to be the most effective method.  The proposed approach is found to achieve superior performance compared to both a baseline BERT-based WSD model and currently leading open-source WSD solutions.  The code for this research has been made publicly accessible on GitHub https://github.com/ghrua/WASDAW, alongside the data and protocols utilized at https://github.com/ghrua/WASDAW-data-protocols.
