This study formulates a genuine integral expression of the reciprocal gamma function in terms of a modified hypersingular integral. It also proves the connection to the traditional complex representation, in addition to obtaining a modified complex representation following the standard Hankel path. A key finding establishes the relation between the reciprocal gamma function and a modified Hankel type integral. Previous attempts at deriving this link have been reviewed. The formulated expressions can be useful in developing integral operators that accurately treat singular behavior in the kernel. As an example, this is demonstrated with an operator that has been employed in a derivative integral equation related to the Mie scattering problem. The new formulation makes the operator more accurate and easier to apply than earlier implementations. The developed method is particularly efficient when employing the Nystrom discretization technique for the integral equations. The proposed implementation is robust and verifiable, as it is based on the highly reliable special function library of C. M. Schneider. This method has been successfully applied to obtain highly precise solutions to a critical equation in the Mie scattering problem, overcoming an earlier limitation of $J_{n/2}\left(z\right)\approx 0$. The new findings can also benefit other applications dealing with similar derivative integral equations. One such example is the scattering problem in stellar systems, particularly for stellar systems consisting of stellar clusters. As computational power continues to increase, solving more complex problems involving higher modes of the scalar function will become feasible. To achieve this, further improvements to the method will be necessary to handle the growing singularity strength. To this end, potential extensions to the formulation that could address this requirement have been identified and discussed. One possible extension involves the Gamma function itself, as well as its relation to the Riemann zeta function. Exploring these connections could lead to accelerated methods for integrating the reciprocal gamma function over the Hankel path. As a result, future developments based on this new understanding could lead to breakthroughs in solving more complex scattering problems in stellar systems. Ultimately, this could enable the computational investigation of stellar systems consisting of stellar clusters. As an added benefit, any such method would also be robust and verifiable. It is further concluded that developing integral operators that accurately handle the singular behavior of the kernel is an essential step in tackling such complex problems. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Top quark single-production cross-sections were also measured for different jet signatures, with results aligning with theoretical predictions. Top quark studies in proton-lead collisions provided insights into the interplay between nucleon size and parton distribution functions, revealing an anomalous enhancement of the antiproton parton distribution function. Furthermore, the introduction of new bounds on the density of nucleon bound-state components, such as meson-like structures within protons, facilitated a more nuanced understanding of the proton's internal structure. These findings paved the way for advanced analyses of top quark data in future deeper and more luminous proton-lead exposures at the LHC.

Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. The implemented code can be found at https://github.com/ghrua/zsparser for reference.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. This work is intended to provide a comprehensive overview of graph-based learning in the context of privacy and serve as a foundational resource for further exploration of this domain. It is hoped that this work will contribute positively to the development of more advanced, graph-based learning models that prioritize privacy protection. In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. Compared to human-generated courses, our results show that our approach can create more demanding driving scenarios in a relatively shorter time. However, there is still room for improvement in terms of testing thoroughness and replicating the precise difficulties encountered in real-world driving scenarios. Nevertheless, our findings suggest that our method can efficiently identify challenging roads, paving the way for the development of more comprehensive testing frameworks. These frameworks will be essential for accelerating the development and refinement of autonomous lane-keeping systems through simulated and real-world testing. Additionally, our work lays the groundwork for investigating other autonomous vehicle capabilities in various environments. Ultimately, we aim to establish a public repository of tested road courses to facilitate the advancement of autonomous vehicle technology. Code and data for this research are available online at the specified repository address.

To facilitate user discovery, product recommendations are often accompanied by descriptions. The rise of personalized music playlists through automatic recommendation introduces the challenge of creating descriptive metadata. This paper introduces an innovative approach called music captioning, which leverages audio content analysis and natural language processing to effectively summarize the tracks within each playlist. Our proposed model specifically addresses this challenge by extracting relevant acoustic features from audio and using a hidden Markov model to select the most descriptive text segments. This approach enables automatic playlist description generation and was evaluated through a crowdsourced survey, revealing that humans perceive the generated captions as legitimate playlist descriptions. Furthermore, our results indicate that music captioning can distinguish between different music genres based on lyrics, demonstrating potential applications in music recommendation and discovery. This pioneering work lays the groundwork for exploring various music captioning themes, such as automatic playlist creation and enhanced user experience through interactive conversation. Our code and data are openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/sharstein/music-captioning. The associated paper is publicly available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04535. Our team also created a live demo of this research, which can be viewed at https://www.spotify.com/us/en/playlist/captioning-the-music/.

Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Through this work, we hope to provide a useful tool for simulating interacting Bose gases out of equilibrium, and make this approach readily accessible to researchers who wish to utilize it to analyze their own scenarios. All necessary code for this study has been made openly available.

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of any difficulty. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized to run a series of experiments involving famous programs and fuzzers. The results show that contemporary fuzzers can detect a significant number of triggerable and detectable mutations, indicating that they are capable of discovering a range of difficult faults, including interactions between program components. Notably, this research demonstrates that combinations of mutations can greatly enhance the effectiveness of fuzzers, surpassing standalone results by up to three orders of magnitude in detecting triggerable mutations and illustrating the significant potential for further optimization. The evaluation toolkit and data have been made publicly available to facilitate future research in evaluating the capability of fuzzers.

Following the success of pretraining techniques in learning representations, various methods utilizing pre-trained models in continual learning have been developed. Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by implementing mechanisms for continual learning with minimal or no updates to the backbone models. In this study, we challenge the necessity of complex models by comparing a basic alternative we devised. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can achieve high performance in continual learning tasks, including the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To test this, we conducted a straightforward comparison: a single-headed, task-free baseline uses the frozen pre-trained model to extract image features and calculate their corresponding mean features for every encountered class. It then determines class predictions by comparing the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and mean features of each class, resulting in a Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This basic approach achieved 88.53% accuracy on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100 benchmark, outperforming state-of-the-art continual learning methods using the same pre-trained transformer model. Furthermore, our NMC outperformed existing multi-head and gradient aggregation methods on the 5-CoRe-50 benchmark, achieving 63.51% accuracy. Our results indicate that complex models, including attention mechanisms and gradual feature extractor updates, may be unnecessary for high-performance continual learning. We have made our code and data available at this link: https://github.com/ghulam-eissa/Continual-Learning-Baseline.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights: combining data from four experiments allowed researchers to identify several 0+ and 2+ excited states below 4.5 MeV, and characterize their properties. Using a Monte Carlo shell model, scientists were able to explain the findings and uncover a surprisingly intricate pattern of shapes existing together, where a high-energy prolate 0+ state at 3463 keV, and a collective 2+ state just above it, 286 keV, marked a first in Ni isotopes. The findings demonstrate that the 64Ni nucleus shares a complex structural landscape with other low-spin Ni nuclei, and that its low-energy spectrum is distinguished by a unique coexistence of multiple shapes. Furthermore, this research reveals that shell-model calculations are capable of accurately predicting the atomic structure when incorporating all possible configurations, and that the proton-neutron interaction plays a crucial role in shaping the nucleus. Additionally, by comparing 64Ni with its neighboring isotopes, scientists were able to follow the evolution of collective phenomena in the Ni chain, and how shell fillings influence proton-neutron pairing and shape coexistence. Lastly, this work sets the stage for exploring other light Ni isotopes, particularly 62 and 63, which exhibit strong low-energy collective transitions, and could provide even more insight into the complex structure of Ni nuclei. Lastly, this work sets the stage for exploring 62 and 63Ni, and offers a framework for comparing these nuclei with heavier Ni isotopes, offering a richer understanding of the Ni nuclear chart.

Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. Our analysis indicates that j-k fold CV facilitates successful parameter tuning, attaining the optimal solution in all tested configurations, as opposed to failing in over 90% of cases. Moreover, the success rate is further enhanced when the training set is divided equally (K=5), and the influence of hyperparameters is also examined, showcasing that the variance-reducing j-k fold CV method is an adaptable strategy with potential applications across the machine learning spectrum. Our code is publicly accessible according to the instructions stipulated in the ICML 2022 Style Guidelines.

Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research leveraging Teacher-Student architectures has successfully combined multiple knowledge-learning objectives with efficient, lightweight student networks. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Moreover, the paper summarizes and highlights the practical applications of Teacher-Student architectures across various purposes, such as classification, recognition, and generation, before exploring promising research directions, particularly on the design of Teacher-Student architectures, the quality of knowledge, and the theoretical studies of regression-based learning. With its in-depth analysis, this survey is poised to provide invaluable insights for industry practitioners and the academic community on the utilization of Teacher-Student architectures in multiple knowledge learning objectives.

This study supplements our earlier research on WIMP-scattered nuclei, specifically examining how the incident velocity of these particles influences the scattering probability as they interact with target nuclei across various recoil angles and narrow energy ranges. Our simulation reveals that not only do the incident velocity characteristics of halo WIMPs play a crucial role, but so does the angle of the recoil itself, resulting in an irregular correlation of the two in specific energy ranges. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. Furthermore, this investigation emphasizes that a comprehensive understanding of the incident velocity characteristics of these particles is necessary for a precise prediction of the associated scattering event rates in future direct detection experiments. Alongside this, we also propose a new approach for deriving the 1-dimensional velocity distribution of WIMP incident velocities from the overall halo velocities and the results of these simulations. This new approach is demonstrated through a hypothetical direct detection experiment with a characteristic recoil energy range of around 1 keV, and we show how the associated scattering event rates can be accurately calculated when this approach is employed. Notably, we find that the traditional method of determining the incident velocity distribution directly from the overall halo velocities results in an average WIMP incident velocity that is approximately 10% lower than expected, and this discrepancy results in an event rate at low energy recoil ranges that is 25% higher than predicted. Conversely, in the higher energy recoil range, this traditional approach results in an event rate that is 10% lower than expected. Ultimately, our research underscores the significance of considering the angle of the recoil itself, rather than treating it as a second-order effect, especially as direct detection experiments with ongoing and future sensitivity to these ranges become more refined. Moreover, this study is accompanied by publicly accessible computer code for the benefit of the scientific community.

Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. Furthermore, they should have access to diverse search engines that can increase their chances of locating all the necessary information. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This technique has potential for broad radiology applications as well.

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo methods to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo method on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Since this test is widely used across many NLP domains, we believe our exact algorithm will be a valuable resource to the community. It is already implemented in the scikit-permutation-importance Python package, which is available under the permissive BSD license. We also include additional examples illustrating how to use this exact algorithm in multiple scenarios. These examples cover applications in machine translation, natural language inference, sentiment analysis, language modeling, topic modeling, document classification, and text classification. We've concurrently released all source code and datasets used in these examples on an open-source basis for the community to use and expand upon. We hope this will help advance research in NLP system evaluation and enable more frequent experimentation with a wider range of importance tests. This is especially crucial given the numerous established methods for computing permutation-based importance. We've already successfully applied our exact algorithm to multiple research projects, leading to new insights such as the observation that the importance of test instances often follows a power-law distribution in multiple NLP systems. We've additionally identified several potential future research directions, including extending our exact algorithm to support more advanced evaluation metrics and exploring new methods for determining importance based on test performance. We're confident that our exact algorithm, along with these new methods, will contribute to a richer understanding of the limitations and strengths of NLP systems in the future. This knowledge will be critical to accelerating the development of robust NLP systems capable of handling real-world tasks and scenarios. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. The experimental findings confirm that Kedge effectively prunes edges instead of nodes, addressing a critical limitation of previous edge sparsification methods. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. Additionally, this study introduces a new feedback-receiving sketch called FreqSketch that, while performing similarly to CountSketch in a single-query scenario, exhibits even greater robustness with limited queries, thereby coming at a lower storage cost. FreqSketch represents a crucial step towards creating safe sketches for learning algorithms that can handle multiple vectors. By either expanding existing sketches like CountSketch or proposing novel ones like FreqSketch, this study's primary objective is to establish a new framework for sketches that are resistant to compromised queries, which is crucial for understanding its behavior in real-world applications. Furthermore, this framework is applied to a well-known problem - the sparse recovery problem - and a new estimator is proposed for its solution. Interestingly, this new estimator is shown to be safe from compromised queries as well as efficiently scalable with respect to its parameters. Ultimately, this study introduces a novel frequency-based sketch called FreqSketch that not only outperforms CountSketch in a limited number of queries but also exhibits comparable performance in single-query scenarios, thereby representing an important step towards creating safe sketches for learning algorithms capable of handling multiple vectors. This peak is essentially a representation of the minimum viscosity-to-entropy ratio in the vortex liquid, which in terms of units $\frac{\hbar}{k_B}$, is much greater than what is observed in common liquids. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Furthermore, our study confirms that MEF approximations are accurate and computationally feasible. Publicly accessible code for the proposed algorithm is available online.

One of the most intriguing phenomena in astrophysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This approach is particularly relevant when considering the intricate processes involved in the CE phase, particularly when multiple stars are involved, and it may also have broader applications to other complex astrophysical phenomena. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Our simulations indicate that CLIC has better sensitivity to the heavier masses in the HEFT, while ILC is more sensitive to the larger scales in the HEFT, and that the bare Higgs self-coupling can be probed up to $\lambda_{HH} \approx 0.3$ at CLIC and $\lambda_{HH} \approx 0.2$ at ILC. In the comparison with the HEFT, we find that the coefficients contributing to the longitudinal contribution to $WW \to HH$ are highly suppressed in the SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude, and demonstrate how the predictions for the cross-section in the two EFTs differ at the TeV scales, with the SMEFT cross-section primarily depending on three leading coefficients in the $WW \to HH$ subprocess. The research further explores the detectability of the two leading SMEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved and its height within the granular layer, but remained relatively consistent across different types and amounts of granular material. Notably, it was strongly influenced by the cylinder's aspect ratio, with anisotropy increasing dramatically as this ratio increased beyond 1. Our study also revealed that the drag experienced by the cylinder could be broken down into two components, one related to the friction between the granular material and the cylinder's surface and the flow of material around the cylinder, and another related to the collapse of material at the cylinder's base, with the latter playing a crucial role in anisotropy. Lastly, our findings suggest that the drag experienced by an object moving through a granular material may be highly nonuniform and dependent on the object's shape and orientation, with potential applications to the development of robots capable of navigating such environments efficiently. These robots could potentially exploit anisotropies in the drag they experience to maintain their balance and propel themselves forward. However, our study also indicates that such robots may struggle to function in situations where the object or its surroundings change significantly, as they may not be able to adapt quickly enough. In such cases, their performance may be limited by their inability to update their movement strategies quickly enough, a problem that may be difficult to mitigate through design or control algorithms. Ultimately, our study highlights the importance of considering the interactions between objects and their surroundings in the design of such robots, with potential pathways for improvement including a deeper understanding of the physics governing their interactions and the development of more flexible and adaptable systems. While our study focused on robotic movement through granular materials, our findings may also have implications for other applications involving the interaction of solids with granular beds, such as medical procedures and industrial processes. In these cases, objects may interact with granular materials in complex ways, with implications for their function and effectiveness. Our study provides a foundation for a deeper exploration of these phenomena and their consequences in these contexts. To facilitate this, we are making our data set publicly available, along with our analysis, in the hope that others may build upon our findings and contribute

Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in building probabilistic models. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, an SBO framework that enables the discovery of system structures from logs, allowing for the incorporation of expert knowledge. By combining this learned structure with expert-provided performance models and dependency information, BoAnon generates a probabilistic graph model. This model accelerates the optimization process, allowing BoAnon to identify efficient configurations significantly faster than existing methods. Through evaluation of a hardware architecture search problem, BoAnon demonstrates a notable improvement in energy-latency objectives, achieving a 5-7x factor improvement over the default architecture. The innovative approach of BoAnon, based on its contextual structure learning pipeline, now makes SBO applicable to various computer systems, such as databases and stream processors. The code for BoAnon is openly accessible on the GitHub platform. https://github.com/parrot-os/boanon.github.io.git

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. These findings demonstrate the intrinsic similarity between triangular and elliptical flow within the context of initial geometry, and suggest the utilization of $v_n/\epsilon_n$ as a quantifier for anisotropic flow responses in various centrality and collision systems. Notably, we discovered an increase in $v_3$ in low-hard centrality collisions compared to mid-central collisions, which may be attributed to initial geometry's influence or specific hard processes. Further investigation is required to distinguish between these scenarios. Our analysis also revealed an enhanced $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions compared to Cu+Cu collisions of comparable centrality, which may be induced by initial geometry or broader soft process differences. Lastly, we found $v_3(p_T)$ to exhibit increased sensitivity to hard process characteristics, particularly in lower centrality collisions. These findings are integral to informing experimental interpretations and theoretical model developments within the context of anisotropic flow.

Over the years, the availability of Linked Data has surged exponentially with more than 10,000 online datasets now available and formatted according to Linked Data standards, enabling seamless machine readability and interconnectivity.  While such datasets provide numerous opportunities, numerous applications remain hindered due to data of poor quality, significantly affecting tasks such as data integration, search, and interlinking.  Existing quality assessment techniques for Linked Data, although limited, suffer from decreased effectiveness with rising data sizes and become unmanageable for single-machine operations.  To address these challenges, our proposed DistQualityAssessment is an open-source, cluster-enabled implementation designed for comprehensive quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets, leveraging the processing capabilities of Apache Spark to distribute quality metrics computation.  This innovative, distributed in-memory approach allows for flexible metric extension via a provided quality assessment pattern and, through seamless integration with the SANSA framework, has been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies.  When compared to the widely adopted MagicLake benchmark, our proposed DistQualityAssessment exhibited reduced overall computation times of up to 2.5 times faster quality assessment of large-scale datasets.  The increased efficiency of our approach is attributed to the more efficient cluster configuration and data partitioning scheme.  The code for this research is available for replication and further development at https://github.com/hpc4mind/DistQualityAssessment and has been incorporated into the SANSA MultiDataSets (MDS) benchmark, along with other comprehensive dataset quality metadata at https://github.com/hpc4mind/SANSA-MDS-Quality.  This comprehensive quality metadata is designed to facilitate in-depth quality evaluation of large-scale RDF datasets on distributed environments through easy replication and comparison of quality metrics.  This allows researchers and practitioners to conduct thorough quality assessments of existing and newly introduced datasets, facilitating more informed comparisons and decisions in various Linked Data applications.  Future work with DistQualityAssessment is set to explore the integration of additional quality assessment metrics and research environments beyond the SANSA framework.  In conclusion, our proposed DistQualityAssessment provides a comprehensive, efficient, and highly customizable distribution of quality assessment for large-scale RDF datasets and has already been successfully applied in at least three external use cases, showcasing its superiority over existing methodologies. This study presents temperature maps for electrons within one kiloparsec of three high-brightness Seyfert galaxies. The findings from Gemini's GMOS-IFU data, acquired at a spatial resolution of 110-280 parsecs, reveal temperature variations between 8000 to >30000 Kelvin. We discovered temperature ranges in these galaxies are significantly influenced by gas outflows producing shocks, particularly in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, while photoionization processes fit the results for Mrk 607. The orientation of these shocks in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348 appears to be perpendicular to the axis of ionization, suggesting the potential for shock ionization to be observed more easily when obscured by a dusty torus. This implies that narrow ionization cones can coexist with wider shock patterns. Furthermore, we observed correlations between electron temperatures and redshifts of ionized clouds in Mrk 79 and Mrk 348, suggesting the direction of gas flows in these galaxies. These findings support the theory that gas outflows play a significant role in the evolution of galaxies by facilitating the dispersal of nutrients and potentially restarting star formation in the surrounding medium. They also highlight the importance of considering the effects of shock ionization when interpreting the spectra from active galaxies and the subsequent impact on host galaxies. This study showcases the capabilities of using integral field units on optical telescopes to analyze the complex physics occurring in active galaxies. It sets the stage for more in-depth analysis of ionized gases in active galaxies using IFU spectroscopy. This includes studying electron temperature maps in a broader spectral range, combining optical and radio data, and conducting numerical simulations to enhance understanding of the observed phenomena. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. Moreover, Frisbee includes a set of developed operators that can execute sophisticated tasks, such as verifying the contents of files and injecting exceptions into processes. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we have applied Frisbee to test an OpenSource IoT application known as Home Automation. Our results show that Frisbee can set up and execute sophisticated tests in a matter of minutes, as opposed to the several hours required by traditional manual and automated testing methods. Furthermore, we compared Frisbee to another prominent testing framework for IoT, Dillinger, and found that it outperformed it significantly in terms of performance. Our study indicates that Frisbee can accelerate the development cycle of IoT applications and reduce the operational costs associated with their deployment in distributed, Edge computing environments. The framework and its source code are publicly available at our repository on GitHub. In addition, we have released all the testbeds and the OpenSource Home Automation application that we used in our study there as well. Our research offers a novel approach to testing the complex software systems used in IoT and it has the added benefit of facilitating the development of more reliable and efficient Edge computing applications in general. Moreover, we believe that our results are relevant to other similar challenging environments such as robotics and the cloud. Lastly, we invite other researchers to collaborate with us and contribute to the ongoing improvement of Frisbee. Its latest version has already been successfully used in the development of several prominent OpenSource IoT applications including one that won the prestigious DFRobot competition in China. In conclusion, Frisbee has the potential to become the leading testing framework for the development of complex software systems in IoT and other similar domains. Its future directions for enhancement and its potential areas of collaboration with other researchers are also outlined in our paper. Finally, our study was presented at the prestigious ICSE 2020 conference but it has been significantly revised since then. Its current version includes various novel features such as a newly developed methodology

The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, our approach allows for the development of highly accurate simulation tools capable of a level of realism necessary for training self-driving vehicles. These tools are also readily customizable to accommodate various scenes and can be made publicly accessible to contribute to the advancement of the autonomous industry. On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel periodic measures that are linked to index-2 normal subgroups within its group representation. These measures outperform the previous known measures, achieving the highest likelihood among all measures found so far. Moreover, we establish the exact temperature at which these measures become accessible in both the full-connected graph and the decoupling limit. Additionally, we classify the structure of these measures, which exhibit rotational symmetry, and visualize one specific example. Furthermore, we investigate the behavior of these measures as the temperature increases, displaying rotational symmetry and bi-partite correlation patterns. Lastly, we explore the relationship between our findings and the Weyl group of the symmetries present in the Ising model.

A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Furthermore, by incorporating the new iteration into a wider framework, it becomes possible to employ any preconditioned iteration as a substitute. Our numerical experiments are conducted across a range of applications, including scalar advection equations, systems of advection equations, the Burgers' equation and the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, resolving a related stability issue. The findings showcase that while the proposed iteration method may not offer a straight performance boost, it still enables the use of flexible schemes for large systems by upholding their intended properties. This advancement has the potential to unlock further innovative numerical schemes. Our code is publicly available under the MIT License at https://github.com/ghwhite/fgmres-preserving. In order to facilitate reproduction of the results presented within this paper, our open-source implementation comprises: (a) multipleexact.m - a reference implementation of numerous exact methods for solving each specific problem under consideration; (b) fgmres.m - the proposed generalised minimum residual iteration with constraint enforcement; and (b) run_solvers.m - a utility for comparing and reproducing the outcomes across all of our numerical experiments. Both the algorithmic innovations and the accompanying software have positive implications for the numerical solution of time-dependent PDEs. A group of integer sequences can be classified as jointly ergodic if for every ergodic system with a measure-preserving nature, their average values, determined by iteratively applying the sequences, converge on average to a specific, integrated product that aligns with the original values. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. Notably, our reasoning employs a novel ergodic variant of a technique initially explored by Peluse and Prendiville in establishing quantitative versions of the finitary Szemer\'edi theorem's application. Additionally, our findings establish an interesting connection between ergodic pairs and their counterparts in the finite context, as evidenced by the inclusion of a non-asymptotic formulation of our condition within the Szemer\'edi's regularity partition framework. This, in turn, enables an innovative approach to addressing certain questions related to the finite version of ergodic theory. Furthermore, we investigate the interplay between ergodicity and the structure of sequences with specific properties, such as being formed by iterative applications of powers of natural numbers or having a particular recursive definition. We also explore implications of our definitions for understanding the behavior of systems with ergodic sequences and present an application involving a modified version of the classical Weyl equidistribution theorem. We conclude by discussing the interplay between our findings and recent research on ergodic sequences. Our work is accompanied by an appendix containing auxiliary material and the basic application of our condition to the finite context. It also includes a brief overview of the necessary background from ergodic theory, sequence entropy, and the interplay between them, as well as a detailed account of the recently introduced ergodic variant of the Szemer\'edi's higher order partition theorem. Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of points falling further than 50m from the vehicle in the nuScenes dataset. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks, including average precision (AP), are insufficiently sensitive to far-field objects because they weigh closer objects more heavily. As a result, detectors are often biased towards favoring the detection of nearer objects over more distant ones. To better understand and improve detection of far-field objects, we created a new evaluation benchmark that isolates performance at great distances and developed a simple approach to tackle this challenge head-on. This new approach, known as directed optimization, enables the autonomous vehicle industry to create and evaluate detectors that excel at detecting both near and far-field objects. To verify the effectiveness of our method, we conducted extensive experiments using the newly created benchmark as well as the widely used nuScenes dataset. The results showed that traditional detectors perform significantly better at detecting far-field objects when given sufficient training data but consistently prioritize detection of nearer objects over more distant ones. Interestingly, our results also revealed that deeper neural network architectures tend to perform better at detecting far-field objects while shallower architectures excel at detecting nearer ones. Moreover, we discovered that directed optimization leads to a significant improvement of about 10% in far-field AP on both created and real-world datasets. Our code, dataset, and findings have been made publicly available so that the autonomous vehicle industry can benefit from this research. Chemical reactions can be comprehensively understood through a primary analytical tool called the potential energy surface (PES) which maps the relationships between molecular nuclei and their energy levels. Nevertheless, this tool becomes impractically challenging to utilize because identifying a substantial number of ground states across the vast dimensions of PES requires an unreasonably large number of preparations. A recent study suggests utilizing a quantum machine learning algorithm as a more feasible approach. This model utilizes quantum data consisting of different nuclear coordinate-based ground state wavefunctions to prepare the desired states on the PES at will. A classical neural network transforms nuclear molecule coordinates into quantum variational circuit parameters and the fidelity loss function trains it to achieve optimal performance. Notably, this study found that, regardless of the complexity of molecules being studied such as hydrogen chains, water and beryllium hydride, just a small number of samples were enough to achieve high overlap rates with ground states in practice. A theoretical aspect also proves a limitation to these protocols suggesting it would be against the laws of physics if such efficient protocol could apply to regions where the ground state significantly drops in energy as in avoided crossings due to limitations imposed by Grover's lower bound. Also the amount of data that could efficiently be processed by the classical neural network is determined with respect to quantum data requirements from a quantum angle. Overall this study suggests that applications involving quantum chemistry are promising candidates to showcase the capabilities of quantum machine learning in action.

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The resulting organ model-based reconstruction can enhance the accuracy of laparoscopic surgery by pointing out and warning against lesions missed during the surgery, along with providing the distance between tumors and major organs, all in near real-time. A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we conclude that the papillon graph encompasses an infinite family of cubic graphs whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of its 3-edge-colouring, leading to a new conclusion that the papillon graph has the E2F condition if and only if it has the PMH-property. Our research also delves into papillon graphs with specific parameters and their relationships to other infinitesimal families of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs, as well as exploring the properties of these graphs. Lastly, our work involves identifying a papillon graph that contains a specific subgraph, namely the line graph of a certain type of graph. This subgraph is of particular interest because it satisfies the PMH-property but does not satisfy the E2F condition, thus providing an example of a PMH-property that is not E2F. This papillon graph with these particular parameters is an instance of a Petersen-agram, a recently defined graph family that has an infinitesimal number of graph instances. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. In the future, we believe that Timeloops has considerable potential to contribute to the development of safe, general-purpose system libraries for microservices operating systems. The source code for this project is currently available under the permissive BSD-3 license on our public code repository.

This study examines the null controllability of a population model that includes an interior control mechanism. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in a single dimension and then deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Notably, the model's unique structure necessitates the development of an alternative approach to standard techniques employed in the context of singular diffusion equations. Additionally, our method introduces an innovative strategy for obtaining a priori estimates in complex scenarios. By combining these new estimates with a standard approach, we ultimately establish the required observability inequality and consequently prove the controllability of the model. This approach may also be applied to a broader class of monotone parabolic systems. In the latter part of the study, we explore its implications for population models and discuss potential future directions in the field.

In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. The model's performance highlights the capability to incorporate contextual information into strategic decisions, and it paves the way for more sophisticated methods to optimize team performance during games. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, both WRI and ESI are tested and compared on the Marmousi model with realistic data from the S-wave component. The results show that WRI and ESI have similar performance, with both outperforming standard FWI, and both facilitating faster convergence by reducing the update size, though at the expense of increased misfit between data sets. Furthermore, both of these methods allow for efficient reduction of frequency-domain wavefields to sparse time-domain records, resulting in substantial storage savings with no noticeable decrease in performance. This innovation enables large-scale seismic imaging projects to be conducted with significantly reduced computational infrastructure demands. Ultimately, both WRI and ESI are viewed as preprocessing tools to standard FWI, with future research being directed towards integrating them with additional seismic imaging methods. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, our results demonstrate that a suitable phase plate 
design remains robust across distinct TEM environments. Finally, our findings 
demonstrate that a programmable phase plate can enhance electron probe quality to the 
extent that image improvement throughients may be insufficient, and direct image 
processing is needed. In practice, this implies that a TEM equipped with such a 
phase plate can attain better than 1 Angstrom resolution without the need for 
further hardware improvements to correct spherical aberration. As a result, we 
propose that a suitable phase plate be viewed as a type of aberration corrector, 
entitled to the same recognition as other corrective technologies. To this end, 
we're advocating the establishment of a new category for this category of correctors 
in the existing taxonomy of TEM aberration correctors. Ultimately, our study 
demonstrates the efficacy of custom-designed phase plates in achieving superior probe 
sizes and, by extension, better image quality, particularly in high-resolution TEM 
imaging applications. In doing so, it provides a valuable reference point for the 
design of more effective phase plate technologies. In practice, this could involve 
exploring alternative materials with higher charge densities, developing multiple-zone 
devices, or creating charge fonts on each element, all of which hold significant 
potential for further improving the effectiveness of such devices. In turn, this could 
ultimately facilitate even greater improvements in electron probe size and current 
density. In such cases, custom-designed phase plates could be particularly 
instrumental, perhaps even necessary, to achieve the necessary levels of resolution 
and current density in TEMs without the need for additional hardware upgrades.

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. This distinction highlights the importance of distinguishing generator quality from encoder representations when evaluating dialogue models. Furthermore, our findings suggest that when evaluating these models, it is not necessarily the overall performance that matters but rather their ability to grasp the underlying structure of dialogue language, which involves anticipating the next utterance. In demonstrations, human evaluators were shown to prioritize certain evaluation tasks over others and their scoring revealed interesting differences according to their individual characteristics, which were accounted for in separate analyses. Ultimately, our study suggests that the understanding of dialogue language should be evaluated through the ability to grasp the underlying structure of dialogue language, which involves anticipating the next utterance, and that this understanding, along with the code, will be made publicly available.

We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The magnitude of this coefficient is directly proportional to the total number of Dirac electrons at each given chemical potential. The specific heat coefficients we obtain are in line with recent experimental measurements. In addition, our results for thermal capacity and compressibility are consistent with those from fully self-consistent many-body calculations using the dynamical coherent potential approximation, although those methods require stronger interactions to converge than do our finite-temperature screenings from interaction at zero temperature. Our results are also in line with recent experimental measurements of thermal capacity and compressibility in doped graphene. In the range of high temperatures, where thermal capacity is heavily influenced by whether the chemical potential lies within or outside the conduction/valence bands, our theoretical calculations are less accurate but still compatible with experimental data. In all cases considered, our thermal screenings at zero temperature are in the range of 2-4, which is in line with previous works using the tight-binding model and are necessary for correct convergence with the dynamical coherent potential approximation methods. Consequently, our study confirms that even in the most disordered and doped forms of graphene, interelectronic interactions play a crucial role, displaying strong screening at zero temperature and significant influence on thermal capacity at all temperatures and in compressibility at all temperatures except the highest. In the case of compressed graphene, its interelectronic interactions could offer the lowest possible limits on the effective Higgs vertex in the context of the Higgs inflation model, again with results that could outperform future direct detection methods. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech incorporates contextual acoustic features into each sentence, enabling a more detailed understanding of semantic relationships. Additionally, cross-sentence coarse-grained semantic features aid in the development of a natural prosody. Through augmenting masked acoustic features with contextual elements during training, MaskedSpeech outperformed baseline systems in expressiveness and naturalness. The benefits of this approach were particularly evident when processing more complex texts. Two variants of MaskedSpeech were explored: a simple approach relying solely on contextual acoustic features and a more advanced system leveraging additional semantic elements. The results show that the latter consistently produces the highest quality speech and has a greater potential for speech that mimics the context. All source code and models are openly available at https://github.com/sonuspeech/MaskedSpeech.
