In this paper, we explore this broader scenario, analyzing both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework and identifying essential conditions for existence in the more complex scenarios. Additionally, we identify a previously unexamined Q-ball state, which we term 'cored', and demonstrate that it could possess stability under specific conditions; a more detailed investigation into its implications will be addressed in a subsequent study. 

A cored Q-ball forms through the combination of two distinct, coexistential Q-ball configurations. These two configurations must have the same scalar fields and symmetry properties but differ in the values of their conserved currents. In our analysis, we establish the conditions necessary for a cored Q-ball to exist and determine whether it is energetically stable in scenarios where both constituent Q-balls have the same mass, a scenario that is mathematically possible only when the theory has two symmetries. 

When the mass of the cored Q-ball lies within the mass gap of its two constituent Q-balls, it is clear that it is the lighter state. However, when the cored Q-ball's mass falls outside of this mass gap, either above or below, we have found that a specific relationship between the two constituent Q-balls is necessary for the cored state to be the minimum energy configuration. This relationship is determined by the total charge of the cored Q-ball, with the cored state being the more stable configuration when this charge exceeds a certain threshold in the case of an extra mass above the two constituent Q-balls, and when this charge is below a certain threshold in the case of an extra mass below the two constituent Q-balls. 

It is worth noting that both the standard and advanced limits within this theoretical framework can be achieved by adding a non-linear Chern-Simons term to the cored Q-ball potential, thereby demonstrating that both the standard and advanced limits can be viewed as particular instances of the more general cored Q-ball scenario. 

Finally, we have found that the field describing the cored Q-ball can be expressed in a form that is analogous to a soliton solution derived from a one-dimensional sigma model, described by a Weierstrass beta function. However, this relationship only holds under the specific condition that the charge of the cored Q-ball is an integer multiple of a particular minimum charge.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our analysis also provides a method for identifying all purely residually free properties of such rings of integers. Consequently, we establish that in cases where G is isomorphic to A4 or S4, the ring of integers in K possesses a completely free additive Galois module property, effectively implying that K itself has a freely additive Galois module property over Q. Our findings extend and refine earlier results presented in [A. Besson, Ann. Inst. Fourier, 2017]. the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. Additionally, we make the datasets for difficult and easy

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). When considering multiple species, a system of two axion-like particles is sufficient to fully comprise the dark matter. This research opens the door for end-to-end surveys of AGNs, treating them as extended astrophysical objects that can be used to investigate the fundamental properties of black holes, and also the potential for dark matter particle investigation in the mass range $10^{-21} - 10^{-14}$eV. This framework can be applied not only to AGNs but also to other compact relativistic jets, such as microquasars. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and
validate a simple mathematical model that successfully replicates the observed migration patterns. Our model
suggests that nuclei at the upper and lower edges of the retina experience greater constraints and tend to stay closer
to their initial positions, leading to the observed migration patterns. Notably, our findings demonstrate that the
orientation of the retinal surface and local tissue constraints significantly contribute to the formation of S-shaped
migration curves commonly associated with IKNM. Furthermore, our results indicate that the efficacy of this migration
strategy is revealed through the uniform distribution of nuclei across the retina. In retinal tissues where cells are
densely packed, as in our zebrafish studies, our model shows that the dominant, S-shaped migration pattern is the
preferred behavior. However, in less dense tissues, we propose that a more efficient, direct migration path would
become the favored method of interkinetic nuclear migration. Our study provides a fundamental understanding of
the intricate balance between migration patterns and environmental constraints, a pivotal aspect of neural development. 
This knowledge is expected to foster exploration of the underlying biological mechanisms governing IKNM in various
tissues and the potential consequences of disruption to this process.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images. This code design problem is cast as a general matrix optimization challenge, with efficient, unsupervised algorithms being devised to compute optimal code patterns for various compressed sensing scenarios, including video compressed sensing, color image demosaicing, and others, leading to significant improvements in reconstruction error and overall performance. Notably, this code design does not require any prior knowledge about the specific image being captured, making it a truly universal solution. Experimental results confirm the superiority of the newly proposed code patterns over conventional, randomly generated codes in various scenarios, resulting in better reconstruction quality and lower reconstruction error. Moreover, the computational complexity of the newly devised algorithms is comparable to that of conventional code generation methods. This innovative code design is anticipated to contribute a key advancement to video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing technology. It also paves the way for the wider adoption of compressed sensing in other applications where coded images are shared over communication channels, such as medical imaging. By optimizing code patterns, higher-quality reconstructions can be achieved with existing algorithms, paving the way for the practical deployment of compressed sensing technology. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately captured using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional up to five-dimensional space; however, we were able to derive precise, dimension-dependent scaling parameters for these dimensions. Our analysis also reveals that polar active fluids exhibit robust coexistence with point inclusions, and we predict that these interactions will influence the polar fluid's behavior when the dimensions are either very small or very large. Furthermore, our hydrodynamic model anticipates that the polar fluid will experience a significant shift in behavior when the dimensions exceed a certain threshold, and we were able to determine that this threshold is indeed greater than three. Additionally, we were able to show that our hydrodynamic theory is consistent with existing numerical simulations and offers a framework for understanding the interplay between polar active fluids and the inclusions that affect their movements. This framework is relevant to the observation of activity patterns in biological systems, such as the movement of cells across epithelial layers and the organization of bacterial colonies. Lastly, our research suggests that the type of inclusion (e.g. obstructions vs. propulsive surfaces) can have a substantial impact on the behavior of polar active fluids and may potentially be used as a means of controlling their movement and organization. This could have applications in the design of asynchronous active metamaterials, and may also provide insight into understanding more complex active matter systems, such as those involving multiple interacting species. This research is particularly significant because it addresses the fundamental challenge of developing accurate hydrodynamic theories for polar active fluids that can be confined to moving persistently in the presence of obstacles, and it offers a framework that can be used to predict how these systems respond to changes in their environment. Researchers within the same institution often rely on their institutional email as their primary means of communication. Due to their accessibility and private data storage, these emails are vulnerable to cyber threats and can serve as lucrative targets. Our proposed approach aims to examine research institutions' internal communication networks for potential security breaches. Initially, we gathered and analyzed over 9,000 email exchanges among 183 senders and recipients from within one institution. Our simulation of a well-known attack algorithm revealed that a significant 79.7% of nodes in the communication network were susceptible to compromise, with 36.5% of nodes being easily attacked and 43.2% requiring additional effort. Notably, our findings indicate that researchers are more likely to fall prey to these breaches due to their frequent interactions with each other and with relatively isolated institutions in their communication networks. Our analysis also showed a notable correlation between the vulnerability of nodes and the attack complexity required, with a strong positive correlation of 0.85. Our study provides a foundation for institutions to enhance their email-based security measures and potentially identify and mitigate potential security risks. Inspired by the pseudogap phenomenon in cuprates, we propose a new idea, 
the concept of an "exceptional" van Hove singularity, where a strong 
electron interaction fragments a continuous Fermi surface into disjoint regions. 
We identify this singularity with the merging of two separated Fermi surface 
segments, and demonstrate that it is close to a van Hove singularity, 
reaching it by adjusting a material parameter affecting its dispersion. 
We assert that, in the broader family of cuprate materials, 
the onset of pseudogap is attainable solely through inducing this exceptional 
van Hove singularity, and that this results in a distinct Lifshitz 
transition distinguished by heightened heat capacity and a nematic susceptibility, 
both consistent with empirical observations. 
However, our theory also predicts that this pseudogap will persist even at 
all temperatures once the singularity is created, contradicting the expected 
behavior in the very near region of the phase diagram. 
Furthermore, we propose that the heavy fermion system $\alpha$-Pu, 
considered a separate entity, might actually be part of the same theoretical 
framework, with its large Fermi surface and extensive flat regions making it 
prone to exceptional van Hove singularities and subsequent pseudogap formation. 
Ultimately, our study suggests that heat capacity peaks observed near 
Fermi surface critical points might be attributed to exceptional van Hove 
singularities, and that this phenomenon holds the key to understanding 
electron systems affected by strong interactions and marked by pseudogap formation. 
Our framework is underpinned by a novel method of determining Fermi surface 
topology, employing an unorthodox combination of density functional theory 
and heavy fluid dynamics. 
This innovative approach allows us to accurately pinpoint the location 
of exceptional van Hove singularities within the electron phase diagram. 
Our theoretical model is validated through its application to the two 
well-studied cases of TlCu$_2$Se$_2$ and $\alpha$-Pu, with our results 
corroborated by available experimental and numerical data. 
Ultimately, we propose that the very notion of an exceptional van Hove 
singularity be added to the electron phase diagram taxonomy. 
By doing so, it becomes clear that TlCu$_2$Se$_2$ and $\alpha$-Pu, 
once considered isolated cases, are actually part of a broader category 
of materials characterized by their association with exceptional van Hove

This paper details a specialized apparatus built for use in Aberdeen Tunnel's laboratory in Hong Kong. The laboratory is uniquely situated to study spallation neutrons produced by cosmic-ray muons with 611 meters of water equivalent in depth. The apparatus consists of six layers of horizontal plastic-scintillator detectors that pinpoint the direction and location of incoming muons. Between these layers, a neutron sensor filled with 650 kilograms of liquid scintillator containing a gadolinium dopant significantly enhances detection efficiency of the produced spallation neutrons. Additionally, we discuss the performance characteristics of this apparatus. During its initial operation from September 2018 to April 2021, the apparatus collected a total of 1595 days of data. It was determined that the apparatus detects cosmic-ray muons at a rate of about 480 per minute. The measured neutron spectrum in slanted mode, with the gadolinium fill layer included, shows a significant enhancement in the low-energy range. This is consistent with expectations. Furthermore, we observed an absolute neutron detection rate of about 18 per minute in the laboratory when the gadolinium fill layer is used. We also studied the contamination of muon tracks by neutrons and found that it occurs in less than one percent of cases. The contamination is likely the result of neutrons being kicked out of the muon bundle during scattering. The apparatus as a whole has a very low background rate of about 10 per minute in the neutron energy range of interest. This is an extremely desirable feature for any future neutron beamline experiments conducted in the laboratory. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing the Keck/HIRES spectrometer, we have conducted in-depth analysis of seven planets discovered through TESS, focusing particularly on planets with masses similar to that of Earth. Our study includes detecting the host star's radial velocity signals, determining the planets' mass and eccentricity, identifying planetary systems' architecture, identifying covariances between orbital periods and mass, and identifying a rock--water--gas planetary composition for one of the discovered planets. We observed significant improvements in precision with our data set, which showed a threshold of 1.5 mas--1 for individual measurements. Our study included seven planets, with three being terrestrial planets with orbital periods less than 20 days. The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best observed through minimally invasive techniques such as optical and radar observations. By analyzing the rotational data of asteroids, scientists aim to identify potential YORP rotation rate changes, which can provide valuable information about an asteroid's shape, size, and internal composition. However, gathering sufficient YORP rotation rate change data is challenging due to the slow effect of YORP and the necessity for extensive observational periods. To enhance the chances of discovering more YORP rotation rate changes, this study reviews and updates existing rotational data in search of unexpected period changes caused by the YORP effect, which are then compared to a predetermined set of criteria. As a result, eight additional asteroids with significant YORP rotation rate changes were identified, increasing the total count to sixteen and strengthening the case for shape and internal composition influences on the YORP effect through statistical analysis. Furthermore, 300 minutes was found to be the critical rotation period separator for an asteroid's internal rotation frequency as a result of this study. Below this threshold, YORP-rotators are rare, while above it, they are common. Therefore, it is hypothesized that the YORP effect drives internal differential rotation in asteroids with short rotation periods, providing a framework for further theoretical modeling and simulations to explore its implications. Additionally, relations between the YORP effect and asteroids' internal structures have been found and potential future targets for ground-based and space-based observations have been suggested. Ultimately, the duration and magnitude of YORP rotation rate changes are key factors in understanding the underlying mechanisms and internal processes of small asteroids through their rotational evolution. 

This study specifically adds sixteen new YORP rotation rate change cases to the existing database of thirty-two asteroids observed from the ground and throughspace-based missions between 2005 and 2021, and analyzes nine of these new cases in depth to illustrate the associated internal dynamics of small asteroids. The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on 10 weeks of data surrounding key elections in Brazil and Italy, observing users who commented on posts from politicians and celebrities. We found communities centered on politics to be more active in discussions, with members producing longer comments containing more emojis, hashtags, and negative language compared to communities focusing on other topics. Additionally, we observed a diverse range of topics over time, with some topics receiving fleeting attention while others centered on fundamental issues continued to be actively discussed. Communities involved in politics displayed dynamic characteristics, with some users consistently contributing to discussions and retaining their status as top commenters. Notably, we found that online discussions reflected real-world election results, with winners' names trending on Instagram and receiving more comments in the short term. However, we also discovered a notable lag between offline elections and the corresponding online discussions, with shifts in the platform's topic centrality occurring 2-4 weeks after real-world events. Our findings indicate that social media plays a significant role in shaping online communities and their discussion topics, with implications for electoral campaigns, research on online communities, and potential uses of centrality metrics in tracking public opinion. This finding contradicts a longstanding conjecture of Kechris, Lyons, and Weiss. We demonstrate a similar non-compactness result for a certain boundary-fixing homeomorphism subgroup on a compact surface with multiple boundaries. A key component of our proof involves developing an almost distal property for a specific family of homeomorphisms on compact surfaces. Alongside these results, we explore the surface homeomorphism subgroups that exhibit topological compactness within the compact-open topology's inherited structure, identifying necessary conditions for a surface homeomorphism subgroup to be topologically compact as highly transitive action within the surface's interior or on its boundary. Lastly, we establish the non-compactness of a surface homeomorphism subgroup requiring only action within the surface's interior being highly transitive, accompanied by its action on the surface's boundary being highly transitive and an almost distal homeomorphism. These findings arise from analyzing homeomorphisms' dynamics, combined with topological properties of compact surfaces and their boundary-fixing homeomorphisms. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database results, building on existing research. By extending two known categories of classification to incorporate self-joined queries with respect to efficiency, this study provides an in-depth analysis and illustrates potential enumeration strategies using self-joins. These advancements lead to more complex proof of intractability in comparison to queries without self-joins. Additionally, this study introduces an existing method to prove intractability in the presence of self-joins and sets criteria for both feasible and infeasible queries with limited complexity, providing answers for low-arity queries and those with cyclic patterns. However, many cases remain unclear. In such scenarios, further theoretical inquiry is necessary to either validate or disprove intractability. In contrast, manageable instances can be enumerated through a combination of self-joins and existentially-bounded joins. In conclusion, while many queries with self-joins fall into unknown categories, our investigation lays the ground for future research and understanding of self-joined database queries. These concepts have implications for other conjugative query languages, such as existential queries, and could inform the design of databases managing complex data sets. Lastly, more practical applications involving complex data management may benefit from these queries. Consequently, further research into these queries is both timely and necessary. To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've demonstrated the efficacy of the new algorithm by applying it to a simplified model of a vertical takeoff and landing aircraft in a confined environment, and we've compared it to an exact reference solution obtained through value function approximation. The results show that the algorithm is up to 1.5 orders of magnitude faster than traditional methods while achieving similar accuracy. Furthermore, we've found that the algorithm can be quite aggressive in its initial iteration but requires a careful initial guess to converge efficiently. We've also found that the algorithm exhibits some interesting behavior in its interior iterations, with some orders exhibiting a form of "alternation" that may be worthy of further study. We believe that this algorithm has significant potential for tackling more complex problems and is an important step towards developing more efficient Eulerian methods for optimal control problems. Additionally, we've open-sourced the code for this algorithm as part of the MPT3 framework and invite the research community to collaborate and contribute to its development. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a modulation network uses a
given input's specific latent code to control the activation of periodic
activations. We also develop an innovative local-function approach to
representation, where each element of the input code affects a particular region
of the space. We demonstrate that our method's ability to generalize across
different types of data leads to superior performance when compared to other
representations. Additionally, our method produces representations that are not
only more accurate but also more semantically meaningful. For instance, we
obtain over 30% improvement in fidelity when representing videos at a
64-dimensionality factor, and over 20% when representing images at a
32-dimensionality factor. We also show that our method produces factors that
are more interpretable, as demonstrated by the extraction of auxiliary
information like lighting conditions from video factors. We hope that our method
will serve as a platform for the development of more general-purpose,
high-fidelity representation learning techniques. All code and data used in this
research are available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/master/duallmp. An accompanying video can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watched?v=H6Und6cH4gA. The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. Furthermore, our findings contribute a stimulus set with multifaceted animal stimuli that can be utilized in future studies of the ventral temporal cortex. A supplementary theory of the animacy spectrum, incorporating both visual categorizability and agency perception, is also proposed. This framework positions agency as a critical factor in the animacy spectrum and may help resolve previous paradoxes, and it offers computational and neurobiological implications for the ventral temporal cortex. Ultimately, our study advocates for a continuum perspective on animacy in VTC and lays the groundwork for more in-depth agency research across the ventral temporal cortex. A companion paper exploring the inter-regional dynamics of the animacy spectrum in VTC is also available.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. Furthermore, this extension enables our logic to natively accommodate the fundamental task of assessing program efficiency, i.e., determining if one program can effectively substitute another while incurring some degree of loss, i.e., programs $f$ and $g$ such that $f$ yields the same result as $g$ with some probability $p$ of error. Interestingly, this formulation reveals that checking the equivalence ($p=1$) and evaluating the efficacy ($p>=\epsilon$ for some acceptable threshold $\epsilon$) of programs constitute two distinct tasks. Ultimately, our approach has been proven compatible with its underlying theory's soundness, and we have demonstrated its practical applicability through successful verification of multiple quantum programs utilizing our quantum relational Hoare logic with "expectations". In particular, this is exemplified by the efficient implementation of a useful application - a quantum random number generator. Notably, this implementation showcases the fundamental capability to evaluate programs of unbounded size, despite only being expressed as sequences of basic instructions (TGC's native language). Additionally, our approach has been compared to an alternative method of checking program equivalence, based on round-trip verification, and we have identified both similarities and differences between these methods. Lastly, we have outlined the possibilities and challenges awaiting further development of quantum relational Hoare logic in its current form. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as effective $R_0$ values. We illustrate in this report that the number of $R_0$ equivalents generated by a single super-spreader event is directly proportional to the effective $R_0$ and depends on the number of individuals the contagious person transmitted to, assuming each of these secondary cases resulted from a fresh transmission chain. Therefore, the significant influence of a single high-transmission event on disease spread can be captured through an increased effective $R_0$ value in modeling efforts. As an example, we analyze the recent outbreak of rabies virus transmissions on an island of the southeast Asian region using data from reliable sources and consider the impact of a single super-spreader event on the epidemic's development. We also discuss various control measures that could prevent similar large transmission events in the future. The findings from this analysis can contribute to strategies for managing public health during viral spread episodes. Furthermore, this study highlights the advantages of incorporating re-exposed patient data into contact tracing efforts. Finally, we suggest modifications to existing public health policies to reduce the risk of future super-spreader events. All data and calculations used in this analysis are openly available for reproduction through an openly accessible repository.  The analysis presented in this report can be reproduced using R code available at https://github.com/rajjoy/rabies-island-outbreak-analysis, where data and calculations used here are fully reproducible.  This study does not aim to provide authoritative guidance on rabies transmission or management practices but rather offers analytical perspectives using existing data. The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The authors suggest that future comparisons between inversion codes be conducted with native Bperp components to distinguish true differences from bias effects. The study's findings have significant implications for using global-scale structures derived from vector magnetic field maps in MHD modeling. The associated code is publicly available upon request. A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to measure the radii of 6097 young star clusters in 31 galaxies from the LEGUS survey. The custom analysis pipeline allowed for a large and contamination-resistant sample, giving us the largest dataset to date of its kind. The study discovered that a vast majority of galaxies exhibit similar radii distribution patterns, with a notable peak at approximately 3 pc. The mass-radius relationship of star clusters in this sample follows a distinct $R_{\mathrm{eff}} \propto M^{0.24}$ pattern. Notably, this relationship applies uniformly to clusters under 1 Gyr old, albeit with a less pronounced slope in cases younger than 10 Myr. Theoretical models suggest that more massive star clusters tend to be nontidally constrained, expanding over time. The study further reveals that a substantial majority of these star clusters in the survey exhibit signs of gravitational binding, especially when viewed at older ages or greater masses. The study's results on the cluster density and surface density show substantial variation, however it seems the dispersion tends to lessen as the age of the cluster increases, where the densest of these youthful star clusters have a typical density of around 100 $M_\odot$ pc$^{-2}$. The variation in cluster density is instead more closely correlated with the host galaxy's mass density, where clusters forming in more densely packed surroundings tend to be less dense. The study's results also offer a means to predict the half-mass dissolution timescale for these clusters, which show a correlation with the host galaxy's mass density, where the timescale tends to be shorter in more densely packed surroundings, specifically in environments above a certain density threshold where the timescale drops below 1 Gyr. The results also indicate a distinct $R_{\mathrm{eff}} \proportional M^{0.24}$ pattern for star clusters in this sample, uniform across all ages under 1 Gyr, albeit with a less pronounced slope in cases younger than 10 Myr. The study's results provide a framework for improved star cluster demography, which has implications for our understanding of star cluster formation throughout the history of the universe. The results also offer a means to predict the demise of these youthful star clusters, which are a key component in many galaxy interactions and mergers, particularly in the case of large star clusters. The study also highlights the value in conducting analysis of star clusters via custom analysis pipelines, which can uncover new patterns and correlations which may go undetected in broader analyses.

We present a novel, direct method for calculating the decay width of hadrons
decaying to two photons, often requiring an indirect estimation via off-shell
form factors. The new method offers an uncomplicated way to study volume effects.
In an example calculation, we apply this approach to $\eta_c\rightarrow 2\gamma$.
Using lattice ensembles with three $N_f=2$ configurations at different lattice
spacings, we derive the final decay width $\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}=6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV,
considering systematics in the charm quark mass. This technique can be extended
to additional processes involving leptons and photons in final states.  Further,
we derive the magnetic moment of the $\eta_c$ meson, yielding results that
bracket the value obtained via chirality rotation.  Our method is versatile
and may be utilized for other hadrons, such as $\J/\psi$ or heavier charmonium
systems, enabling a more precise determination of $\eta_c$ through $\J/\psi$
spectral shape analysis.  Additional, we highlight the importance of
considering systematics in charm quark mass corrections for volume effects in
$\eta_c$ decay width calculations.  Finally, we outline possible lattice
method enhancements, such as configurational averaging and systematic study
of systematics, to further increase the precision of our results.  In the case
of $\eta_c$, we find that a $10\%$ precision for the decay width calculation
may be achievable with current generation lattice simulations.  This is largely
achieved using the direct method proposal presented here.  We encourage
theoretical and experimental communities to re-evaluate $\eta_c$ decay width
measurements in search of an explanation for the observed discrepancy between
lattice and experimental/evaluative values.  In the case of $\eta_c$, the
lattice value for the decay width into two photons exceeds the experimental
value by about $2\sigma$ despite our very precise calculation.  We derive
the decay width of the $\eta_c$ meson into two photons, often denoted as
$\Gamma_{\eta_c\gamma\gamma}$, to be $6.57(15)_{\textrm{stat}}(8)_{\textrm{syst}}$ keV.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Our technique is exemplified through an investigation of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with electron-phonon interactions. By employing ab initio range reduction in combination with our method, we are able to tackle an unprecedented 64-site system with a filling level of four electrons. Our algorithm is an essential component for future computational physics research on intractably large systems. This paper examines the relationship between integers that are y-friable (or y-smooth) and the Dickman function. By assuming the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), we had a previous estimate of the count of y-friable integers up to x in terms of the Dickman function but it was limited to integers y greater than or equal to $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$ due to previous work by Hildebrand and Saias. Without making any assumptions, we derive a more general formula that gives the count of y-friable integers for the larger range of $y \ge (1+\varepsilon)\log x$. This formula reveals a pattern that follows $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ times correction factors. The correction factors consider the influences of zeta zeros and prime powers. By having this more general formula, we resolve two long-standing conjectures of Hildebrand and Pomerance. 

Hildebrand initially hypothesized that once $y$ is smaller than $(\log x)^{2+\varepsilon}$, the count of y-friable integers would no longer follow the estimated $x \rho(\log x/\log y)$ pattern, which we confirm to be true. 

As for Pomerance, he posed the question whether $\Psi(x,y) \ge x \rho(\log x/ \log y)$ would always hold for any y such that $x/2 \ge y \ge 2$, even under the condition where RH is true. We prove that in cases where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ except for very small values close to the critical value, $x/2\ge y \ge 2$ and that it fails infinitely many times when RH is not true. 

Our new estimates and our derivation for the count of y-friable integers for any y such that $x/2\ge y \ge 2$ also raises questions as to whether this relationship might hold only when $y$ is far away from $x$. In fact, under the condition where RH is true and for sufficiently large $x$ and any given $\varepsilon>0$, it will always fail an infinite number of times between $y=(1+\varepsilon)\log x$ and $y=x/2$.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code can be accessed via the link provided in the paper.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. When the set S has four elements, we directly determine all possible homeomorphisms between the boolean complexes and their projections, offering a comprehensive classification in this case. Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the elementary abelian group of rank n, the dihedral group of order 2n, and the Coxeter group of type B_n, among others. By examining discrete Morse theory on the boolean complex itself, rather than its dual, our methods offer a more intuitive understanding of the underlying Coxeter system. Lastly, we establish a connection between the homotopy type of the boolean complex and the descent set of an involution, providing a significant implication for the study of Coxeter groups and their connection to the combinatorial structure of polytopes.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study provides new insights into the propagation of online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic and offers cutting-edge forest models for predicting a rumor's peak influence. Additionally, we released the largest-scale dataset to date on medical rumors, incorporating 5083 labeled samples, in the hope of sparking more extensive research on this critical issue. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE dataset of the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive sample of 1350 planetary nebulae was collected from 259 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with a specific host galaxy based on its spatial location, and a comprehensive data set is compiled that includes the frequency of planetary nebulae within a certain radius from the galaxy's central point. By normalizing this frequency by the stellar mass within that area, a distinct pattern of planetary nebulae frequency is obtained for each galaxy, allowing for a comparative analysis of the space densities of planetary nebulae across various radii within individual galaxies. A statistical analysis of the observed data and theoretical predictions confirms that the vast majority of extragalactic planetary nebulae reside within their host galaxies' gravitational potential. Therefore, a comprehensive model is developed that connects the predicted frequencies of planetary nebulae based on galaxies' mass profiles to their cumulative counts, effectively providing a method to determine the distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. Additionally, LifeStream facilitates the development of analysis protocols by enabling researchers to define easy-to-understand workflows, reducing the necessary expertise from $11$ to $3$ (on average) and speeding up protocol development by $5\times$. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To further explore this concept, we conducted experiments across four image classification datasets. Our results showed that, using a fixed dataset and model architecture, we could obtain precision rates of up to 0.93%, outperforming the established Adam optimizer and delivering results on par with federated learning methods. A comparative analysis of various loss functions, including their mathematical properties, was conducted to guide our research, leading us to develop a novel loss function-based federated learning approach. In our study, we discovered that loss function selection amounts to optimizing a probability distribution, prompting us to apply insights from probability theory. Notably, we observed that the mean squared error loss function corresponds to the optimal low-rank estimator in the context of matrix factorization, and that loss functions like KL divergence yield superior outcomes compared to their Euclidean-based counterparts. Our research culminated in the development of a novel, loss-function-based approach to federated learning, which we hope will pave the way for further exploration of loss functions in the context of learning theory. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which results in a complex magnetic susceptibility in the nematic superconducting state. A key consequence of this complex susceptibility is that a non-trivial magnetic domain may be stabilized in the presence of a sufficient transverse magnetic field, even if the long-range magnetic field is not sufficient to overcome the superconducting critical current. Notably, this non-trivial magnetic domain can survive in the absence of any symmetry protection, which provides a possible explanation for the experimental observation of non-trivial magnetic domains in high-temperature superconductors like Bi$_2$Sr$_2$CaCu$_2$O$_8$. Additionally, we find that the chirality of the superconducting order parameter is sensitive to the in-plane component of an applied magnetic field, which results in a non-trivial magnetic domain with a non-uniform magnetic field distribution within the sample. These theoretical predictions can be experimentally verified in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and may also be applicable to other spin-triplet nematic superconductors. Furthermore, we suggest that magnetic hysteresis and magnetic domain wall pinning may provide a possible explanation for the anomalous transport phenomena observed in high-temperature superconductors. One significant issue in Imitation Learning (IL) is that obtaining perfect optimal demonstrations from a teacher is a challenging task due to the complexities involved, especially in robotics. Providing quality feedback is further constrained by the need to supply demonstrations for multiple state actions at once. To overcome these difficulties, researchers propose an alternative where the teacher can provide corrective feedback in the form of preferences or rewards instead of demonstrations. However, existing algorithms are designed to work with specific types of noisy feedback, limiting their application across various teachers and tasks. To tackle this problem, we suggest a different approach, one where we model a variety of feedback types as different loss functions. Using this approach, we can leverage any online learning algorithm to minimize the combined losses and learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed method can handle different forms of feedback by treating the teacher's cost function as latent. By applying a general corrective feedback meta-algorithm that unifies prior work, we can achieve similar regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by successfully learning to perform a complex household navigation task on a robotic platform using a variety of noisy feedback. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Moreover, our approach proves resilient to various labeling configurations and offers a scalable and user-friendly interface for efficient human-in-the-loop learning. The code is available at https://github.com/ruipengzhang/hrc-lever. We have also included additional details in the supplement at https://ruipengzhang.github.io/hrc-lever-supplement. Our approach now incorporates a translated version of the leverspace paper at https://ruipengzhang.github.io/hrc-lever-leverspace-translation. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. However, the maximality of model companions differs from a maximality axiom in set theory, as the latter would imply the existence of an ultimate model for set theory. A significant aspect of our study involves the comparison of model companions in various extensions of set theory, which involves nearly optimal preservation properties. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the concept of model companions provides a coherent and substantial framework for analyzing fundamental questions in set theory. This work is a preliminary outcome of the research project "Maximality in Set Theory" (PI: R. Kuekembilian), which is supported by the French National Research Agency (ANR-19-CE28-0008).

Evaluating a person's risk of drug abuse is crucial, and online surveys have proven effective for gathering relevant data. The data collection process included a comprehensive range of characteristics, including personality traits, impulsivity levels, and sensation seeking tendencies. The data set analyzed substance consumption patterns for 18 different central nervous system-altering substances. The research revealed that certain substances are frequently consumed in clusters, characterized by strong correlations, known as "pleiades." Notable clusters were identified around the substances ecstasy, heroin, and benzodiazepines. By exploring various classification techniques and features, a data-driven approach identified the most effective methods to categorize individuals as users or non-users for each specific substance or cluster. Among the techniques examined, including tree models and probability estimations, a top-performing classifier was chosen for each drug. The accuracy of these classifications exceeded 70 percent for nearly all substances when using a rigorous evaluation method. The best performance was seen for the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, legal highs, LSD, and volatile substance abuse, achieving a high classification accuracy of above 75 percent. The best-performing techniques for the drugs benzodiazepines, ecstasy (again), LSD, and prescription opioids were then applied to predict clusters within the data set. The results showed a strong correlation with previous studies and confirmed the existence of pleiades around the substances ecstasy and prescription opioids. The clusters were found to be similar to those identified in previous research. Notably, the data set showed an alarming trend of rising misuse of the substances cannabis, crack, ecstasy, LSD, and volatile substance abuse. Furthermore, compared to previous studies, the data set indicated an increase in the prevalence of misuse for the substances benzodiazepines, ecstasy, LSD, and prescription opioids. The research provides online resources in the form of publicly accessible code and data set at https://github.com/jheusen/Drug Consumption Characterization. The code includes the implementation of all classification techniques and cluster predictions along with visualizations of the data sets at https://jheusen.github.io/Drug Consumption Characterization/. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that takes into account the limitations of such hardware. NISQ-HHL is then employed to conduct a real-world portfolio optimization, utilizing S&P 500 company data and the prices from the day of the query, to compare its outcome with that of the classical approach. The results show that NISQ-HHL's output is only marginally worse than the optimal solution, while the performance difference with the classical approach is relatively minor. This groundbreaking study marks the very first time a hybrid quantum-classical portfolio optimization project has been undertaken. The underlying NISQ-HHL framework is not only applicable to portfolio optimization, but may also be adapted to tackle other computational challenges facing the financial sector. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This technique also achieves notable improvements of 3.8% and 6.4% in accuracy when applied to the Google Speech dataset with unpaired Wikipedia text. This approach is found to be particularly effective at improving ASR models' performance in low-resource setting scenarios. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, converge in distribution to independent, uniformly distributed random variables $U_{1,n}$ through $U_{k_n,n}$. The number $k_n$ can be any function of $n$ that satisfies $k_n = o(n)$ and $k_n/n$ is positive and bounded away from zero. This result extends the known behavior of the smallest parking position, for which it shows the exact rate of approach to uniformity. We also establish a central limit theorem for the sum of the first $k_n$ uniform variables, showing that $S_{\pi_n}(1)+\cdots+S_{\pi_n}(k_n)$ converges to a normal distribution with mean $k_n/2$ and variance $k_n/12$. These results follow from an underlying renewal theory and are applicable to any sequence of non-decreasing probabilities that satisfy a regularity condition. We demonstrate the practical utility of these results by confirming the predicted asymptotic properties for specific distributions. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of these results to other types of parking functions and offer a new heuristic explanation for the observed behavior. Our approach is efficient and straightforward, involving no advanced mathematical theory. Rather, it is grounded in basic principles of renewal theory and is entirely compatible with intuitive analysis. Along the way, we establish a central result that may be of independent interest within the broader context of parking function research. We also explore connections to previous work by Diaconis and Hicks, Flaxman, and Janson, among others. Although our results are primarily focused on uniform distributions, it is clear that similar approaches could be adapted to examine other distribution types. Notably, this method for analyzing place values could plausibly be applied to various other sequences of random variables that share similar characteristics. Ultimately, this research offers a fresh perspective on parking functions and suggests numerous avenues for further investigation into these captivating objects of study.

Our study offers an explanation of the structural properties of a thermal medium like quark-gluon plasma, using the framework of electron scattering via virtual photons on this medium. In particular, we investigate deep-inelastic scattering processes and derive moment sum rules from structure functions. These sum rules can be expressed as the thermal expectation values of twist-two operators, and such calculations are feasible using lattice QCD for a small set of initial moments. We demonstrate how lattice simulations can determine the minimum virtuality for a photon needed for Bjorken scaling to apply to structure functions. In line with typical DIS on protons, a kinematic parameter $x$ here directly represents the momentum carried by the partons, with its value spanning from zero to infinity. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Moreover, our approach excels in novelty view prediction from unseen categories, achieving a 51.5% improvement in FVD score. The code for our novel view video prediction approach can be found at https://github.com/ruilong0530/nvvp. Our research demonstrates the novel capability of novel view video prediction from just RGB frames, a crucial step towards developing more realistic novel view video synthesis.

Our approach offers a straightforward and efficient method for designing complex photonic functions using the inter-orbital coupling phenomenon.

This note outlines the algorithm devised by J. M. Eisenlohr and S. L. Farris to
systematically generate all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Furthermore, this algorithm is employed to construct a novel polyhedron within three-dimensional Euclidean space. Fully transitive polyhedra are geometric structures that exhibit complete transitivity and do so in multiple dimensions. Eisenlohr and Farris developed an method to produce all fully transitive polyhedra in $d$-dimensional Euclidean space by iteratively applying a set of generating polyhedra. We have expanded upon their work by automating their algorithm via a computer program. Utilizing this program, we discovered a previously unknown polyhedron in three-dimensional Euclidean space. The volume of this new polyhedron is comparable to that of the Dodecahedron. An analytical approach to define all fully transitive polyhedra is also an issue of significant interest. Given the discovery of this novel polyhedron, it is clear that further analysis is still decidedly necessary. We intend to explore additional aspects of this polyhedron in future research. 

Keywords: fully transitive polyhedra, euclidean spaces, polyhedra construction.

Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Notably, this could enable reliable copying of specific items, such as programs, with minimal compromise, even in scenarios where a user may intentionally collaborate with the adversary. Our work on unclonable encryption also presents novel opportunities and challenges in the field of cryptography. We hope this will spark further research into and exploration of these concepts. We also establish a condition for a conformal Ricci soliton to be a gradient Ricci soliton, and provide a characterization of the soliton in terms of its contraction or expansion rate. Both celestial bodies can experience mass loss due to an expansive outward flow,
often regulated or redirected by magnetic fields that create a surrounding
magnetospheric field. Powerful star winds are generated by the scattering of the
star's radiative force, whereas in smaller stars and our Sun, weaker mass loss is
caused by thermal expansion of the mechanically heated outer layer. This process
can also occur in planets around low-mass stars, resulting in thermal expansion or
mechanical wear on their atmospheres. Magnetospheres in stars arise from wind flow
containment, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by the external impact of
the star's wind. However, in both cases, magnetic reconnection due to the strain can
lead to detectable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to
summarize the underlying physics of these processes and their shared and unique
aspects in stars and planets. It additionally discusses recent space mission
achievements in this field and is accompanied by an invitation to participate in
the upcoming Exo-Life Mission Concept Study.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and magnetosusceptibility, were investigated in Bilayer WSe2, where one WSe2 layer was in contact with a Fermi sea of gold. The study revealed that increased Spin-Orbit Coupling in the coupled WSe2 layer results in resistance suppression and enhanced susceptibility under magnetic fields, and the effect of Spin-Orbit Coupling was found to influence two-gate WSe2 layers in a device setup, showing resistance controllability via both electric and magnetic fields. The findings have potential applications in spintronic and magneto-electronic devices utilizing transition metal dichalcogenides. Furthermore, the investigation provides practical methods for detecting Spin-Orbit Coupling in solid-state systems. The study also presents an electronic phase-diagram of bilayer WSe2 involving Spin-Orbit Coupling and electron-electron interactions, and the results may contribute to a deeper understanding of transport phenomena in transition metal dichalcogenides, especially in multi-layer systems where interlayer interactions play a significant role. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. We hope our findings will contribute to a deeper understanding of how to train more reliable and sensitive neural networks. We also introduced a novel metric that measures the difference between a neural network's actual and maximum possible Lipschitz constants, and made our source code publicly available.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity
to learn complex language hierarchies and grammatical patterns naturally
occurring in human language.
As a case study for understanding the implicit comprehension of sentence
structure and the adoption of a complex yet systematic morphological system,
we explore agreement prediction in Basque, which demands a thorough analysis
of both.
Our analysis of the results of verb number prediction and suffix recovery in
two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.
Our exploratory findings based on diagnostic tools indicate that neural
networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.
