We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. Furthermore, this code can be adapted to facilitate the search for monojets produced through the collision of protons at the LHC. In this scenario, quantum chromodynamics effects are anticipated to be substantial and will be addressed by the code. In addition, this code is capable of integrating with comprehensive event-simulation programs, such as APERA, to generate detailed descriptions of the production of ditau events, from the primary particle-collision stage to the detection of the resulting particles as they interact with the LHC's detection apparatus. By doing so, it is possible to perform an accurate comparison between theoretical predictions and the actual data collected by the LHC, thereby constraining the properties of vector leptoquarks more effectively. The code is publicly available under an permissive open-source license. In a related context, we also examine the production of monojets at the LHC, an exotic process that could provide valuable insights into the world of subatomic particles. In this process, quantum chromodynamics plays a significant role and is a key area for further study. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. Moreover, compared to existing transfer learning methods, this model exhibits superior performance in out-of-distribution robustness. Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The evaluation of the proposed model in comparison to popular signal distance metrics such as RSS-LOS, RSS-NLOS, and Rician distribution was conducted and revealed that it is robust in multiple scenarios and outperforms other metrics in most cases while exhibiting minimal variability in error rates across different datasets. Furthermore, to provide a complete understanding of the model's performance in different scenarios, the researchers conducted evaluations on various datasets at different training and testing data ratios as well as using different training techniques such as stochastic gradient descent. The findings indicated that the model's accuracy in certain cases could drop as low as 1.29 meters when the training size is extremely small but generally averages around 1.07 meters when the training size is adequate. To facilitate replication of these findings and inform positioning research within unknown environments, the researchers have made the model available for public use. Nonetheless, due to the nature of indoor settings as unique environments, replication of these findings is still dependent on validation using newly collected datasets from unknown locations. To this end, the researchers invite the academic community to contribute their collected datasets for training and testing the proposed model in various scenarios. Ultimately, the ultimate goal of this research is to create a publicly accessible, open-source dataset that can be used to inform and evaluate positioning methods and algorithms in academic literature. Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis (LFDA) is a localized adaptation of the traditional Fisher Discriminant Analysis, widely employed for supervised dimensionality reduction techniques. The LFDA R package allows users to execute various LFDA methodologies like Kernel Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis and Semi-Supervised Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. The package also facilitates dimensionality reduction result visualization, utilizing 3D (rgl) and 2D (ggfortify in ggplot2) graphical tools. Moreover, to ensure consistency, the package includes utilities for generating random number sequences and data (especially for categorization), along with sample data sets. The package's primary goal is to provide an easy-to-use framework for LFDA-related methodologies and related tools. Unlike other R dimensionality reduction packages (e.g., RDA, PCA, ICA, MDA, NPCA), LFDA does not support unsupervised or reduced dimensionality input. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the robot to acquire skills while adhering to prerequisites such as joint positions and avoidance of obstacles. Nevertheless, conventional constrained imitation learning methods either dismiss external influences or develop complicated optimization algorithms. In response, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) for conjugating imitation learning with kinodynamic and external constraints. EKMP facilitates effortless incorporation of constraints into kernelized learning and enables data-efficient skill acquisition from single demonstration trajectories. Evaluations using a collaborative robot in a manufacturing setting and a quadrocopter in an environment with moving obstacles demonstrate that EKMP surpasses state-of-the-art conventional kernelized learning methods. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we analyzed the effects of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman field on superconductivity in a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with doping. Our findings reveal that Rashba coupling enhances s-wave superconductivity, overcoming Zeeman field-induced pair-breaking when present. Additionally, we demonstrate that Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field through mixing, thus restoring superconductivity. Furthermore, we established that Rashba coupling's favorable impact on superconductivity originates from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the likelihood of a pair of electrons traveling in reverse time-states. Our analysis also predicts that under suitable Rashba coupling and Zeeman field conditions, the superconducting state exhibits topologically non-trivial characteristics, as confirmed through inspection of the interacting model's Fermi surface.

By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The discovered phase shift, occurring at magnetic fields higher than 35 T and very low temperatures below the critical point without magnetic field, can be identified by measuring the stiffness of the interlocked vortex lattice, at a doping concentration of $x=p=0.17$. Our theoretical calculations using the Eilenberger theory for interlocked vortices demonstrate that this transition represents the expected rotation of the square lattice structure by 45 degrees predicted for materials that are $d$-wave superconductors near a point of high singularity. 

This study provides the first empirical confirmation of a predicted phenomenon in the physics of interlocked vortices and offers a possible method for indirectly confirming the $d$-wave nature of La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ through magnetic field-state transitions in this material. Furthermore, we have established that the newly discovered transition occurs beyond the point of optimal doping ($x=p=0.17$) in the material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$, which contradicts our initial hypothesis that it could be observed only at the point of optimal doping. 

In addition, we have determined that the strength of magnetic fields required for this transition decreases with increasing doping concentration ($x$), and it appears that it may no longer be observable at $x \geq 0.20$ due to the destruction of the $d$-wave symmetry by excessive doping. We have also discovered that the newly identified state transition is distinguishable from the "65-K" transition, another recently discovered transition in this material, by Interlocking Vortex Lattice Melting Temperature and that it only occurs in materials that are $d$-wave superconductors. 

Finally, our findings suggest that this transition may no longer be observable in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$ above magnetic fields of 37 T and all temperatures below the point of zero-resistance even at low levels of doping ($x=0.12$), which may indicate that it is no longer present in the well-doped (upper phase plane) of this material. More research is needed to confirm these findings.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to a better comprehension of group decision-making processes and action coordination among individual agents within dynamic, ever-changing environments. We demonstrate the applicability of our methods through concrete examples and thorough simulations across diverse scenarios. In addition, we preclude the possibility of achieving a constant-factor approximation when applying it to NP-hard combinatorial optimization domains by constructing a NP-hardness proof for a simplified variant of one such domain, specifically arborescence domain, despite being unable to obtain an explicit lower bound due to the limitations of the 1.6 approximation factor technique by [Feige et al.'11]. We hope that our work will spark further inquiry into the efficacy of action sequences for resolving combinatorial optimization problems and encourage researchers to investigate additional query-based approximation schemes. We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. In our sample set, we identified four new wide binary asteroid 
candidates, alongside recovering two established binary asteroid orbits and one 
additional wide binary asteroid previously documented in (Johnston, 2019). All 
analytical techniques, data extraction, and candidate selection were 
automated/execute with Python tools.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data. The fifth section uses real-world data to analyze the impact of friends' income on individual income, focusing on professional soccer players. The paper's third section offers a novel approach to account for unobserved variables that affect the connection between two individuals. The method involves utilizing an auxiliary network where the same individuals are connected, but the nature of the connection (e.g., friendship versus acquaintance) is different. The auxiliary network allows for controlling the confounding variables that affect the connection between two individuals. The method is then applied to analyze the influence of friends' and acquaintances' income on individual income. The paper includes a Monte Carlo simulation of a model with endogenous peer effects and estimates the large sample behavior of the least squares estimator in this setup. We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,
such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user
interactivity. Additionally, the adoption of modern web frameworks facilitates
extensive customization, making our visualization tools effortlessly integratable
into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is
also compatible with Aladin Lite and other popular third-party web tools. To use
these visualizers, simply click the three dots on the SED catalog page and follow
the instructions. We've also included a comprehensive tutorial in the documentation
for users wishing to locally host and customize these visualization tools. We've
integrated these visualizers into the second edition of the RCSED galaxy energy
distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org) and made the code publicly available
on GitHub at voxastro/rcsed2-visualizers. We hope these visualization tools will
facilitate community engagement with the RCSED catalog and inspire users to create
their own customized visualizers. We'd appreciate any contributions or suggestions
to enhance this framework, which we intend to extend to additional astronomical
catalogs and datasets in the future. We'd be delighted to receive any feedback or
collaborative ideas at support@voxastro.org. We're excited to present the second
edition of the RCSED catalog, featuring over 200,000 galaxies with accompanying
visualizers, and we look forward to integrating these tools with more astronomical
catalogs and datasets. We'd like to express our gratitude to the square kilometer
array survey for giving us access to their data and for their financial support.
We'd also like to extend our appreciation to the community contributors listed in
the documentation. We're excited to present the second edition of the RCSED catalog
and we hope you enjoy exploring it at rcsed2.voxastro.org. We're eager to receive
any community feedback at support@voxastro.org. We're committed to continually
upgrading and expanding this framework with additional features, more visualizers,
and more datasets, which we'll regularly update on our website voxastro.org

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  This is evident in sedimentary basin patterns, magmatic and metamorphic rocks, and polycyclic Precambrian crust in West Africa.  This research was carried out as part of the MOntenegro Project, with data analysis completed in the EarthByte consultancy. A proven strategy to enhance multiple tasks using limited labeled data is
unsupervised pre-training.  Despite being a viable approach, contrastive
learning poses challenges in forming relevant pairs for an unsupervised
segmentation task. To circumvent these challenges, our proposed framework
utilizes two primary components:  using unsupervised over-segmentation with
mutual information maximization and a pre-training task along with boundary-
preserving learning.  The experimental outcomes of applying our proposed
framework to two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate its
efficacy in improving segmentation accuracy with limited annotated images. 
Notably, our method achieves a notable 5.8% gain in DICE score on the
BrainPro dataset when utilizing just 5% of the annotated data, and our code
and model are openly accessible on GitHub and CloudHanLab. for further details. 
Our method has been accepted as an ORAL presentation at the 2022 IEEE Conference
on Computer Vision.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Furthermore, we uncover that a Dungeon Master that integrates a single player's thoughts outperforms a system that considers the thoughts of all players simultaneously. Ultimately, our experiments demonstrate that a Dungeon Master trained on diverse D&D conversations excels in more complex worlds, ultimately outperforming a system trained on its own D&D conversations within the same world. Our work offers initial yet substantial insights into the G4C challenge within the context of D&D, underscoring the value of accounting for a theory-of-mind in the guidance of unaided learning through conversation, as well as the significance of grounding these systems within diverse, embodied contexts of shared world and history. Our approach paves the way for the development of more sophisticated systems that can effectively guide their own reasoning through verbal interaction, ultimately contributing to the development of more versatile, general-purpose learning frameworks. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. Our primary dataset consists of 10,000 German words with rich semantic histories, spanning from 1850 to present, based on adapted versions of Subtlex-DE. We also introduce an automated filtering method for both type-based and token-based methodologies. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. Our approach also facilitates the classification of knotoids, a recently identified class of minimal knots, and reveals that proteins with shallow knotoids exhibit similar folding patterns to those with trefoil knots. Notably, about half of protein knotoids are likely formed through intracellular folding processes. Since these proteins have a high tendency to form aggregates, our research suggests that understanding the folding of protein knotoids could contribute to tackling protein aggregation-related diseases. Moreover, our analysis of protein knotoids' geometry reveals that they have a higher tendency to target mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum. Consequently, our study proposes that cellular components could influence protein folding and, ultimately, shape the geography of protein interiors. By exploring the intricate connections between protein geometry, folding, location, and function, our research provides a statistical framework that is applicable to any type of protein knots and knotoids. This framework is particularly relevant to the many proteins whose folding processes have yet to be analyzed in depth. By doing so, our study is a step towards answering the fundamental question of how the intricate geometry of proteins is linked to their folding processes and, ultimately, their function. In this regard, we are launching the KNOTBASE 2.0 database, a comprehensive repository that includes the comparative analysis of knotted proteins along with their folding predictions and pathways. This database is an open resource for researchers to explore protein folding pathways and to identify patterns in protein geometry and biology. It is available at https://knotbase.org. For methodological details, please refer to the supplementary materials. A data visualization toolkit is also included in the supplementary materials for further customization. To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. Notably, this analysis does not rely on variations of EDE models and does not consider interactions with other components, instead focusing solely on EDE's impact on the evolution of the universe. Consequently, our study suggests that EDE could account for as much as $10\%$ of the universe's total energy density, potentially addressing the Hubble tension, and deserves further investigation within the context of the Standard Model of cosmology. Furthermore, we discovered that EDE's properties are consistent across different EDE model variations, reinforcing its viability. In addition, we found that EDE's effects on the universe's evolution are robust across varying parameters, supporting its role in explaining the Hubble tension. Nonetheless, other scenarios that do not involve EDE remain possible, emphasizing the need for additional, more precise constraints from various ongoing and future experiments, including stage IV experiments, to fully comprehend the universe's evolution and ultimately resolve the Hubble tension. In this study, we outline the methodologies that can provide such independent, precise constraints on EDE or other fundamental cosmological parameters. These methodologies involve integrating individual dataset pairs in a multi-dimensional likelihood space using an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood, and leveraging existing simulations as a framework for this study. Employing this approach, we are able to determine a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.) and explore various parameter choices that influence EDE's properties. Consequently, this analysis can provide a framework for independent, precise constraints on EDE or other fundamental cosmological parameters in various ongoing and future experiments, including stage IV experiments. Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite. Additionally, we establish that the symplectic mapping class group itself has an infinite order. This achievement opposes a $2016$ prediction of Fuentes, Mu\~noz, Rojas, and the third listed author. Our proof includes a novel, previously unstated argument which verifies that any characteristic class of $K_[\frac{1}{2}]$ on a symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is zero, a fact with implications for the study of $K_[\frac{1}{2}]$ in similar contexts. This finding may have a broader significance due to its connection to the recently introduced 'half-class' functor $K_[\frac{1}{2}]$. This work builds upon previous research which demonstrated that $K_[\frac{1}{2}]$ is an effective tool for analyzing the locally standard symplectic blowup of any symplectic manifold with an irrational Kaehler form, such as $(T^4,\omega)$. This new evidence highlights the capabilities of $K_[\frac{1}{2}]$ in yielding geometrically meaningful information about the properties of such manifolds. Lastly, this note presents an example which illustrates that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of any one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite, as well as proves that this group has an infinite order for any $\omega$ which is an arbitrarily minor adjustment of a given specific form. This achievement may have additional implications for our current understanding of the dynamics associated with the symplectic mapping class group. A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the criteria necessary for true NG boson generation and the mechanism for producing the masses of massive NG bosons. A key finding also emerged from examining the effective potential in the kaon condensation model: it revealed that the generation of massive modes within the NG sector can be understood through the lens of a Heisenberg algebra, which arises as a result of Lie algebra symmetry breaking. Consequently, a direct relationship has been established between the mechanisms driving symmetry breaking, the resulting Heisenberg algebra, the mode-mode interactions, and the generation of mass within the NG sector. Finally, some intriguing connections between the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem have been presented. Although these connections are purely speculative, they do offer a framework for exploring both the Riemann hypothesis and the anomalous NG theorem within the context of string theory and M-theory. A discussion on future research directions is also included as part of these investigations. Consequently, this project can be viewed as an initial step in a broader investigative endeavor aimed at comprehending the fundamental principles governing the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone theorem. Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings. while others were derived from the specific structure of these circulant graphs. Our research
also explores the relationship between total and standard chromatic numbers for the given graphs.

standard chromatic number. Some of the circulant graphs we considered also have a total
chromatic number equal to 2, which indicates they are 2-total-colorable. Our analysis also

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided. Moreover, a particular $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear code of rank two has been identified, demonstrating a particular type of non-uniqueness known as a Gray image of a $\Z_3 \Z_9$-additive code's image, adding to the existing knowledge that a unique $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code exists for p = 3, 5. Some $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes of rank one have been constructed from repeated $\Z_p$-linear codes and it has been established that these codes are equivalent to the original $\Z_p$-linear codes, leading to a better comprehension of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes and their relationship to $\Z_p$-linear codes. Lastly, several $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes of rank one have been identified and their properties analyzed in order to provide a foundation for investigating higher rank $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes.

The technology of graded viscosity banks, specifically tapering for polymer flooding,
has been analyzed using various models of mixing zone behavior. By considering different
viscosity functions, researchers have mathematically determined the optimal polymer injection
profile, given transverse flow equilibrium assumptions, for both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models.
Moreover, a numerical assessment has been conducted to evaluate potential polymer gains relative
to flooding using a finite number of polymer slugs. Furthermore, the impact of graded polymer
flooding has been examined in relation to polymer flooding using a single polymer slug,
considering both the Koval and Todd-Longstaff models. Finally, the feasibility of implementing
graded polymer flooding in real-field applications is discussed.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.  The technique also proves particularly useful in situations where limited annotated data exists.  The implemented code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang84/smls. Full research findings are published in the paper "Single-to-multi-label sampling for generative adversarial networks," available on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.10748.}

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms. For example, it yields an abstract adjoint representation of the algebra's symmetry group on the state's Hilbert space. This representation drives the derivation of Wigner's selection rules in high-energy physics. Moreover, it leads to an abstract symplectic form, related to the Tomasiewicz-Bogoliubov formula, that connects the algebra's state sum with the partition function in statistical mechanics. This new perspective on the GNS construction's inverse operation may lead to further mathematical discoveries with far-reaching implications in physics. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  Therefore, we propose that hadronic radiation from nearby radio galaxies could be responsible for a substantial amount of high energy cosmic radiation on Earth.  Furthermore, it's possible that finding more radio galaxies at greater distances will be essential to comprehending the origin of high energy cosmic radiation.  Additionally, we suggest that the gamma-rays from these galaxies could be identified through a collaborative effort between gamma-ray and radio telescopes.  Finally, it's also possible that a significant aspect of the gamma-ray background, specifically the component above 100 GeV, could be attributed to gamma-rays produced when magnetic fields from nearby radio galaxies interact with high energy cosmic rays. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. We tackle current, striking discrepancies in flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems, specifically addressing CP-violating Kaon decay and lepton-flavor universality violation in $B$ meson decays, with the introduction of heavy flavorful vector bosons at an energy scale of $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$. If these vector bosons are substantially heavier, around $\sim 1\,\mathrm{TeV}$ or above, a problem arises, as we then encounter difficulty in resolving the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly consistently with the $K^0$-$\overline{K^0}$ mixing constraints. However, the proposed framework is compatible with the given data within the one-sigma confidence threshold for each anomaly, with the parameter space to be examined by experiments such as NA62 and KOTO and through direct searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Moreover, this framework offers a plausible explanation for the $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ anomaly at a $3\sigma$ confidence level. Furthermore, we find that the proposed framework successfully reconciles the $B^0_{s}$-$\overline{B^0_s}$ and $B^0$-$\overline{B^0}$ mixing constraints with the observed values, and it also predicts an enhancement in the branching fraction of the decay $\Delta C$ mode, specifically $\frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{PS}}}\left(\Delta C\right) \simeq 7.5\times 10^{-2}$. This proposal also entails a distinctive pattern of flavor-changing processes, which can be examined at the Large Hadron Collider through searches for top quark production in association with antimatter mesons. Ultimately, this framework offers a compelling framework for addressing the flavor anomalies observed within the $K$ and $B$ meson systems.

Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code

It's interesting to note that when r = 1 and the sequence and channel alphabets have the same cardinality, the problem's channel capacity equivalent is the minimum number of channels required to reconstruct the transmitted sequence.

Our research also offers an encoding-decoding scheme that achieves the sequence reconstruction problem's channel capacity upper bound in the case of binary alphabets.

Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. The project's code is shareable on https://github.com/kuangqi/fsl-music, with data and experiments detailed on https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/GQ0f4s2s6thbG6G6uQzG6nQ0f4s2s6thbG6.

Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP researchers. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. The code and dataset are available at this link https://github/qasper.

This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. Our analytical approach employs the speed process of the TASEP system and a utility maximization argument. This innovative strategy may also provide insight into solving the analogous problem for the KPZ equation. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, collaborations between mathematicians, epidemiologists, and public health officials are crucial to developing actionable insights and to ensure that the valuable tools of mathematical epidemiology continue to serve the community in the face of future global health crises. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior and how an external linear potential affects their entropy and average energy. Our results reveal that the entropy and energy exhibit periodic increases in relation to the chemical potential, albeit in a limited range due to the particle-antiparticle identity restriction imposed by the linear external potential. This study ultimately lays the groundwork for exploring real-space Majorana fermion statistics within topological insulator segments.

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. Additionally, user-generated datasets can be incorporated into the system, enabling continuous improvement and increase in coverage of new acronyms. Alongside the project, a comprehensive evaluation including 135k examples from both the open domain and controlled settings has been conducted, showcasing the system's effectiveness with F1-scores ranging from 0.809 to 0.938 in various settings. The project's code is currently being expanded to accommodate additional domains and can be contributed to at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. Moreover, user-created datasets are welcome at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog-datasets. Consequently, this publicly accessible project aims to facilitate the development and testing of acronym-related theories and hypotheses. Ultimately, the successful deployment of this system in real-world applications is anticipated to contribute to the maturation of the field. This project has been presented at the 2021 Conference on Empirical Methods in Artificial Intelligence and the 2022 Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. Both presentations are available at https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLs6sD5sFVcN4Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q8. Lastly, the project is currently hosted at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog with code contributions welcome. Consequently, this publicly accessible project aims to facilitate the development and testing of acronym-related theories and hypotheses.

A Bose-Einstein condensate of rubidium atoms, positioned in two hyperfine states of the ground fraction, undergoes detailed investigations of its interplay with atom-molecule coexistence. A theoretical framework is used to analyze the impact of two key processes: first, combining spins results in the creation of molecule pairs, influenced by light association and a plethora of collision-related effects; second, photoassociation of atoms into molecules with specific energy levels. Our study specifically examines the interplay of these processes with the spin structure of the condensate, as well as the impact of light association on the molecule pairs, which results in a pairing imbalance. Notably, we find that the spin-exchange collisions play a crucial role in pairing spin-zero atoms into molecules, resulting in the predominate production of atom-molecule pairs with a single atom having nonzero spin. Furthermore, our findings also indicate that the molecule pairs produced through this mechanism exhibit a notable correlation between their spin states. In contrast, atom-molecule pairs formed as a result of photoassociation exhibit random spin relationships. Our data also illustrates the temporal evolution of pair formation in the $F=1$ system, showing that atom-molecule pair formation occurs far more quickly than molecule-molecule pair formation. Notably, we also observe a substantial increase in the number of molecule-molecule pairs when illuminating the condensate with light association, whereas a significant increase in atom-molecule pairs results from the spin-exchange collisions alone. Our study offers a comprehensive theoretical framework for a complex interplay of atom-molecule physics, present in various Bose-Einstein condensate systems of multicomponent gases. Moreover, our findings provide valuable insights into the intricate dynamics of these systems. In particular, we believe that our results will stimulate experimental investigations to further explore the intricate phenomena of molecule-molecule, atom-molecule, and molecule-photoassociation interactions in multicomponent Bose-Einstein condensates. Additionally, our study may serve as a starting point for examining multiple Bose-Einstein condensates involving different components and containing atom-molecule coexistence. In such cases, we anticipate that the interplay between different components will give rise to novel phenomena awaiting experimental validation. In our $^{85}$Rb system, we also anticipate that future studies are directed towards implementing optical association of atom-molecule pairs into molecules and offering a means to control chemical reactions within these systems. Ultimately, achieving a robust understanding of these complex many-body systems is crucial in successfully employing them as a functional platform for chemical reactions and photoassociation

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects. The advantages of our proposed architecture are showcased through an example of a large-scale, distributed data storage system, encompassing an extensive collection of scientific knowledge. This encompasses over 10,000 object data, equivalent in size to about 2 Gigabytes of compressed text. The methodology is then evaluated against conventional data storage solutions, in terms of both scalability and performance, with our DNA-storage method demonstrating comparable read throughput and better write throughput, while the overall approach is deemed a promising direction for the exploration of novel, biomolecule-based data storage architectures. However, it is also acknowledged that significant advancements are required before the approach can be considered a viable option for general-purpose data storage. Nevertheless, it is believed that the unique features of DNA storage make it particularly well-suited to specific use cases and applications. Consequently, a set of criteria has been established to identify suitable candidates for DNA storage, encompassing data formats that are inherently compatible with PCR addressing, such as hash tables and binary trees. Moreover, DNA storage is shown to offer an interesting alternative for the long-term preservation of content, such as articles and social media posts. Ultimately, this work is intended to spark further innovation and exploration in the field of biomolecule-based data storage, rather than presenting a fully functional storage system. The associated code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/alexejz/dnastore. The index used for the CancerGenomics Atlas is also accessible at https://cancer.sjcdn.org. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research has made notable strides in understanding and replicating topological effects through artificial materials, particularly photonic, phononic crystals, metamaterials, and electrical circuits, centered around Dirac/Weyl points. Conversely, topological nodal lines – one-dimensional singularities in momentum space – are relatively understudied. This review aims to illuminate the theoretical basis of topological nodal lines and outline recent developments using artificial materials, featuring examples of non-Abelian charges observed in nodal lines in momentum space and their realizations in photonic systems. Furthermore, it discusses the challenges associated with both experimental and theoretical investigations of topological nodal lines. This includes assessing the suitability of artificial materials that also host Weyl points and discussing the need for more sophisticated methods to analyze nodal lines in momentum space. This review is concluded by highlighting potential future directions for the field, which could be shaped by the unique properties of artifical topological materials, the diversity of momentum-space anatomy, and the versatility of photonic systems, enabling the exploration of novel concepts and phenomena in nodal-line systems. This could involve integrating multiple point defects into artificial materials and directing the flow of electrons through nodal lines by incorporating topological magnets. These developments hold the promise of propelling the field of topological artifical materials forward. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that uses MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal views.  The model is trained on the Figshare dataset containing images of three tumor types, meningioma, glioma, and pituitary tumors, and outperforms existing models through numerous trials while requiring the fewest parameters.  Evaluation of the model shows high accuracy in detecting tumors and distinguishing between types, with results comparable to those obtained from radiologists.  The model's ability to segment tumors in different views is equally impressive, with high dice similarity coefficients in all views.  Code for the MAG-Net model is available on GitHub, marking a significant step towards developing practical diagnosis tools that can be incorporated into healthcare systems.  Further improvement can be achieved by incorporating more datasets containing images from different views.  The model's ability to handle cases with incomplete data also needs to be explored in future research.  As a result, this study paves the way for the development of more effective diagnosis tools that can be utilized in conjunction with healthcare professionals.  The model's code is hosted on GitHub, and potential enhancements could be realized by incorporating additional datasets containing images from diverse perspectives.  Lastly, investigating the model's capability with incomplete data is a subject for further study. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Moreover, this method offers a modular framework that is versatile enough to be applied to various applications, including texture transfer, composite material analysis, face reconstruction, and model-to-scene transfer. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with several experiments and data transfers. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/yin-yang-lab/accu-sphere-rendering.

A popular technique, widely used for enhancing video playback on television and recording, is interlacing. This technique doubles the perceived frame rate without boosting the bandwidth, yet generates undesirable effects like visual distortion and flicker during playback. Present methods fail to balance real-time processing with satisfactory quality. They either prioritize real-time processing over visual clarity or improve quality at the expense of processing speed. This research proposes a groundbreaking approach utilizing deep convolutional neural networks, capable of delivering both high-quality results and real-time performance. Diverging from traditional super-resolution models that assume pixel invariance, our approach incorporates data from both interlaced half-frames to regenerate missing scan lines. This innovative system runs on a single GPU, achieving real-time processing speeds through the use of a shared architecture. Comparative tests confirm that this method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. In particular, our experiment shows that our algorithm performs significantly better than the baseline model and the widely-used collaborative deep network during both the training and testing stages. Additionally, our method exhibits a notable improvement over the super-resolution model that assumes pixel invariance and proves equal to the best existing self-deblurring model while outperforming all other competing methods. Moreover, our approach demonstrates superior robustness when dealing with distorted input data. Furthermore, our experiment involving real-world footage confirms that our method is capable of producing visually acceptable results even in the absence of training data. Consequently, our innovative interlacing technique serves as an all-encompassing solution for deinterlacing, suitable for both consumer electronics and cinematic applications. Our code and model have been made publicly available at https://github.com/hiemonguyen/deinterlacing. Our experiment involves the use of two datasets, comprising synthetic and real-world images, and shows that our method surpasses all existing techniques in both accuracy and processing speed. Notably, our approach outperforms the collaborative deep network, the baseline model, and all other competing methods, exhibiting a notable improvement over the self-deblurring model that assumes pixel invariance, outperforming it even when the model is distorted, and producing visually acceptable results even in real-world applications without the need for additional training. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the computation of the riverbed's expected value and various statistical moments. Secondly, a machine learning algorithm is trained to predict flow velocities based on the equations of motion, using the riverbed's statistical moments as inputs. This approach facilitates the derivation of an efficient closed-form expression for the expected flow velocity at an arbitrary point, thus making it feasible to compute the velocity field quickly. Furthermore, robustness to model inaccuracies is achieved by incorporating the riverbed's moment maps into the prediction model, allowing for reliable estimation of velocity boundaries even in the presence of uncertainties in the riverbed profile. Experimental evaluations using real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed methods. In particular, it is shown that the new method outperforms conventional numerical solvers, while the closed-form expression for expected flow velocity proves valuable for computational workflows. Additionally, future research directions are identified. One such potential direction involves exploring other machine learning algorithms to further improve flow velocity predictions. Another direction is focused on developing methods for efficient riverbed profile updates following changes to the riverbed. Moreover, there is also scope for applying this two-step approach to tackle similar challenges in other canals and streams. In conclusion, this study offers an innovative two-step approach to river flow velocity prediction, delivering both a robust and efficient closed-form expression for expected flow velocity as well as a machine learning-based model. This work has the potential to contribute to various applications including flood risk management, riverbed monitoring, and navigation system development. In addition, it is likely to be of interest to researchers working on machine learning for geophysical data analysis, river science, and hydrodynamics. Consequently, this study may ultimately lead to more effective use of machine learning algorithms in conjunction with physical models of river flows, resulting in better model robustness and ability to handle complex scenarios. Ultimately, this could result in outcomes that are more reliable and efficient in streaming data environments. In such scenarios, fast convergence and low latency are critical, enabling faster deployment of models in these settings. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This research presents a
technique for automatically determining optimal exposure settings for smartphone
images by utilizing the camera's inherent characteristics. Furthermore, an innovative
image fusion method is introduced, leveraging optimization and weighted averages.
These techniques are applied to a mobile HDR application, demonstrating the
feasibility of the approach. Comparative assessments are also conducted to
demonstrate the introduced solution's efficiency and effectiveness in comparison to
established methods. The implemented software is freely accessible online.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions. As such, authors are encouraged to incorporate their methods within this framework through an easy-to-use protocol, making it an openly accessible and community-driven knowledge base. For more information about individual comparisons or the protocol itself, please contact the authors at this paper's email address. With this community-driven approach, we aim to create a comprehensive and authoritative catalog for causal deep learning methods, providing a valuable resource for researchers to compare and benchmark their approaches and facilitating informed discussions in future related work sections. As such, we hope this initiative will contribute to the progression of the field, enriching the practice of causal inference and machine learning as a whole. This community effort is now live and we look forward to integrating your methods!

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, corroborated by optical temperature probe measurements, with an average error of 1.5°C. The presented MRI thermometry technique presents new avenues for the in-depth study of mass and heat transfer in gas-solid fixed beds, potentially being adapted for further applications in reactive gas-solid systems in the future.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different spatial finite element mesh sizes affect solution efficiency; how different orders of finite element basis functions influence solution efficiency; and how different muscle tissue mechanical property parameters, such as tissue hardness, affect solution efficiency. For each variable, a comprehensive examination is undertaken using a range of values typical to those seen in cardiac mechanics simulations. The study finds that both the BDDC method and AMG algorithm are highly effective at speeding up the solution of complex cardiac mechanics problems, reducing the time required to complete a simulation by as much as three orders of magnitude. However, the study also reveals that while BDDC can solve large cardiac mechanics problems in under two hours when the finite element grid is relatively small, it may take over ten hours to do so with larger grids, highlighting the need for further improvements to the algorithm to handle even larger problems in the future. The research was conducted using high-performance computing resources at the University of Houston's Trestles cluster and the National Center for Supercomputing Education's OnDemand system. The project involved several key contributors including graduate students, faculty members and researchers from several institutions. The project's data and code are now available to the public on GitHub, enabling other researchers to compare their results and contribute their own findings. The project's findings are also featured in an upcoming issue of the SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing.
