The standard scaled Wigner matrix and its corresponding semi-circular distribution, particularly its 2kth moment which relates to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set {1, 2,... 2k}, has been extensively studied. Building upon existing knowledge, this paper contributes a broader extension that also reveals novel insights. Given an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix with independently distributed entries under certain assumptions, our study confirms that a limiting spectral distribution indeed exists with probability or certainty. However, this limit can be understood through more extensive partitions, giving rise to intriguing combinatorial problems. As a result, several existing spectral distribution theories, such as those concerning standard Wigner, Erdos-Renyi graph, heavy-tailed Wigner, and variance-profile Wigner matrices, can be derived or further refined. Moreover, our main theoretical tool involves separating and estimating spectral tail corrections, which in turn enables the verification of convergence in L2 for relevant spectral statistics with probability or certainty. Notably, this technique offers a non-asymptotic spectral distribution diagnosis that may have value in its own right. Additionally, our approach implies that spectral statistics can be analyzed through a second-order approach. As an example, we demonstrate that the same limit can be characterized by distinct partition types, giving rise to different location and scaling parameters that can be close together, thereby indicating the limitations of first-order methods in some instances. As an independent development, our study also introduces novel combinatorial formulas for calculating moments of of the semi-circular distribution. Lastly, our work is accompanied by user-friendly software tools that can be useful for tackling related problems. In particular, our findings provide the basis for a more general conjecture concerning the limiting spectral distribution of matrices with independent entries, which we term the 'Big Block-Big Fourier' (BBBF) conjecture. The BBBF conjecture offers a highly refined description of the spectral distribution that is poised to significantly enrich our understanding of the spectral characteristics of various matrix models. As such, it merits further investigation and exploration. As an initial step in this endeavor, we offer several theoretical developments and analytical techniques that are both relevant to the BBBF conjecture and more broadly applicable to other related problems. As an instance, we confirm a key aspect of the BBBF conjecture concerning a specific type of matrix known as a Wigner matrix with non-zero entries. We believe that our study will not only contribute to a deeper understanding of the spectral characteristics of various matrix models but also provide novel insights and methods for analyzing related problems.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Notably, our analysis reveals that the diversity of time-dependent diffusion characteristics can be characterized through a single scalar quantity, effectively prioritizing their influence on the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. This finding is subsequently validated through simulation. We also derive conditions under which the population's distribution conforms to a specific pattern, such as a normal distribution or the Cauchy distribution, based on the properties of the individual particles that make up the population. Our theoretical findings are accompanied by numerical examples verifying our results through the simulation of relevant scenarios. These scenarios include a population of walkers where some individuals possess normal diffusion characteristics while others exhibit power-law diffusion, resulting in a population distribution that follows the Cauchy distribution. Additionally, we demonstrate that the diversity of the population's distribution can change over time by incorporating walkers that adopt non-standard diffusion methods, such as nonlinear diffusion, which generates a bimodal distribution. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between the diverse diffusion characteristics of individual particles and the resulting population distribution in complex systems. This understanding can be applied to analyze and predict the spatial distribution of populations consisting of particles that engage in non-standard diffusion. Our results also highlight the significance of considering the diversity of diffusion characteristics in each particle when analyzing the spatial distribution of populations, particularly in instances where the population's standard diffusion model is insufficient. Our approach is a crucial step towards developing a more general framework that can describe and predict the evolution of complex systems characterized by diverse diffusion processes. This framework has the potential to contribute to a deeper understanding of systems that defy standard description, such as those displaying subdiffusive or superdiffusive behavior. Our study focuses on the static aspects of the population's distribution, and future research can build on these findings to investigate dynamic aspects, such as the behavior of frontiers and the formation of stationary patterns within the population. This will provide a more comprehensive understanding of the relationships between individual characteristics, population distribution, and the dynamic behavior of complex systems. A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the framework being applicable across various geometries and modes. The general approach allows for a wide range of phenomena resulting from linear interactions, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity, such as mode coupling and phase modulation, to be analyzed. The developed theory is specifically utilized to investigate the nonlinear interactions within two dimensionless ring resonators, revealing how these interactions modify mode spectra and patterns of light within the resonators, and how they affect the amplitude and phase of modes at different frequencies. The study shows that linear coupling and scattering lead to mode mixing, while Kerr nonlinearity results in the creation of optical vortices and stable isolated waves, offering a possible explanation for the formation of isolated waves observed in resonators with spatial symmetry. The proposed theory and findings could contribute to the development of more precise and efficient computational methods for simulating mode interactions in optical resonators, ultimately informing the design of novel photonic devices and technologies. The general approach to the problem is also discussed in the context of existing numerical methods, with possible improvements and extensions being identified. The work lays the groundwork for further experimental and computational investigations, with potential applications in the development of novel photonic devices, phases, and materials, and could contribute to a deeper understanding of nonlinear interactions in isolated systems at the macroscopic and mesoscopic levels. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Additionally, it successfully handles tasks involving unseen classes and uncovers the underlying uncertainty distribution of the data. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. Additionally, our work offers a valuable resource for researchers to explore, as it's available as an open-source toolkit, encompassing both the environment and benchmark tasks. This comprehensive toolkit can be utilized as a key component in any evaluation setup and offers a range of flexible CONTINUUM-based composition options for customizing learning scenarios and curricula. Our work includes both a paper detailing our approach and a supplementary video showcasing the environment and associated results. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it against changing real processes to ensure its effectiveness and accuracy. Our approach and associated test data are available online. Despite existing approaches to process discovery, our is distinctive in utilizing DCR graphs and resulting models in a pure form, without presupposing specific process assumptions. Moreover, our method stands out for using event data without prerequisites, incorporating all occurrences within a process. Consequently, our approach is particularly suited to processes involving exceptions and varied behaviors. Furthermore, our algorithm is particularly effective with small to medium-sized processes in mind. However, larger processes might yield overfitting results and fail to generalize well. Furthermore, our approach is most effective with process variations occurring frequently rather than infrequently. Lastly, our method performs best with anomaly rates of around 30% or less. Although our algorithm is primarily designed for business processes, it could equally be applied to analyze workflows in computational biology. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. Specifically, it highlights how the compactification of moduli spaces, achieved via the minimal model program and algebraic geometry, is connected to the use of L^2 cohomology and Chern-Weil forms in Hodge theory. This connection is illustrated through the example of compact complex surfaces. Some previously known results in this context are reviewed, and further research directions are suggested, centered on extending this relationship to higher-dimensional algebraic varieties and discussing philosophical implications for algebraic geometry and Hodge theory. No new theorems are established in this brief overview. Ultimately, it aims to position the recently proven projectivity of moduli spaces of ample line bundles on surfaces within the broader context of the interplay between algebraic geometry and Hodge theory. This development is seen as an instance of how the minimality of a variety can be interpreted as a non-triviality condition on its L^2 cohomology, and how this non-triviality is sufficient to ensure the non-singularity of the variety. In this process, the role of the birational geometry of the variety is replaced by the topology induced from its Chow variety, and the resulting relationship between algebraic geometry and Hodge theory through the compactification of moduli spaces is seen as a fundamental aspect of the subject. Some previously known but less well-known results in this context are reviewed, and further research directions are suggested, centered on extending this relationship to higher-dimensional algebraic varieties and discussing philosophical implications for algebraic geometry and Hodge theory. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Furthermore, the characteristics required for the model to exhibit MMO behavior, and thus the required conditions for the population to exhibit MMO behavior, include a critical period of coexistence for the three species and the presence of a specific form of algebraic instability in the reduced model. The results of the analysis are verified through numerical simulation and used to interpret real-world data from a three-species ecosystem in the Serengeti ecosystem. The findings of the study highlight the difficulties associated with identifying early warning signals for a significant population shift in a dynamic ecosystem, especially one subject to rapid change, due to the prolonged duration of MMOs and the need for improved data analysis methods. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the value of multi-scale analysis, numerical experimentation, and the comparison of theoretical and empirical data in the study of dynamic ecosystems. It also highlights the need for the development of more effective algorithms to analyze complex biological systems. Lastly, the study suggests that the model presented could be adapted to investigate the dynamics of infectious diseases in a multi-level ecosystem. The extended version of the model presented in the study is now available on the Harvard Dataverse platform under the name 'EcoCOVID'. The 'EcoCOVID' model can be obtained from Harvard Dataverse with the identifier https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataverse/Eco

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit flattened SFR profiles. Notably, the SFR in bulges is correlated with the S\'ersic index, with a linear relation of $\Delta (SFR) = 0.062(2.0-n)$. This finding implies that the star formation rate in massive galaxies' bulges is an ongoing process, with a rate that decreases as the S\'ersic index increases. Consequently, the NUV$-r$ color of the central bulge contributes significantly to the shape of the mass-star formation rate relation, particularly in the massive galaxy regime. By comparing observations to predictions from a model of hierarchical galaxy formation, it became clear that the observed main sequence, including its flattened section at high masses, can arise from a cosmological simulation. However, removing the central bulge in simulations results in a main sequence with a less pronounced peak at massive ends. Therefore, the growth of bulges with increasing mass is the key factor causing the main sequence to level off at high mass ends. Overall, the findings of the study demonstrate the significant role that bulges play in the formation of star-forming galaxies and suggest that bulge growth is a crucial process in forming massive galaxies. Consequently, a significant portion of the gas in massive galaxies is consumed by bulge formation, with implications for unsolved puzzles in galaxy formation and evolution. Lastly, the study discovered that bulges with flat S\'ersic profiles are more likely to exhibit flattened SFR profiles, while those with sharp profiles are more likely to exhibit a more mature SFR profile. This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian. The findings show that zero-shot
learning yields the best results across both languages and setups, outperforming
the traditional supervised model on the test set for Slovene by 0.048 in
macro-F1 and 0.026 for Croatian. The model's performance on Croatian achieves the
best F1 score of 0.924 in zero-shot learning within the single-task setting. 
The inclusion of the Slovene dataset in zero-shot learning leads to a 0.073 
increase in macro-F1 on Croatian, while the opposite setup shows a 0.042 
increase in macro-F1 on Slovene. The paper also compares the model's performance
with a highly tuned system, achieving a higher F1 score of 0.931 on the test set
for Slovene in the few-shot learning setup. The source code is available at 
https://github.com/Jnous/Zero-Shot-Sentiment-Analysis. The dataset used in this
study is available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/GQdI6sU6s6t6. The paper's
results can be replicated by executing the zero-shot.py and few-shot.py scripts.

Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to previously unseen program behaviors and potential security vulnerabilities. In response to this threat, we are proposing a new approach to enhance the security of protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade. This protocol modification includes a novel cache coherence algorithm and a specific set of instructions to detect and mitigate memory reordering attacks from malicious programs. We also demonstrated the applicability and effectiveness of our solution to the SHARC processor. Furthermore, our study indicates that introducing security measures to protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade may result in acceptable performance overhead. We achieved this by minimizing the additional instructions required to detect memory reordering attacks and incorporating a simple detection mechanism with limited branch prediction resources. Our findings reveal that the performance impact of this security feature is minimal, resulting in less than 10% performance decrease compared to an insecure baseline. We also examined various workloads and found that our secure cache coherence protocol generates around 10 million instructions per second on a modern desktop computer. Consequently, we believe our solution can serve as a relevant security feature for single-issue, out-of-order processors that employ cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade. Moreover, our study provides valuable insights on the performance characteristics of our secure cache coherence protocol, which can be fine-tuned to minimize performance overhead while maintaining robust security. Additionally, we included a novel aspect in our research where programmers are given the option to develop programs securely, enabling multiple valid program versions that can coexist safely across different cache configurations. We also introduced an innovative approach to assigning different priority levels to program versions to prevent memory reordering attacks. However, integrating this feature would necessitate a significant redesign of processor architecture and programming models. Nonetheless, we still believe that our basic security feature concept is worth exploring and could be an useful point of reference for further research and development. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. Several benchmark tests have been conducted to evaluate the performance of the CAPP, revealing its ability to achieve speeds of up to 8.3 million searches per second and 1.4 GB/s data transfers. Furthermore, a Python-based CAPP API has been developed to streamline application development and is now available on GitHub. This API includes multiple utility functions and a command-line tool that showcases the CAPP's capabilities. Additionally, we have successfully run various CAPP-themed algorithms and applications, including flood fill, graph lookups, and data replication, and have distributed the code openly on GitHub. In addition, we have successfully adapted the CAPP to employ Michael-Scott non-blocking cache coherence algorithm, providing a working prototype that can handle up to four CAPP modules. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. This is manifested by an aligned major-axis of galaxies in relation to nearby filaments, presenting observational evidence of accretion streams on galaxy evolution. This is exhibited by massive, centrally-concentrated, star-forming galaxies in the later stage. This findings offer new insights into galaxy evolution processes, highlighting the impact of accretion streams, quenching, star-formation, and the construction of bulges, along with the influence of galaxy interactions on their evolution. We re-examine and revise the predictions of the Universal Texture Zero (UTZ) flavour model as initially presented in the study arXiv:1710.01741. The revision is made with reference to more accurate experimental restrictions and refined numerical analysis methods. Specifically, our team developed an in-house Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to extensively evaluate the viable parameter range of the UTZ model, encompassing primary and secondary contributions in its effective operator expansion. Furthermore, we obtained for the first time precise UTZ predictions for previously underdetermined CP-violating phases of lepton interactions, and related neutrino mass characterizing ratio observables, that could be probed via oscillations, beta decay, and cosmological processes. Consequently, our revised analysis significantly surpasses the initial analysis and confirms that the UTZ theory remains a coherent and compelling flavour theory. The findings also highlight the capability of robustly assessing multi-parameter flavour models with MCMC techniques. Nonetheless, the revised scenario still retains an irreconcilable discrepancy between theoretical predictions and the constraints imposed by the data, specifically regarding the UTZ value of the effective electron neutrino mass, which falls below the sensitivity limit of beta decay experiments by several orders of magnitude. Consequently, the most straightforward way to differentiate the UTZ theory from the sterile neutrino scenario through electron decay measurements appears unfeasible with any existing or near-term experiments. To disentangle or falsify the UTZ theory in comparison to the sterile neutrino model, future experiments should be capable of constraining the UTZ parameter space in a way that differently impacts these two theories. To facilitate further research on this topic, we outline the modifications required to the current implementation of the UTZ flavour model within the Effective Operator Expansion (EOE) framework. Moreover, we outline the modifications needed to evolve the parameters of this model within a numerical framework that considers the renormalisation group effects of the UTZ model. This evolution could provide a solid foundation for predicting flavour-related new physics signatures in the UTZ scenario at the next-generation particle colliders operating around the TeV energy scale. In this study, we exclusively explored the flavour sector of the UTZ model. Consequently, we did not investigate the renormalisation group effects on its parameters, instead assuming the UTZ dimensionless flavour predictions remain unaffected for our consideration. Nonetheless, investigating the influence of the UTZ parameter evolution on its flavour predictions in the face of the upcoming constraints from the LHC and future colliders will be an interesting topic for further research

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence. Modeling indicates that on November 7th, 2004, a substantial number of neutrons would have reached the surface, largely absent in previous events, and could have been detected with appropriate ground-based neutron detectors at lower elevations. Moreover, increased counts above background levels were observed in four out of five monitored counters, suggesting that further studies are needed to fully grasp the implications of this event's potential for ionizing radiation at lower elevations. In future events of a similar scale, researchers believe that appropriate ground-based detectors could provide valuable information about the interactions of high-energy neutrons with the atmosphere and surface, offering insights crucial for a deeper understanding of these complex phenomena. Moreover, such data could have significant implications for the protection of both aircraft and ground crews during intense solar proton events. As a result, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) plans to install neutron monitors at high elevations in Mexico and Bolivia as part of the Global Heliosphere Monitoring initiative. These detectors are now under development to accurately measure neutron decay protons, a key component of Energetic Particle Detectors previously tested in space. In conclusion, further analysis of November 7th, 2004, provides a crucial opportunity to investigate the behavior of high-energy neutrons at the surface of the Earth and could pave the way for a greater understanding of these events and their potential impact on both aircraft and ground crews. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 12 diverse data streams. The study was conducted using critical performance metrics including precision, recall, F1 score, mean absolute error, and average distance from inliers, with results showing our quantum-inspired method consistently performs at or near the top across all benchmark datasets and scenarios. The implementation of this research is available as part of the Quantum-Inspired Anomaly Detection framework on GitHub. Alongside the code, we include a comprehensive Anomaly Detection Toolbox featuring 12 established algorithms. Notably, our results were obtained without fine-tuning or hyperparameter tuning. Consequently, this could provide a valuable reference for those seeking to apply real-time anomaly detection in streaming data contexts. Furthermore, the study offers novel quantum-inspired algorithms amenable to offline settings. The research is further contextualized by an open discussion on key challenges and potential solutions for continuous real-time anomaly detection. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action taken has already provided implicit evidence accessible to the authorities. Instead of addressing this overarching goal, this paper introduces a framework that identifies specific actions where any implicit evidence effectively becomes a foregone conclusion. At its core, this framework places the onus on the government to prove it is not leveraging the respondent's compliance. Building upon this, we introduce 'demonstrability' as a central concept to describe actions compelled by the authorities. Moreover, we develop a language that discerns whether an action is as efficacious as the government's intended goal. Subsequently, we apply our framework to evaluate the compelled actability of several cryptographic tools, such as decryption, multifactor authentication, and hash functions, and arrive at a novel conclusion about compelled decryption. Contrary to existing consensus, we believe that compelled decryption does not necessarily entail compelled actability. This study presents a novel, high-order numerical method for solving the linear Fokker-Planck equation under a constant diffusion term. The devised method integrates elements from the Lagrange-Galerkin and semi-Lagrangian techniques, yielding an explicit, conservative, consistent, and robust scheme capable of handling substantial time step sizes. A convergence analysis for the exactly integrated Lagrange-Galerkin approach is provided, along with an implementable alternative that employs approximate integration. The method is particularly useful in modeling time-dependent mean field games systems, enabling high-order solution approximations. A key advantage of the proposed method is its high order despite being easy to realize with high-order Lagrange basis functions and explicit time-stepping. To verify the method's convergence and robustness, it was applied to two linear FP equations with analytical solutions. The efficient implementation of the method on a one-dimensional domain with smooth initial and boundary conditions is discussed, along with its evaluation on a range of time step sizes. The results demonstrate the method's capacity to effectively preserve initial conditions, achieve significant precision on moderate to large time step sizes, and converge to second-order accuracy. The method is then employed to solve a significant problem in time-dependent mean field games systems. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Nevertheless, this finding highlights the importance of closely monitoring a range of low to intermediate mass giant stars in the future. By doing so, we aim to identify additional stars with analogous internal rotation patterns and further understand the underlying processes shaping their internal structures. Through such discoveries, we hope to refine our comprehension of angular momentum management in giant stars and ultimately contribute to a greater understanding of the prescience of giant stars on planetary formation and evolution. 

This study is part of a larger project that employs stellar seismic data to study the internal rotation patterns of low to intermediate mass stars in their giant phases. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a significant obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming and impractical in real-world settings. To address this challenge, an end-to-end fake news detection system called MetaFEND has been proposed, allowing for the rapid learning to identify false information on unexpected events with limited information from verified sources. This system leverages the strength of both meta-learning and neural process methods, incorporates a module to address label embedding, and employs a hard attention mechanism to enhance the effectiveness by dealing with category information and eliminating unnecessary information. Experiments conducted on large multimedia datasets obtained from Twitter and Weibo demonstrate the effectiveness of the MetaFEND system in detecting false information on previously unseen events and outperforms the current state-of-the-art techniques. Moreover, the flexibility of this system enables the rapid adaptation to new events with limited labeled data, proving its practical feasibility in real-world scenarios. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. Finally, we examine the efficacy of first-come-first-served (FCFS) and last-come-first-served (LCFS) queueing disciplines on AoI distribution and mean value. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Further, a connection between GCA and binary Reed-Muller codes is explored and some interesting properties concerning GLA and GQA are revealed. Lastly, several examples and their corresponding properties are provided, offering additional insight into GCA constructs. 

Keywords: Golay complementary arrays, multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays, ring identities, binary Reed-Muller codes.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by conducting experiments on real patient data alongside a comparison with common image processing methods, revealing significant improvements in performance and precision. Additionally, experiments demonstrate the capability of Progressive BLS to generate diverse scenarios and increase the accuracy of therapy evaluation in various conditions. Ultimately, the study shows that Progressive BLS offers higher precision in evaluating the effectiveness of LITT treatment compared to standard approaches, delivering a more accurate definition of the treated brain area with lower entropy, minimal temperature increase, and no scarring. Consequently, Progressive BLS has the potential to contribute to improved LITT treatment outcomes and enhance the understanding of brain anatomy. The speed at which massive spectroscopic surveys collect data directly corresponds to the number of optical fibers used in each observation. This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Ultimately, the algorithm successfully coordinates astrobots in real-world applications with the SDSS-V. The astrobot coordination algorithm serves as an open-source tool available on GitHub, offering a Python implementation that can be adapted for other applications. The algorithm's code has been integrated into the BRICKS framework as the default method for coordinating astrobots in the SDSS-V. The algorithm has a high degree of modularity, allowing any modifications to cooperate with the base force-balancing algorithm. The current implementation covers all astrobots in the SDSS-V and includes various configuration files. The algorithm has over 1500 degrees of freedom in the SDSS-V and achieves complete convergence in a reasonable amount of time. The code has been optimized for performance, resulting in convergence times of less than 15 seconds for all astrobots in the SDSS-V. The algorithm's code is an early example of an artificial force metabolism algorithm in action, and its modular design makes it an open-source cooperative control code available for public use. The algorithm has been successfully applied to actual observations with the SDSS-V. The code has been used to coordinate astrobots in at least four successful proposals with the SDSS-V, winning funding from the NSF. The algorithm has been an essential component in securing funding for the SDSS-V's flagship proposal and has been instrumental in the development of the SDSS-V's concept. The code has been discussed in various meetings with the SDSS-V's directors and scientists. The algorithm has been presented in multiple conferences related to the field. The code has been recognized for its innovation and effectiveness by renowned experts in the field.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates and uninterpretable results due to the'selectivity effect', which selects only one variable from each group while disregarding the categorical structure. To address this, we propose a novel algorithm called CategLasso, which leverages an exclusive and hierarchical framework for categorical variables to achieve a linguistically meaningful sparse solution. By applying an exponential family formulation and a generalized Lasso penalty, CategLasso enables the identification of distinct categories and eliminates redundant variables. Moreover, we introduce a progressive strategy for categorizing variables of unknown type and establish the consistency of the estimated model under certain conditions. Moreover, we provide a suitable Q-Q plot for model assessment and include a computer code for the algorithm. Through simulations and real-data analysis, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over traditional approaches. Furthermore, we illustrate the challenge of variable selection in real-world applications due to the selectivity effect and highlight the significance of our results with an example from consumer behavior. Lastly, we emphasize the practical value of our results for linguistically oriented natural language processing tasks. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous tasks such as text classification, question answering, and generation. However, creating training data from structured knowledge stored in knowledge graphs proves to be more effective than using natural language sentences for the tasks that involve these graphs. This advantage comes from the ability to perform inference between entities and their relationships. Currently, methods that combine knowledge graphs with large language models typically rely on graph embeddings and treat entities and relations equally. These approaches typically produce fixed-size vector representations of the graphs in the embedding space and assume that all entities and relations have equal importance. In our work, we propose a novel method that uses multi-head attention in transformer-based architectures to process knowledge graphs. This allows our model to differentiate between entities and relations and to produce dynamic-sized vector representations of the graphs in the embedding space. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to three inference tasks - answering knowledge graph questions, link prediction, and identifying missing entities - and show that our results outperform existing graph embedding methods and the baselines that use only node information. Our results indicate that our method's performance is on par with the state-of-the-art approaches for the three tasks, with particular improvements in the low-data setting. We also analyze our method's performance from different angles and provide insights that could guide related research. Our code is available for use at https://github.com/ashish72/GraphAttentionTransformer. This article examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models, where interactions are limited to a finite distance $\delta$ and investigates how they are defined in a bounded area with various boundary conditions representing inhomogeneous data. The article compares their solutions with classical PDE models under specific localization limits, as well as how rescaled fractional kernels relate to inhomogeneous fractional boundary value problems. These discussions shed light on the challenges and issues that arise in nonlocal problems with inhomogeneous data within bounded domains. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Moreover, detailed analysis of factors influencing performance and methods without prior knowledge of focal lengths are also examined. The implemented algorithms have been made publicly available as part of the MIPANS library. The experimental findings are viewable in the paper's supplementary material along with further details about the implemented methods and results from the evaluation without prior knowledge of focal lengths. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. This outflow in turn may prevent mergers from forming massive galaxy clusters in the early stages of the universe. More observations are necessary to confirm these findings and better understand how active galaxies, including those with low to moderate infrared outputs, contribute to the outflow of gas across the universe. These findings are consistent with earlier results from our team using lower spatial resolution data and broaden our understanding of the interaction between galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas across various infrared outputs. The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. In particular, our results show that using the new interpolation function leads to lower errors compared to the traditional multivariate multiquadric when a proper value of weight 'c' is chosen. In cases with unstructured data, our method outperforms the multivariate multiquadric under appropriate conditions. It is observed that our method is susceptible to overshooting for large data sizes and when a large value of 'h' is used, suggesting that further improvements are necessary for these scenarios. Notably, our method consistently produces lower errors than the multivariate multiquadric for all tested data sets, even if the optimal value of 'c' is not achieved. In summary, the proposed new interpolation function offers an efficient alternative to the multivariate multiquadric, especially for small data sets and moderate distances. It is anticipated that this new interpolation function will contribute positively to the further development of quasi-interpolation methods. In particular, adapting this concept to other quasi-interpolation methods is deemed worthwhile. It would also be desirable to explore higher-dimensional applications of this new interpolation function. Ultimately, implementing this new interpolation function within widely available software packages such as MATLAB is seen as a feasible goal. It is hoped that this new interpolation function will be of interest to researchers in the field of approximation and interpolation. It is anticipated that it will be used to inspire further innovation, particularly in higher-dimensional settings. It is also believed that it has the potential to be a useful tool for scientists and engineers who rely on quasi-interpolation methods. It is further expected that it will be used to address challenging interpolation problems in various fields such as geoscience, engineering, economics, and biology. It is also hoped that it will be used to provide a more efficient and accurate alternative to the multivariate multiquadric. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. 
The unparalleled diversity of the dataset is achieved through the combination of images captured by multiple cameras at varying speeds and orientations, resulting in a distinctive set of images that accurately represent the driving experience.
A thorough evaluation of our method is conducted with several benchmark models and through experiments involving limited and real-world data. 
The outstanding performance of the RFS dataset is further highlighted by the minimal domain shift observed when applying the trained models to real-world data, demonstrating their potential as a starting point for further fine-tuning in real-world scenarios. 
The code and dataset are available online at https://github.com/anzb/RFS. 
Early versions of this work were presented at the 2020 IEEE Intelligent Vehicles Symposium and the 2021 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Additionally, comparisons with other convolutions-based models using the same number of parameters confirmed the DPCRN's superiority. Source code is available at https://github.com/JiaKaiWang/DPCRN.

A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts. The method provides a new approach to analyzing the fundamental properties of cluster halos and offers a promising tool for distinguishing between various cosmological models through forthcoming observations with future surveys like DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder, although more simulations are needed to improve precision. Additionally, this method may be applicable to other types of halo turn-around radii in different contexts. Nevertheless, distinguishing between $\Lambda$CDM and fR5+$0.06$eV cosmologies might be more challenging due to overlapping probability distributions at $>1\sigma$ confidence level for all the analyzed redshifts. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our study offers a comprehensive understanding of multipartite entanglement generation using the Jaynes-Cummings model. Moreover, this understanding could enhance the development of more complex, realistic models involving multiple Jaynes-Cummings interactions. This in turn, may facilitate the design of practical protocols for creating genuine multipartite entanglement in realistic scenarios. In such contexts, our analysis provides valuable guidelines for selecting suitable parameters and arrangements of JC-interactions. In broader terms, our study contributes to the ongoing research on using cavity-catalyed entanglement generation as a resource for other applications. This is particularly relevant given the Jaynes-Cummings model's widespread use as a standard description for interaction between light and matter in optical cavities. Our findings are applicable across various systems based on different quantum systems used, such as superconducting qubits, atomic setups, or optical cavities containing one or more atoms. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced. This new design incorporated a redesigned data processing system, integrated circuit for readout, and improved two-stage data compression. The prototype also introduced a new filtering approach called the Low Gain Avalanche Detector, integrated into the sensor layers. The LHC was operated at 450/650 TeV energy levels and 25/30 nanopsec bunch spacing during 2015/2016, and subsequently at 2.5/3.5 TeV and 25 nanoseconds at the outset of the shutdown. The data collected from the upgraded prototype were analyzed to assess its precision, specifically particle location accuracy and charge integration precision. The results showed location accuracy of 8.4/9.1 micrometers and charge precision of 1172/1465 electrons. The implementation of the new design elements was successful in meeting the requirements for the upgraded CMS tracker set to debut with the LHC at 300 GeV in 2026. Furthermore, the improvements will be integral to the future experiments at the LHC with upgraded detectors. The development of the forward pixel detector prototype has been detailed, and its evolution discussed in the context of its potential to drive significant progress in the development of future LHC experiments. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. We
concluded that the commonly used Stancing AI dataset is not a representative sample of
the emotions expressed on Twitter. To validate our findings, we conducted two experiments.
First, a simple sentiment analysis model was trained using the combined dataset and tested
against the annotators' classifications. The model's performance varied depending on the dataset
used for training, with the most accurate results obtained when trained with the combined
dataset. Second, a more complex experiment involved using the model to analyze the sentiment
expressed towards listed companies' Twitter accounts. We found that the model performed best
when trained with the combined dataset, outperforming a baseline model trained with the
Stancing AI dataset alone. Our findings can be applied to improve the accuracy of social
media monitoring and sentiment analysis. Additionally, we contribute a newly created
dataset that can be utilized for initializing and fine-tuning pre-trained language models
for the task of Twitter sentiment analysis. This project's code and dataset are available for
download at https://github.com/rahulpujari/Twitter- Sentiment-Analysis. Our paper's findings
can be viewed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.02226.

We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Our study indicates that shadow radius can serve as an indicator for understanding thermodynamic phase transitions in black holes from the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills gravity framework. Ultimately, our findings could contribute to a deeper comprehension of black hole physics through optical observations, or observations of black hole shadows. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd. Our paper has been accepted for publication in CVPR 2022.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph~$G$ comprises a selection of vertices~$S$, which allows for the coverage of the remaining vertices in~$G$, by establishing unique shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in~$S$. The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. This study introduces the Strong Geodetic Recognition problem (SGR), which requires identifying if a specific vertex subset~$S$ within a graph~$G$ constitutes a strong geodetic subset. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized in imitation learning to speed up the learning process. We show that using these suboptimal paths enables imitation learning to learn a policy more quickly than if it only used the small set of high-quality expert examples in isolation. This is because the information from the suboptimal paths is incorporated through an auxiliary task that is learned using a different loss function, allowing the policy to benefit from the added data while maintaining its performance on expert examples. We evaluate our approach on multiple systems and demonstrate that speeding up imitation learning is possible when there's a vast amount of suboptimal data available. Moreover, when the suboptimal data is extremely limited, our approach is comparable to the baseline method that is only trained with expert examples alone. Nonetheless, when the amount of suboptimal data becomes quite large, our method may suffer from noise and bias, leading to decreased performance. Nonetheless, we observe that this issue can be mitigated by utilizing a different loss function or different optimization methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. The code for this research is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/ghulamali/CoImitationLearning.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that using our proposed metric function, medium to high-rate PAC codes can achieve error-correct performance near that of the SC-list decoder for polar codes, with a list size of 16 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost. In particular, the computation complexity of a 1024-bit code with a rate of $4/5$ under search-limited PAC decoding is approximately $10^{11}$ computations, which is comparable to the computation complexity of a 1024-bit polar code with a code length of 1024, a code rate of $4/5$, a list size of 16, and a CRC length of 11, under search-limited polar decoding, which is approximately $10^{12}$ computations. Hence, our results indicate that PAC codes have potential as a simple and efficient alternative to polar codes. Moreover, the proposed metric function can be applied to the efficient decoding of conventional convolutional codes, particularly in scenarios where code memory and computational resources are limited. Lastly, our results validate the effectiveness of the proposed metric function in reducing PAC code decoder computations across multiple code lengths and rates.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy. Notably, our approach distinguishes itself from traditional approaches relying on fiducial markers by eliminating the need for alignment, optical character recognition, and marker detection, thus streamlining the process and eliminating sources of error. Additionally, our method does not require expertise in opencv or other computer vision libraries and can be easily integrated with end-effector design to create a fully functional product ready for real-world deployment.
