The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. Conversely, we've also seen that users' intentional behavior alone is insufficient to fully account for the degree of online polarization observed. Consequently, we propose that users' unconscious biases play a crucial role in polarization's amplification. Notably, we've discovered that users' browsing habits are influenced not just by their deliberate actions but also by the online environment itself. To better understand these complex dynamics, we've developed a simplified framework for reference. Lastly, we believe our research holds significant value in guiding the development of strategies to mitigate online polarization.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size. This analysis establishes a higher lower bound than the previously known exponential lower bound for solving V's word problem via a Turing machine with a onetime read of the input. Additionally, we demonstrate that the context of this investigation can be broadened to incorporate various variants of Thompson's groups, and that our findings regarding the time complexity of solving V's word problem are not limited to its core form. Our research also leads to an investigation of the context of (bracket) systems, a framework initially introduced by Chomsky, and we identify a crucial distinction between system identities and the context-free languages they generate. Lastly, our study paves the way for further exploration into the computational properties of Thompson's groups through the lens of context-free systems. because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment. 
This discovery is consistent with the view that information flows rather than 
energy flows in open systems. In addition, we were able to direct the flow of 
photons between different locations by managing the phase of the driving field. 
Notably, we were able to replicate the characteristics of a system in a true laboratory 
setting using a fake laboratory represented by the matrix of the system's Hamiltonian. 
This breakthrough paves the way for the development of innovative, adiabatic 
techniques for controlling the non-equilibrium steady state in open quantum systems.

non-equilibrium steady state.

While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems. Our work also establishes a connection between the density of subsets in base p/q systems and the density of their counterparts in integer systems. Lastly, our research provides an example showing that when p is sufficiently large in relation to q, the base p/q system exhibits considerable density, enabling the recognition of essentially all subsets in (Np/q)d. Our paper also presents a method for converting base p/q systems to integer systems and leverages this to solve non-uniform decision problems in base p/q systems. This is accomplished by converting the base p/q system to its equivalent integer system and then solving the problem in the integer system. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. Influenced by these observations, this study proposes Edge-Gated CNNs (EG-CNNs), an easily integrable module that complements standard encoder-decoder networks, capable of processing edge and texture information simultaneously. By prioritizing edge extraction and incorporating an auxiliary supervision, the EG-CNN module refines its output and merges it with original network predictions. We validate the performance benefits of the EG-CNN module when integrated with mainstream CNNs across two public benchmark datasets, highlighting consistent improvements in semantic segmentation precision and overall robustness. Moreover, the egated architecture demonstrates superior scalability and consistency when tested with additional public datasets. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. As such, we were able to identify previously unrecognized properties of these protocols, including conflict detection and retry behavior. Our work is relevant to any application using MongoDB transactions, as it provides a clear understanding of the underlying transaction protocols, consistency guarantees, and implied properties, which can be utilized for further research in database protocols. Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019). Further, we connect this result to the enumeration of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three and detail the underlying statistics contributing to the resulting expressions. Moreover, we identify the combinatorial representation underlying the $e$-positivity of an even stronger class, encompassing all Dyck paths with bounce number three, although in this case, the associated Schur functions sum to a single $s_{(1,1,1,1)}$. Lastly, we discuss implications for a broader class of monomials within the elementary symmetric function basis.

However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets. Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Furthermore, our findings highlight the potential of our framework to guide the selection of unbiased training datasets, ultimately enabling the development of more reliable and generalizable medical image analysis models. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. This finding implies that spin-based networks, resembling those found in neural connections, are capable of complex behavior arising directly from their triangular structure, without the necessity of intrinsic randomness. Lastly, a clear distinction between two different noise patterns was observed, and their relationship with the network's assembly dynamics was demonstrated. This theoretical investigation could provide a foundation for analyzing noisy patterns observed in hysteresis loops in neural networks and clarifying the effects of different stimulation protocols. In practice, this could ultimately lead to more accurate clinical assessments in the diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases. In conclusion, this study offers an original framework for analyzing geometrically intricate systems, defining a novel set of rules that govern the dynamics of spin-based networks and featuring an unusual noise pattern that is an irreversible byproduct of the network's internal workings. This discovery paves the way for a deeper exploration of these systems in neural networks and encourages a multidisciplinary investigation of complex networks in neuroscience, physics, and neuroscience. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on data from six different instruments, combining them to get a comprehensive picture of solar wind characteristics including energy, density, and particle speed. Our data showed a clear pattern where energy flux increased as you moved closer to the sun, up to about 1.5 times the average value as you approach the solar surface, or about 100 times the energy released by a typical solar flare. Nothing like this has been seen before in such close observations of the sun, and it challenges our current understanding of solar wind behavior and how it's influenced by the solar magnetic field. Further study of data from even closer approaches to the sun, which much of this data is based on, may hold even bigger surprises, and could ultimately help us figure out the source and characteristics of the solar wind. Finally, we found evidence that big whirlpool-shaped regions, known as magnetic nulls, play a major role in the structure and behavior of solar wind plasma, particularly as you get closer to the solar surface, and that they may hold the key to understanding the entire solar wind. Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through further analysis and data refinement. The approach is shown
to yield meaningful estimates for flight times in various scenarios, and the code
is openly accessible under an permissive license. The project is part of the EU's
flying-high project and is openly accessible on GitHub under an permissive license.

Notably, our results uncover the critical velocities at which acoustic emissions originate from irreversible work and the onset of stick-slip motion. The techniques developed here open up fresh avenues for scientific research, offering the potential to uncover the intricate nonlinear dynamics governing other systems' behavior through acoustic emission analysis. In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, was consistently found to be around the/electron temperature and BCS gap size, and was found to depend on the area of the junction, with smaller areas requiring higher threshold temperatures. SQUID loops demonstrated a more substantial temperature range before reaching T*, yet ultimately reached the same threshold at very small areas. Our theoretical model suggests that T* is governed by minimum unit capacitance in Josephson junctions, and in SQUIDs, it is determined by the loop area and the interloop tunnel coupling. These findings provide valuable insights into the quantum coherence of planar Josephson devices at high temperatures near T*.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Finally, this research is relevant to the broader field of derivative pricing, which continues to evolve with emerging technologies like high-performance computing and machine learning, and can provide valuable insights for both practitioners and regulators in the financial industry. By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators. Ultimately, our investigation paves the way for tackling more intricate material structures. We also explore a scalar example featuring an increasingly thin periodic subdomain to demonstrate that the limit functional may not be absolutely continuous with respect to the original energy functional. Lastly, we establish that incorporating material non-autointeraction leads to the appearance of a boundary integral term within the limit functional. This conceptual framework has far-reaching potential for applications in electromagnetism and elasticity. We also propose an alternative formulation utilizing volume constraints, along with a related homogenization problem involving periodically embedded solids. We then discuss an additional application in phase transition models within nonlinear elasticity, even in the absence of rotational diffeomorphisms. We conclude by outlining an existence result for a related double well energy model. This study was initially motivated by an exchange with Antonio Savato.

We undertook a statistical investigation into the tidal features of early-type galaxies with high stellar masses. Our study utilized the STRONGLENS-10K sample, which comprises approximately 10,000 strong lenses constructed from the CFHTLenS and EDGES datasets. These strong lenses were identified through a systematic analysis of 10,880 galaxy mass maps, and our research focused on 2,635 massive early-type galaxies for which tidal features analysis was feasible. Our findings showed that about 27% of tidal features have a flux fraction greater than 1%, and their average radius is approximately 22.6 kpc, which is roughly 0.53 times the effective radius of the associated galaxies. The orientation of these tidal features spans the range from 0.12 to 0.84 radians, and they are more commonly aligned with the major axes of the galaxies. Our results indicate that a substantial proportion of massive early-type galaxies with prominent tidal features have undergone mergers with smaller companion galaxies. These tidal features are retained in the galaxies over extended periods, consistent with recent numerical simulations of hierarchical galaxy formation. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. Finally, we discuss how our model may be applied to analyze real-world scenarios, such as education systems and social networks, and consider potential directions for further research in this area. Despite its simplicity, the model possesses features that can contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between socioeconomical mobility and the passage of time. The proposed model also finds applications in forecasting and evaluating public policies in various societal contexts. In conclusion, assigning priority to lower socioeconomical situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings is beneficial to maximize long-term payoffs. However, accurately modeling these laser systems using CPA and NLO is a complex task due to their interconnected linear and nonlinear processes, and the high variability in available modeling frameworks. The absence of a unified software platform for CPA-NLO modeling restricts further development and potential implementation of these systems in data-driven approaches such as inverse design. We introduce a modular software model that encompasses various amplifier configurations and nonlinear techniques to provide time and frequency-resolved electromagnetic field data and essential physical properties, enabling characteristics of energy, fluence, and spectral distribution. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The results from the 2016 and 2018 data highlighted significant shifts in horizontal and vertical beam sizes at the level of individual bunches at the maximum design luminosity spots, amounting to around 7-8 $\sigma_x$ and 2-3 $\sigma_y$. The data further revealed significant long-range beam-beam induced shake of the low-luminosity bunches at 29 RHIC-like equivalent luminosity spots. The analysis of 2018 data revealed a notable decrease in the size of the (10,10) bunch in the horizontal direction at the design maximum luminosity spot, likely caused by the increased long-range beam-beam effect on this bunch in 2018. The results from the 2018 data also indicated the need for an additional corrector kick in the train to correct for the increased long-range beam-beam effect on the (10,10) bunch. The implementation of this correction in 2018 resulted in the desired beamspot size at the design maximum luminosity spot. The results from the 2018 data, featuring the additional corrector kick and resulting beamspot size, will be incorporated into the final beam-based optimization strategy for the CMS experiment at the LHC in 2022. The study highlights the significance of the emittance scans in providing critical insights into beam behavior and closed orbits, ultimately enabling the development of sophisticated beam-based optimization strategies to maximize the effectiveness of physics runs. The TRAIN code's capabilities to accurately predict long-range beam-beam effects at various luminosity levels have been validated by the measurements, and this study emphasizes the code's value in informing beam-based optimization decisions. The success of this study serves as a model for the implementation of emittance scans in other particle physics experiments in the future. The approach developed at the LHC can be applied to future colliders, such as the Future Circular Collider, where emittance scans will play a crucial role in developing beam-based optimization strategies to deliver the maximum scientific payload. This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study. Compared to existing approaches, our proposed method is more resilient to adverse conditions and able to handle larger losses in communication. The characteristics of the algorithm make it suitable for time-critical optimization problems in collaborative filtering and matrix factorization. The code for the proposed algorithm and associated experiments is available online. This research is part of a larger project that aims to develop reliable and efficient algorithms for cooperative tasks involving untrustworthy agents. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques.'s4cmb' can be run in a cloud environment, either interactively for quick tests or in a distributed mode with large data sets, and features a simple and efficient command-line interface for user convenience. This approach represents a significant improvement over previous approaches, such as CMBSim, due to its superior performance, flexibility, and precision, with's4cmb' exhibiting up to 10 times faster data generation rates depending on the specific use case. This development is crucial for the design and optimisation of future experiments, such as the CMB-S4, which will consist of 152 antennas across four configurations, and is set to begin data collection in 2029. The's4cmb' package is openly available under the Apache 2.0 license at the https://github.com/cmb4all/s4cmb repository. The code has been publicly released to facilitate collaboration and to encourage other researchers to contribute to its development, especially in areas such as increased realism, more sophisticated instrumental models and cloud-based simulations, and is ready for use in future CMB experiments, such as the Planck Legacy Surveyor and the Simbol-X survey, among others. The paper also includes several examples of's4cmb''s capabilities, such as generating simulated data that mimics actual data collected by the S4's demonstrator instrument, incorporating scan patterns and instrumental systematic effects, and comparing's4cmb''s performance with other cosmic microwave background data simulators, such as four-dimensional Fourier transform and Nside-based approaches. In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that its performance is largely attributed to its utilization of part-of-speech tags, syntactic dependencies, and semantic roles. Furthermore, we introduce a method to incorporate the BART's order preferences, resulting in a simpler approach that surpasses the current state-of-the-art baseline in three out of four evaluation metrics on the WiC dataset. Our proposed method's results also demonstrate a strong correlation with the order preferences derived from BART, with a coefficient of determination (R^2) of 0.76 in the case of easy questions. Additionally, we find easy questions to exhibit a more linear order and to have a smaller distribution shift compared to the whole WiC dataset, which facilitates larger-scale ordering tasks in the future. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/wic-ordering. Prior work on ordering words has been conducted under the assumption that the input words constitute a coherent text, without examining the case where words originate from distinct sections of a document, including articles with removed headings. Intuitively, this scenario appears amenable to the proposed approach, given the significant structural differences often present in documents. Consequently, we introduce two new datasets consisting of articles with deleted headings, where the task is to restore the original order, together with a simple evaluation metric that is highly correlated with human judgments. Lastly, our results indicate that simply ordering words based on their part-of-speech tags or syntactic dependencies can lead to baselines that outperform the current state-of-the-art models on easy questions, with our proposed approach producing order preferences that correlate with BART's ordering preferences at a rate of determination of 0.76 in easy questions. The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Furthermore, the MD-CSDNetwork exhibits superior robustness against resolution changes and real-world variations without the need for additional fine-tuning. With minimal custom training required, our system delivers impressive performance, achieving a classification accuracy of over 75% across all videos in the FaceForeniscs++ benchmark. The code for the MD-CSDNetwork has been made publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/huburtan/MD-CSDNetwork. Despite its high performance, we stress that no detection method can guarantee 100% accuracy and that the only definitive way to confirm the authenticity of visual content is through human evaluation. Consequently, our code is intended to facilitate the development of high-performance deepfake detection methods, rather than their deployment in real-world settings without human oversight.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs. However, at higher degree correlations, LDPC code performance significantly deteriorates. In contrast, LDPC codes exhibiting strong positive degree-degree correlations can still maintain respectable error tolerances, albeit inferior to those achieved with negligible correlations. We also establish design guidelines for LDPC codes featuring degree-degree correlations and provide unequal error protection designs outperforming their degree-degree uncorrelated counterparts. In particular, we demonstrate that correlation designs can provide a fourfold improvement in error tolerance for specific protection configurations. Lastly, we propose two new construction methods for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC codes and highlight several key features and advantages of these approaches. As an additional finding, we show that LDPC codes featuring strong positive degree-degree correlations can serve as effective tools for error detection, potentially surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art error-correcting codes like polar codes. In conclusion, our research reveals the performance benefits of degree-degree correlated LDPC codes and presents novel construction methods enabling the generation of highly performant unequal error protection codes. These designs may find useful applications in various communication systems, particularly those with correlated user endpoints, such as correlated sources or correlated sensor readings in sensor networks. To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources. Furthermore, we explore key technological enablers and set out a roadmap for the design of highly efficient, adaptive, and resilient future MNs. These networks will be capable of managing the complexities of modern applications, providing seamless connectivity, and guaranteeing optimal performance, security, and quality of experience for all users. Lastly, we highlight the critical research challenges and potential opportunities for further investigation in this field.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Additionally, it demonstrates that this framework allows for the integration of Euclidean space structure onto certain metric spaces equipped with an angle function. The article also introduces the notion of orthogonality and demonstrates that it is compatible with the revised angle function definition. Finally, it offers an example showing that the introduction of the property of betweenness is necessary for its integrated structure with orthogonality and angle function. The article also presents an interesting distinction between the metric space structure and the Euclidean space structure through the concept of angle function and the properties of hyperbolic metric geometry. Lastly, it presents an interesting problem concerning the embedding of spaces with an angle function into the structure of Euclidean spaces. This problem could provide valuable insights into the focus of researchers on the topic of metric geometry. This article is dedicated to the memory of K. Menger. It is part of mathematician V. Jovanovic's doctoral research, supervised by mathematician S. Kikkawa. Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Notably, our findings imply that in fields of degree 8 or higher, there are infinitely many isomorphism classes of orders with a specific minima pattern, namely $\lambda_1^2\ll\lambda_2$, and offer a prime number theory interpretation of Lagrange's left-over theorem. Additionally, we describe the structure of orders with extended divisibility properties related to their minima and identify infinitely many families of number fields with particular inequality structures in their orders, thereby extending our earlier work in this area. Our methods draw from combinatorial design theory, Galois theory, discriminant bounds, and field construction techniques. Moreover, our results provide answers to several of Lenstra's open questions. 

This work is part of the author's PhD thesis, supervised by Richard Kaye.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that backscattering between opposing modes at the contact locations is present. The result shows that neutral modes hold relevant information and can be used for a nonlocal reconstruction of a dc charge current. The described protocol may be employed to detect any neutral mode that counter-propagates with respect to charge modes, and this detection approach is applicable not only to the edge modes of quantum Hall systems but also to systems possessing neutral modes that do not originate from quantum Hall effects. Finally, an experimental demonstration of this concept is proposed. The study presented here builds on previous work that showed the ability to measure the counter-propagating mode in quantum Hall systems using nonlocal measurements. The findings have implications for the development of scalable, nonlocal quantum interferometry. The discussion is concluded by addressing potential techniques to enhance the visibility of the counter-propagating mode in future experiments. In our research paper, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by taking into account the changes in data distribution. By incorporating the Kullback-Liebler penalty into the robust min-max optimization framework, we transform the problem into an efficiently solvable form and propose a robust decentralized optimization method, specifically DR-DSGD, based on the Decentralized Stochastic Gradient Descent (DSGD). Under specific conditions and a sufficiently large regularization parameter, we analytically prove that our algorithm achieves a rate of convergence of $\mathcal{O}\left(1/\sqrt{KT} + K/T\right)$. Furthermore, experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of DR-DSGD, yielding an improvement of up to $10\%$ in test accuracy over various data distributions. DR-DSGD exhibits greater communication efficiency, with reduced communication rounds by up to $20$, compared to traditional DSGD, while also ensuring fairness across decentralized devices. Our findings highlight the advantages of DR-DSGD in scenarios involving shift data distributions. The code for this research is available online at https://github.com/lingyin87/DR-DSGD. Our paper includes additional related work on distributionally robust learning and decentralized optimization, along with key assumptions and theoretical proofs for DR-DSGD. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, our findings reveal how the Forsage scheme operates, how it evolved to circumvent mechanisms designed to limit its growth, and how it was capable of moving funds between users with seemingly unlimited capacity. Furthermore, our study identifies several security vulnerabilities that enabled the scheme's success and allowed the scheme to maintain control over the majority of its funds until the present day. Our research also provides a unique perspective on the Forsage scheme's place within the broader context of blockchain-based multi-level marketing initiatives. Due to the visibility granted by the scheme's blockchain implementation and its unprecedented scale, our study offers a previously unattainable glimpse into the inner workings of a pyramid scheme, one of the most enduring and dangerous types of investment scams. Forsage has been designed as a blockchain-based multi-level marketing project and was launched in April 2020 by Sergey and Kate Shutenko. It has been promoted extensively on YouTube and has attracted over 300,000 participants from nearly 150 countries, with users investing nearly $300 million in the scheme. In return, Forsage has paid out roughly $340 million to its top participants, with the majority of user investments being lost. Our analysis of the scheme has been conducted with the code and transaction records available up to block height 8,500,000 and date May 2022. Our research has been independently verified by security researchers and blockchain analysts. Due to legal concerns related to the scheme, our study focuses exclusively on Forsage's technology and transactions, without mentioning individuals or groups that have been defrauded by the scheme. Our analysis intends to contribute to the existing body of research on pyramid schemes, multi-level marketing, blockchains, and cryptocurrency, with our findings offering a previously unattainable empirical examination of one of these schemes

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We included a list of suggested research priorities for the remaining potential globular clusters within the galaxy's bulge based on proximity to the galaxy's plane, freedom from heavy elements, and movement through space. Ultimately, we expect at least 20 to 30 globular clusters within the galaxy's bulge based on density and movement patterns, which would bring the total number of galaxy bulge clusters to at least 60 to 70 when including those found outside heavy element regions.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two instances: silicon around a gap and a semiconductor with a band gap manipulated through elemental doping. The effectiveness of the two approaches is assessed based on the correlation between their energy diagrams and those obtained from first-principle simulations, taking into consideration the impact of wave function localization, size of the supercell, and method of calculation for the Wannier functions. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise representation of energy levels, especially when the Wannier functions are poorly localized, whereas the velocity-based model is more accurate when the Wannier functions are well localized and the associated energy levels are far removed from the conduction band of the pure material. Notably, when the band structure of the doped material is considered, both methods provide a comparable level of precision. The outcomes of this analysis are highly relevant to the development of efficient and reliable tight-binding models for doped semiconductors, where both the band structure and wave function localization need to be accurately captured to achieve meaningful insights. The methodology described herein can be applied to any instance of light-matter interaction, enabling the identification of optimal tight-binding parameters that faithfully replicate the behavior of ab initio simulations. In this particular case, we utilized a range of Wannier function localization factors and sizes of finite supercells, all of which are commonly encountered in the simulation of doped semiconductors, thereby providing a set of TB models that can be made freely available for download at the corresponding author's webpage. In doing so, researchers will be able to compare their own results with those obtained using these well-established TB models, thereby facilitating a more precise validation of their own simulation methods. In addition, this study includes a detailed comparison of two alternative approaches for calculating the dipole-based TB models, both of which result in distinct energy diagrams and demonstrate a level of robustness that can be employed with confidence in any light-matter interaction scenario. Ultimately, this analysis offers a much-needed framework for evaluating and improving the precision of TB models derived from first-principle

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's also advisable to establish results with strong baselines like simple
Multi-layer Perceptron. Moreover, our findings suggest that deep learning can
be an effective choice for predicting process event characteristics and times of
occurrence but also highlight the necessity for thorough and rigorous testing. 
Our experiments, research findings and data are openly available to facilitate
progress in predictive process-modeling through public experimentation and feedback. 
This initiative is an early step towards developing a community for process
learning that is open, transparent and collaborative. 
All data, implementations, along with further analysis can be found at
https://github.com/jiashu-zhang/Predictive-Process-Model.git.

Leveraging these formulas, we simulate quasiparticle RPA phonons within prolate rotating nuclei and investigate shape-coexistence phenomena, particularly focusing on the mixing of intrinsic ground states and low-lying collective vibrations in $^{192}$Pb. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Furthermore, our findings can also inform practitioners on key factors to consider when choosing clustering algorithms for time-dependent systems, such as velocity's impact on algorithm performance and the occurrence of artifacts caused by dense flow lines. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. The ability of these representations to encode key sentence elements is further highlighted by their performance in auxiliary sentence encoding tasks, showcasing the generality of the representations generated by the SparseGAN model. These results suggest that our approach not only facilitates efficient and accurate adversarial text generation but also provides valuable sentence representations with inherent semantic meaning. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Nonetheless, no adjustment in bias due to variable selection in capture-recapture models was observed.  Ultimately, our method allows wildlife researchers to investigate two significant questions--how animals utilize space and how they utilize resources--through a unified framework, incorporating different data sources, including capture data from varied sources and telemetry data, with potential applications in multidisciplinary studies combining biological and environmental data.  We also provide a publicly accessible software package that incorporates these methods, giving users multiple analysis options, including model selection and parameter estimation through Markov Chain Monte Carlo.  We showcase this software by applying it to a real-world data set, offering users easy-to-execute code along with data and model files.  This research is part of a larger study investigating the ecology and management of a declining jaguar population in Mexico, a region facing numerous environmental challenges posed by human activities, deforestation, and ecosystem alterations, with data collected prior to the COVID pandemic using a comprehensive field research approach. Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that enables the detection of multiple states within a single time series. By implementing a distinctive structure for model weights and constructing an appropriate likelihood function, HiP-RSSMs was able to effectively learn multiple states and their associations. Through various experiments, HiP-RSSMs demonstrated superior performance compared to conventional state-space models and alternative methods for multi-state analysis. By recognizing the underlying structure as a mixture of weibull distributions, HiP-RSSMs also provided valuable insights into data quality and system stability. The code for this project is publicly available on HiP-RSSMs.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best performance following normalization. Our research lays the groundwork for a thorough evaluation and comparison of different structural polarization measurement methods. Additionally, we constructed a suite of artificial networks to facilitate empirical evaluations in the future. Long-term goals encompass integrating temporal network data and exploring methods for identifying polarized groups in social systems. The code and additional data are available at https://github.com/kevmiller/polarization_measurements. Our analysis was featured in an upcoming book on social network analysis edited by Stanley Wasserman.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we can investigate the stability of these solutions by analyzing the reduced system and obtaining insights into the multilayer system's Jacobian. Our method is adaptable to different interlayer node connections. Ultimately, our research enables the exploration of multilayer networks through simplified representations, facilitating a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics underlying these systems. As such, we hope this approach inspires further innovations in the analysis of multilayer networks.

This paper develops an inverse method to recover the full Cauchy stress operator from its compatibility conditions, using only one of its components. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once modified, the code can be tested again to verify the effectiveness of the change. Our approach also enables several advanced features, including automated generation of test cases and a visual display of the causes of errors in a way that is navigable. This verification and testing process is efficient because it leverages the capabilities of modern computers to perform operations that could take days or weeks just a few years ago in a relatively short period. Our research includes an evaluation of several sample programs to measure the performance of this integrated verification and testing process. The results show that this approach works effectively across different programming languages and can locate and fix even complex errors efficiently. Moreover, our method achieves a level of reliability where a mistake is either correctly identified and fixed, or further analysis is needed to determine the next steps, in a single iteration of the verification and testing cycle. This is because the chances of missing a real error or fixing a non-existent one are so low that they can be considered virtually nonexistent. Additionally, our method allows us to reduce the time and effort required to complete each stage of software development, making it possible to deliver working versions of software more quickly. Finally, our technique enables us to measure and compare the dependability of software by counting the number of errors found and fixed during development. This approach also opens up possibilities for new computer science research areas, such as the visualization of program proofs and the automatic detection of software reuse opportunities. Furthermore, our method could be adapted for use in other fields, such as the analysis of scientific data and the verification of hardware components. Ultimately, our goal is to create a comprehensive integrated verification and testing tool that can be employed by software developers to produce reliable and dependable software, and by doing so, contributes to the advancement of computer science research in this domain. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency. Through thorough experimentation on diverse models and benchmarks, such as the GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks for BERT, HyperPrompt has consistently outperformed prominent multi-task learning approaches like Prompt-Tuning, HyperFormer++ and T5. The code for HyperPrompt is openly accessible on GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt. The official repository for HyperPrompt also contains additional details about HyperPrompt's HyperNetwork architecture, experiments, and findings.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The algorithm's design and analysis are comprehensive, involving an overview of the why-and-how of its construction, an examination of potential attacks and their circumventions, and a detailed explanation of the algorithm's fundamentals. Additionally, our discussion encompasses an examination of related topics. Our work offers an innovative approach to addressing the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse, complex network's size in the presence of unknown nodes. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations, and we delve into potential applications, including community detection, rumor spreading, and network localization. Lastly, we outline directions for further research and possible adaptations of the algorithm in various networks. Our algorithm is made publicly available to facilitate replication of our results and exploration of related open questions. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Notably, this method also enables a direct link between spacetime conformal connections and the extrinsic curvature of spatial slices, facilitating new insights into the dynamics of gravitational waves. Overall, this approach offers a more controllable and versatile framework for constructing initial data in numerical relativity simulations.

The search for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ decays utilizing $pp$ collision data collected by LHCb, at centre-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV and an accumulated luminosity of 3 $fb^{-1}$, yields 4 standard deviation excess beyond predicted background counts with no noticeable features found in dimuon invariant mass spectra. Upper limits on the branching ratio of $\Sigma^+ $ decay to a dimuon pair are set, ranging from $4.3 \times 10^{-8}$ to $6.5 \times 10^{-8}$, depending on resonance width, significantly tightening the existing upper limit by a factor of over 40. Under similar analysis conditions, upper limits on the $\Lambda \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ branching ratio are tightened to $4.0 \times 10^{-8}$, a 25 times lower limit than the previous upper limit. Both results contribute to a deeper understanding of the $\Sigma^+$ and $\Lambda$ systems. Moreover, with an accumulated luminosity of $13$ $fb^{-1}$ at 7 and 8 TeV centre-of-mass energies, an upper limit on the $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ branching ratio is set at $2.0 \times 10^{-8}$. This excess, observed in 2012 data below $p_K^* = 1.8$, remains unexplained. Further study is needed to fully elucidate its nature. Upgraded LHCb sensitivity, coupled with future experiments, will be crucial in resolving this anomaly. Until then, it remains a intriguing phenomenon in the field of hadron physics. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate significant variations in the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials when varying temperature and material thickness. Notably, we observed an inverse proportionality between the anomalous Hall conductivity and conductivity, which implies that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is influenced by the spatial thermal gradient distribution and electron scattering at the sample surface. Consequently, our study provides a theoretical framework for understanding the surface-induced spin-dependent thermal transport in magnetic materials, which is crucial for designing high-performance spintronic devices. Moreover, this research paves the way for a comprehensive investigation of the spin-dependent thermal transport phenomena in various materials and structures, which is essential for a deeper understanding of the underlying physics and successful development of such devices. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Source code is available at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/PTE/tree/PILE.

Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time use in conjunction with measurements. Despite these developments, users without machine learning expertise often face significant barriers to integrating this technology into their experiments. To overcome these obstacles, this work presents several examples of machine learning models designed for real-time analysis across multiple beamlines at the National Synchrotron Light Source II (NSLS-II), with a focus on incorporating them into existing workflows to enable easy integration into experiments. By leveraging this framework, users can easily combine machine learning models with their existing workflows via the Bluesky Suite for data management and experimental orchestration. As a result, this approach enables users to perform real-time data analysis during experiments and make informed decisions to modify measurements in real-time. This technique is being demonstrated across four beamlines at NSLS-II, offering several machine learning models for various measurements, including X-ray scattering, spectroscopy, diffraction, and microscopy. By doing so, this framework provides researchers with powerful tools to unlock the full potential of their measurements, improving data quality and enabling more precise and faster scientific discoveries. Furthermore, this work highlights the benefits and challenges of integrating machine learning into user facilities and showcases the path to wider adoption at synchrotron light sources. By presenting this work, we hope to inspire a broader collaboration among the machine learning and scientific communities at these facilities, facilitating faster, more precise, and more inclusive research. Finally, this project is part of the Machine Learning for Accelerated Science initiative at NSLS-II and is available on GitHub under the Bluesky Suite repository.

Notably, we address subquadratic growth conditions on the function $f$, i.e., where $f(x,\xi)\approx a(x)|\xi|^p$ and $1<p<2$ and map $a$ also belongs to a Sobolev space, where $\Omega$ and $x,\xi\in \Omega$.
