A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, we demonstrate that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods, a consequence stemming from block-diagonalization and symmetry-related crossing during QA. Nevertheless, we find that adding a specific decoherence process can facilitate successful ground-state achievement for these problematic cases, a phenomenon attributed to environmental interference disrupting symmetry in quantum systems. This counterintuitive outcome yields profound insights into the fundamental workings of quantum annealing. Moreover, our research offers environmental setups that can demonstrate successful ground-state achievement despite undergoing quantum annealing processes. In addition, we identify the conditions under which quantum annealing successfully reaches the target ground state within both closed and open system scenarios. Furthermore, our research reveals that certain environmental setups can enhance quantum annealing success rates, a finding with significant implications for the development of more effective and reliable quantum annealing protocols.

This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his lack of exploration into the broader implications of his findings, potentially stemming from limited creativity or vision. Throughout nearly his entire directorate, van Rhijn struggled to secure additional funding due to severe challenges including the 1930s Depression, the Second World War and its aftermath, his personal health issues during the 1940s, the lab's distant location, and a governmentally favored infrastructure in Leiden. Lastly, the circumstances that led to Adriaan Blaauw accepting the position of director in 1957, setting in motion the revitalization of the lab, are analyzed in the latter half of this study. Alongside a more detailed account of the appointments of the three directors following van Rhijn, this essay concludes with some personal reflections on the state of the lab in 2000, 43 years after the revitalization, and offers a forward-looking perspective on its future prospects. This research is an extension of my 2000 thesis titled 'De ontwikkeling van de Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory tot de komst van Adriaan Blaauw (1921-1957)' which was an requirement for my MA in History of Science at the University of Utrecht. Although my 2000 thesis included an extensive bibliography it has been left out of this essay due to its online availability at the UWRAC website. Furthermore this essay has been written as a result of my ongoing involvement with the KAP as a volunteer and as part-time communications officer. It has been acknowledged by the board of the KAP but it has not been peer-reviewed by academic historians of science. It is available online at the UWRAC website. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. We demonstrate that this method not only converges to an optimal solution, but also facilitates structural optimization. The proposed method also significantly reduces training time and decreases the memory usage per machine. The code is openly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/Local-critic-training. The project also includes example use cases for image classification using ResNet-20 and sentence classification using LSTM. The results show that our method achieves a 15% faster convergence rate with a 25% smaller memory footprint on a machine with 8 GPUs, compared to the baseline MPC method. Furthermore, local critic training enables structural optimization, as evident from the 0.8% improvement in test accuracy for the Cifar-10 dataset without additional data. The project also introduces EasyMP, an efficient model-parallel training framework that is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/hjdw2/EasyMP. This algorithm excels in environments where there is only limited, high-noise data from ongoing experiments. It achieves exceptional results by making the most of various types of secondary information about the dynamics, such as basic physical laws and the system's general properties. The algorithm essentially finds the best possible solution to an optimization problem by gradually refining a dynamic system model that incorporates unknown components. This model is based on streaming data from ongoing experiments. The algorithm uses a method to predict all the possible system outcomes and establish a theoretical limit on its performance when the actual dynamics are known. The algorithm's effectiveness is confirmed by simulations on advanced flight simulator and video game-like environments, and the experiments demonstrate comparable performance to machine learning algorithms that are trained over vast datasets. Notably, the method outperforms existing techniques combining dynamic system modeling and optimal control methods in the tested scenarios. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on the ability of university students to keep up with the pace of instruction in a physics course. Focusing on the varying effects of remote learning on diverse demographic groups, data was collected from online learning modules in the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters. Three indicators measured students' ability to stay on track: module submission rate, extra credit module submission rate, and engagement level with modules. Four demographic variables were analyzed - Gender, Ethnicity, Transfer Status, and First-generation status - and students were categorized into two groups based on each variable. Comparative analyses between each pair of demographic groups within the same semester, and between groups across semesters, were conducted to identify significant differences in student performance. In addition, exam and course scores in Fall 2020 were compared against those of the Fall 2019 semester, and against demographics groups. Findings showed that remote learning led to a decline in on-time and early module submission rates among first-generation students, but resulted in increased early submission rates among transfer students. Under-represented minority students demonstrated enhanced engagement with modules, while non-URM students exhibited similar levels of engagement before and during the pandemic. These outcomes highlight the varying effects of remote learning on students from different demographic backgrounds and underscore the importance of adaptable instructional designs that cater to the unique needs of a diverse higher-education student population. Moreover, these findings can inform the development of more effective instructional strategies to mitigate potential negative consequences of online learning for certain demographic groups. In the current study, first-generation students were defined as those whose parents did not complete a higher education level; however, it is crucial to acknowledge that this definition is merely one of many possible categorizations and may not fully capture the complexities of this demographic group's experiences. Ultimately, this investigation emphasizes the value of Adaptable Design-Based Research in addressing the unique learning needs of a diverse student body, particularly in the context of online learning environments. truths. We have devised a user-friendly axiomatic system, dubbed BZFC, by adapting
the ZFC-axioms to the parameters of a four-valued logic in a systematic manner.
Our key innovation involves the anti-classicality axiom, asserting the existence
of non-classical sets, with the unexpected outcome that the existence of a single
non-classical set allows for the generation of a wide array of non-classical sets.
Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the relationship between our proposed system
BZFC and classical ZFC, demonstrating that the two logics exhibit bidirectional
interpretability. We also demonstrate an interesting application concerning Tarski
semantics by showing how the traditional definition of the satisfaction relation
faithfully represents the non-classical properties inherent in our proposed meta-theory. 
Ultimately, our findings underscore the geometric interpretation of intensional
truth-finite models, leading to an original formulation of the Georgescu-Tarski
conjecture in the context of the new system. 
This innovative approach to set theory is made accessible to a broader audience
by employing the FDE-lens, a user-friendly notation for four-valued logics. We
also explore potential connections with other paracomplete and paraconsistent theories. 
Our proposed system BZFC is available online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/1903.02803.pdf. 
We invite comments and feedback from experts in the field. 
Keywords: set theory, paracomplete logic, paraconsistent logic, non-classical
sets, intensional truth-finite models, Tarski semantics, FDE-lens.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. A video illustration of this approach can be found at https://youtu.be/ies8s3sQ4qk. Findings from this study were validated through repeated trials with multiple participants and demonstrated the feasibility of developing a BCI that could accurately and safely operate modern prosthetic devices for walking. In future work, the research will focus on adapting this system for use in individuals with spinal cord injuries. This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions. Implementing this methodology, we developed a Python package called HS2, which is now freely available on GitHub.

If a right-angled Artin group acting minimally on a tree that is not a line has a non-trivial action, we prove that its graph $\Gamma$ contains a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree. Additionally, if the tree is not a tree of diameter 2, we demonstrate that this component's underlying graph is connected to all other components in $\Gamma$. Furthermore, we establish that the right-angled Artin group with graph $\Gamma$ has a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree if and only if its graph $\Gamma$ has no isolated vertices. Moreover, we show that the graph $\Gamma$ has a connected component whose subgroup acts transitively on an edge of the tree if and only if the right-angled Artin group with graph $\Gamma$ has a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree of diameter 2. Lastly, we provide a condition under which a right-angled Artin group with a graph that contains an component whose underlying graph is a star, has a non-trivial, minimal action on a tree. This condition can be described in terms of the vertex labels within that star component. 

This research is inspired by the work of Bestvest, Forester, and Minster on right-angled Artin groups acting on trees. Our investigation is also motivated by the graph theory queries of F. J. McGetton. 

Keywords: Right-angled Artin groups, group actions on trees, graph theory.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. We expect DECENNT to contribute to further research in dynamic graph modeling and its applications in multiple disciplines. The code is now available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/aichler/DECENNT.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. To facilitate accurate phylogeny reconstruction, various stochastic processes have been developed to generate random phylogenetic trees or networks, which can be used to validate results or inform Bayesian analysis. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a range of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks as a function of the number of reticulations present. The comparative assessment is conducted across four distinct reticulation types and encompasses a comprehensive examination of three network generators. Moreover, two additional network analysis tools are employed to further compare the generated networks on a broader scale. Our exhaustive investigation yields novel insights into the properties of phylogenetic networks generated through statistical processes, which can contribute meaningfully to further research and development in this field. Notwithstanding the comparative analysis, we also explore the topological characteristics of the generated networks in relation to the underlying reticulation processes. Additionally, we highlight key aspects that need to be considered in the design of network generators, including the impact of different reticulation types and the influence of input trees. To facilitate easy access to the compared network generators, we have created a comprehensive dataset that is freely available for download at https://github.com/AmitDixit1/ComparingPhylogeneticNetworkGenerators. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. The developed algorithm has significant potential to contribute to various computer vision applications such as wildlife monitoring, healthcare, security, and industrial processes. The code for the proposed approach is available online at https://github.com/aalexondz/biolocomotion_detection. The dataset created for this research can be found at https://deepmind.github.io/biolocomotion_dataset/. The code for the alternative approach is available online at https://github.com/aalexondz/biolocomotion_detection/tree/master/alt_method. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. A notable benefit of NN is its minimal additional memory usage per GPU, making it suitable for large-scale linear system solving and matrix inversion within a single GPU framework. A Python implementation of NN is provided, along with three explicit matrix inversion applications to demonstrate its effectiveness. The code has been successfully run on a single NVIDIA V100 16GB GPU. The software used for the experiments can be found at https://github.com/zheng0625/Nested-Neumann. The benefits of NN include its low memory usage, high order convergence, and efficient implementation on a single GPU. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our predictions can be verified using atomic or photonic systems with site-dependent disorder.

This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. Various approaches are utilized to derive and compare curve invariants, including the Feynman parameter method, lightcone parameters, and Baikov parameters in both their comprehensive and incremental forms. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research is grounded in the context of harmonic sums that underlie the sunset integrals and Elliott Box Feynman integrals. The analysis also offers a geometric explanation for the isogeny relationship between curves in genus one, providing a broader computational framework for genus zero and one Feynman geometry. The study concludes with an examination of the elliptic double-box Feynman integral in terms of its geometric components, including isogenies, elliptic K3 surfaces, and genus one curves. The research is set to contribute to the ongoing discussion on computational methods' inherent properties within physics. The investigation is supported by diverse computational tools, including Wolfram Mathematica, Singular, and Magma. The associated data has been openly available since May 2023 at https://doi.org/10.48543/xwq_jezW9d. The study is further backed by two companion studies, one on the elliptic double-box integral in $d=6$ and another on the hyperelliptic curve of the double-box integral in $d=7$. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The implementation is available for download at [1]. The code can be utilized to compute the threshold expansion of the physical $\mathcal{CP}$-even and $\mathcal{CP}$-odd light and heavy Higgs boson masses in the complex MSSM, with inputs following the constraints of the effective renormalizable theory defined at the scale of the SUSY scale $\sim \mathcal{O}(1)$ TeV. The discussion also addresses the distinction between on-shell and threshold masses for the neutral Higgs bosons, with a numerical comparison demonstrating their equivalence within the desired precision for the parameters of interest. The code has been admitted to the parton level tools collection of the $\texttt{SCET}$ workshop on QCD [2]. For further information, please contact A. Pich. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance. Implementation of the test is achieved through an R package, providing users with an accessible quasi-score linearity test. This includes functionality for both fixed and increasing network dimensions, as well as associated p-value calculation methods. The package is available on GitHub. In conclusion, the proposed quasi-score linearity test offers an effective approach for evaluating linearity in network autoregressive models, complementing the current literature. Full details of the test's implementation and associated results can be found in the accompanying technical appendix. The R package and technical appendix are available at https://github.com/ycyong9/quasilinity. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. The accompanying code has been made freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/xiangning/yu2023deepdeclarative networks. The associated repository comprises Python implementations utilizing the Jax library for the declarative networks discussed in this research. In addition, we have incorporated examples illustrating how to utilize these Declarative Network functions within training loops and experiments. The code enables the reproduction of the results presented in this research, including the evaluations of robust vector pooling and optimal transport. The code has been made available under the permissive BSD-3 license for the benefit of the broader research community. The innovative use of optimal transport in deep declarative networks was inspired by an earlier concept first introduced in the 2019 paper by Solomon and Weinstein. The conceptual efficiency of optimal transport in deep declarative networks was further developed and refined in an earlier research paper co-authored by the present study's first author. The associated code for this earlier research has been made freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/xiangning/2019_ot_deeplearning. The code has since undergone significant revisions to accommodate the new developments and computational optimizations discussed in this research. The revised code is fully compatible with the extensions and modifications highlighted in this research. The code has been successfully tested with both TensorFlow 2 and PyTorch. Nevertheless, the current implementation is exclusively based on the Jax library. Any contributions to further enhance the computational performance or broaden the applicability of this code are welcome and may be contributed back to the research community through the GitHub repository. A cell's behavior during spreading and movement is influenced by various interrelated events that are activated by external stimuli at different scales. Due to the cell's living nature and complex response mechanisms, it is not sufficient to apply traditional material mechanics principles to it. Rather, cells comprise constituents with repeatable reactions such as contractility in single fibers and actin networks but also exhibit non-deterministic reorganization upon external stimuli. With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. We will prioritize the development of a mechanistic approach, focusing on illustrative two-dimensional simulations of membrane protein interactions, fiber contractility in cytosol, and actin network reorganization. Our proposed method offers a coherent framework for incorporating various cellular constituent behaviors and reacting to external stimuli, thus providing valuable insights for tackling more intricate challenges in cellular dynamics. We hope this framework will spark further development for applications in three dimensions and in even more complex cellular systems. We have publicly shared the code for our single-filament solver and the associated reaction dynamics solver on our GitHub repository. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transfers. Notably, our approach is versatile and adaptable to other cryptocurrency blockchains with suitable modifications tailored to the characteristics of the underlying cryptocurrency. By leveraging our feature set, which includes unique attributes of cryptocurrency transactions like sender-receiver relationships, transaction amounts, and weights, we are able to differentiate them from regular transactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing our temporal cyclic transfer discoveries with existing databases of known malicious activities. In conclusion, our innovative money trail analysis provides an effective solution for identifying unknown malicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains, revealing hidden patterns in temporal transaction graphs that can be applied across various cryptocurrency platforms. By showcasing our methods on the Ethereum blockchain, we are able to uncover two novel cyclic transfer scenarios not previously documented. Additionally, our study highlights the pressing need for greater cybersecurity among users of these platforms and urges the development of more secure transaction protocols to prevent the exploitation of vulnerabilities in blockchain technology. Lastly, we recommend that cryptocurrency exchanges and platforms implement real-time analysis of transaction graphs, combined with offline data analysis, to detect and prevent malicious activities before they occur. By taking this integrated approach, we can proactively mitigate the evolution of new cyberattacks within cryptocurrency blockchains. Ultimately, our study provides a foundational framework for a secure cryptocurrency ecosystem, one that prioritizes the development of more secure transaction protocols to prevent the exploitation of weaknesses in blockchain technology. As such, we hope this research will inspire the community to adopt these methods and contribute to the ongoing discussion of these challenges. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Furthermore, we showed that these deepQ learning decoders could learn general noise patterns that transfer to new, unseen environments. In contrast, traditional decoders perform suboptimally in these situations. While we do not claim these solutions represent the optimal decoding method, they do offer valuable insights into combining deep reinforcement learning with quantum information theory. Moreover, they are available online for public use at [URL] for the community to explore and extend. Leveraging these decoders, we also found that multiple decoders can learn unique noise patterns that correlate with specific physical systems, raising the possibility that they might distinguish different quantum systems based on fault-tolerant quantum dynamics rather than initial states. This could provide a new approach to quantum system identification. With further development, these efficient decoding approaches might also find applications in other code scenarios, such as the Bargen code, enabling the exploration of larger codes in the near term. Ultimately, integrating deepQ learning into the quantum computing cycle could facilitate a more adaptive approach to quantum error correction, promoting a co-evolution between learning decoders and developing new codes that can handle diverse noise environments. This could prove crucial for the success of large-scale quantum computing projects in the long term. While we already have basic decoders online, we invite the community to collaborate and expand on this research. More information about this work and how to get involved can be found at [URL]. Another approach is offered by quantum jump metrology, a method that extracts information by continuously monitoring an open quantum system and inducing correlations with the assistance of quantum feedback control. This method is utilised to study the measurement of relative phases in optical systems consisting of two interconnected cavities, and controlled by quantum feedback from laser pulses. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. The excess's magnitude at the largest angles and lowest hadron $p_T$ values is $\sim$1.5 times the $p$$+$$p$ yield. These results provide evidence that the medium created in Au$+$Au collisions interacts with hadrons, potentially influencing their formation, and offer insights into the interplay between hadron formation and medium interaction for various direct photon sources. Additionally, these data may hold implications for the development of models that aim to reconcile direct photon and hadron data within the same collision system.

Over time, the trend of companies adopting remote working has been on the rise, leading many to adapt Agile methodologies such as Scrum to cope with distributed teams. However, the global shift to fully remote working brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic was a unprecedented phenomenon. This research involves a two-phase, multi-method approach. Initially, it investigates how working from home affected Scrum practitioners through a qualitative survey. Subsequently, it proposes and empirically tests a theoretical framework using PLS-SEM with data from a sample of 200 software engineers who collaborated on Scrum projects from home. Our results demonstrate the reliability of all key constructs and the validity of all hypotheses, while also highlighting the advantages of combining home working and Scrum practices through an IPMA analysis. Notably, supporting employees' inherent needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness is crucial in the remote working context. Our findings indicate that both home working and Scrum use contribute to project success, with Scrum playing a mediating role. Furthermore, home working and Scrum use are interdependent, with Scrum relying on certain home working conditions to function effectively. In addition, our results show that home working and Scrum use jointly contribute to project success, with Scrum acting as a success accelerator under home working conditions. Our research offers several recommendations for practitioners, including adopting Scrum and taking steps to support employees' psychological needs in the remote working context. Ultimately, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of how to combine home working and Scrum use, and highlights the importance of successful project management in the distributed Scrum context. Our findings are set to spark further research in this evolving field. Our study is built on data collected between 2020 and 2021, a period of significant change and growth for software development companies. Consequently, our results are highly relevant to professionals working from home with Scrum teams during the COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath. Our study provides a theoretical framework that is both novel and comprehensive in the context of distributed Scrum projects. Our approach involves combining earlier Scrum theory with the principles underlying home working, and incorporating the relatedness need from Self-Determination Theory. Our framework comprises eight constructs, including four key variables and four moderators, which are all empirically validated through PLS-SEM with a sample of 200 software engineers. Our study involves a pioneering use of IPMA analysis in the Scrum context, which offers a fresh perspective on combining home working and Scrum practices. Our approach may serve as a point of departure for further research

Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Various particle types exhibit distinct radial flow patterns that complicate their differentiation through event-shape selection.  Models simulating nuclear matter development, specifically idealized viscous fluid dynamics and PYTHIA, are compared to our data, revealing that while they replicate basic event-shape selection patterns, they fail to fully capture the complexity of our observations.  An adjustment to the initial condition correlation observed in our data is proposed.  Events with the same average flow but varying elliptic flow are found to have initial conditions that, when compared, reveal a higher than expected elliptic flow for a given initial condition condition among more steeper distributed events.  This discovery, born from our data, sheds light on the event-shape selection's impact on the elliptic flow coefficient in nuclear collisions.  A deeper understanding of this relationship could provide valuable insights into nuclear matter development.  Furthermore, our study sets the groundwork for exploring other event-shape selection effects in various particle types and multiplicity distributions.  Ultimately, this could lead to new constraints on models simulating nuclear collisions.  Additionally, we analyze our data with the goal of identifying potential biases that could influence results on particle types with low yields, such as anti-protons and D-mesons.  To do this, we use two methods: first, events are separated into two groups with varying average flow but similar centrality; second, events are organized into two groups based on transverse particle density, resulting in outcomes that, while not entirely unbiased, allow for a clearer distinction between particle types.  Ultimately, our study provides a foundation for further research into nuclear matter development, particularly events with higher particle densities, and sets the stage for comparisons with models that simulate nuclear collisions.  Finally, our analysis of events with varied average flow has broad applications, enabling a more intricate comparison of model outcomes with our data, and shedding light on the complex development of nuclear matter in collisions.  Our research also paves the way for additional studies, such as a closer examination of radial flow patterns

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Furthermore, our results for a highly turbulent case with larger particles indicated that our algorithm could enhance the accuracy of simulations. We concluded that our multiple-time-step integration algorithm is an efficient and accurate method for simulating complex sediment transport with numerous particles, and can be an valuable tool for other multi-scale fluid-particle simulations. Additionally, this algorithm has been made publicly available on GitHub for the community to use and contribute to.

A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached a height of 14.9cm, a distance short of the desired height due to energetic losses. To validate the feasibility of the DEM model, a one-legged robot with a 10cm tall leg was built and tested on the actual soft ground represented in the simulation. While the robot jumped 8.8cm high, the results indicated that the discrepancies between the desired trajectory and the actual trajectory could be attributed to the failure of the RFT to account for the robot's foot dynamics, in addition to energetic losses during hopping. To improve the robot's performance, modifying the model of ground reaction forces or enhancing the feedback controller is seen as necessary steps. This groundbreaking research lays the groundwork for developing more sophisticated controllers and better models of ground reaction forces, ultimately paving the way for robots to efficiently navigate various types of deformable terrain. In this project, several valuable lessons were learned that can be applied to more complex multi-legged robots, allowing them to fully utilize their additional degrees of freedom and maximize their performance when moving on soft ground. In doing so, they may be capable of propelling themselves at speeds rivaled by the fastest animals. In this research, a one-legged hopping robot was used as a fundamental base for this investigation, offering an uncluttered environment to focus solely on the interplay between the robot, ground

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In contrast, simpler models like BERT-based CONDAQA achieved a mere 25% accuracy, highlighting the extensive gap that needs to be bridged through further research. Our CONDAQA dataset is now publicly accessible at this link https://github.com/huggingface/datasets/tree/fe9c6e8d8d9fd14e8d3d5d3d4f2c5f1f/hf-iter/condaqa. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. When assessed against three evaluation metrics, our method consistently outperforms all major competitors, including several widely-used topic modeling approaches. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the derived hierarchies can inform and direct users in an interactive information system, as shown by user feedback in our experiment. Our code is freely available online.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. Notably, the dynamics of quench and annealing exhibit a universal connection that transcends the specific Hamiltonian at hand, thereby implying that similar strategies could be applicable across a broad spectrum of discrete optimization tasks. Furthermore, real-world neural network training can be viewed as a quantum annealing process, and its performance may be enhanced via the proposed protocols, without necessitating a deeper comprehension of the underlying Hamiltonian. In this context, the most significant achievement of this study is the development of a new neural network that learns from a quench, rather than annealing, dynamics, resulting in exceptional overall performance being attained. When confronted with instances of the exact cover problem, even when they are highly complex, this new network consistently exhibits optimal solution-finding efficiency, outperforming not just the conventional teacher-student protocol, but also any known generalization technique, across all conceivable scenario combinations, including up to 20 random target covers among 20 options, and over four distinct neural network training sizes. The source code for the developed models is available at https://github.com/strmerg/qannealing-nn.

A crucial aspect investigated is how to accurately determine alignment-based conformance measures for incomplete process runs. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
This study demonstrates how varying the screening within this infinite layered
nickelate series can result in a range of one-band or two-band models, with
parameters shifting in accordance with the electron count in the series. 
Therefore, to comprehensively understand nickelates, it is necessary to
consider the screening effects within this infinite series for a thorough
understanding, rather than drawing conclusions based on isolated examples alone. 
Our study is then further substantiated through comparisons with existing
experimental and theoretical studies.

effort be directed towards the 4$u.f.$ case with weak correlations to uncover
the self-doped, insulating, and isolated $d_{x^2-y^2}$-only chain running through
the nickelate series.

layered nickelate series using the most reliable two-band model and to

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption, with numerous countries enforcing strict lockdowns and millions of lives affected. In an effort to cope with the emotional impact, people are increasingly expressing their sentiments on social networks, utilizing microblogging platforms as a means of seeking comfort. Twitter has emerged as a prime platform for exchanging ideas, with users posting diverse sentiments aimed at promoting awareness about staying home and maintaining social distancing. However, there is a growing concern regarding the dissemination of fake news that aims to frighten people, emphasizing the need to differentiate between positive, negative, and neutral thoughts to effectively disseminate beneficial opinions to a wider audience. Consequently, identifying and interpreting the context of large datasets on Twitter has become a significant challenge. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of Twitter data using various machine learning algorithms was conducted to evaluate sentiment, and subsequent context learning of the dataset based on sentiment was explored. Our research utilized a range of 0.92 to 0.95 accuracy levels for sentiment classification, demonstrating the efficacy of different machine learning models including Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and Multinomial Naive Bayes. Furthermore, context learning of the dataset was successfully achieved with an F-score of 0.79, indicating that there is a strong correlation between context and feature learning. Our research offers a novel approach to context learning of large datasets from limited annotated data, facilitating easier understanding of large datasets in low-dimensional space. Additionally, context learning was successfully applied to a real-world scenario, namely the COVID-19 pandemic, aiming to ease the dissemination of beneficial opinions to a wider audience. As a result, we propose a Context Aware Sentiment Analysis Framework, incorporating a flexible context-aware scheme that caters to diverse applications and context types. The proposed framework is particularly useful in addressing challenges related to big data analytics, deep learning, social media, and machine learning. All the implemented algorithms as well as the related data are freely accessible at https://github.com/rahmanajih/Context-Aware-Sentiment-Analysis. Consequently, we hope that our research will motivate further context-aware sentiment analysis in big datasets, offering numerous applications in various domains. As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties. Furthermore, this could lead to Rees-Irvine processes occurring in hybrid stars, resulting in dust formation when massive stars with quark cores undergo supernovae explosions. The established Tai mapping between two trees $T_1$ and $T_2$ is a unique one-to-one correlation of their nodes that maintains the ancestral hierarchy. However, determining the maximum-weight Tai mapping between two unordered trees is a well-known NP-complete problem. We now introduce a contrasting concept - anti Tai mapping - as a binary relationship between two trees. An anti Tai mapping, defined as the subset $M$ of $V_1\times V_2$, excludes any node pairs $(x,y)$ and $(x',y')$ that would conflict with each other's ancestral hierarchy, given that $x<x'$ indicates $x$ is an ancestor of $x'$. Calculating the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping plays a significant role in solving the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem through integer programming by applying the cutting plane method. We provide an efficient algorithm for computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one tree is a path. Additionally, we show that by applying a restricted version of anti Tai mapping, where nodes sharing the same path as their ancestors must not correspond, we can obtain a polynomially computable lower bound for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between any two trees. We also present an efficient algorithm for solving this restricted version directly on unordered trees within $O(|V_1|^2|V_2|^2)$ time. Finally, we exclude the possibility of computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping in the same time complexity by showing that such an algorithm would imply an efficient solution to the maximum-weight Tai mapping problem via counterexample. Consequently, this leads to a $0$-1 integer programming application of computing a maximum-weight anti Tai mapping when one input tree is a path, demonstrating further value in solving general maximum-weight Tai mapping problems via integer programming methods. We highlight the challenges and opportunities for research related to the broader field of tree correspondence and its connection to 0-1 integer programming. We conclude by outlining potential future research directions within this domain. We offer our computed results and related data for the maximum-weight anti Tai mapping between trees in a publicly accessible repository for reference and further exploration. We hope that our new concept of anti Tai mapping will contribute meaningfully to the field of tree correspondence and encourage collaborative research efforts. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. With dust development playing a key role in VSI's behavior, future observations of protoplanetary disks should prioritize studying dust development and its interactions with VSI-driven turbulence. Additionally, dust development may impact other disk processes, such as photochemical reactions and disk accretion, and should be given more research attention. While dust development's effects on VSI are complex and need further study, it is clear that it has significant implications for our understanding of protoplanetary disk systems.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Our proof draws from an earlier strategy employed by the second author, although our approach includes distinct components such as a new technique for establishing a maximum principle and a new approach to applying Liouville's theorem. Notably, our method also confirms that harmonic functions with sublinear growth can be represented as a finite linear combination of soliton functions. Moreover, this result can be extended to harmonic maps into a manifold of the same dimension. We have also obtained a new estimate measuring the size of harmonic maps when the target manifold has a non-negative Ricci curvature. This estimate is expressed in terms of the square of the distance from the harmonic map to its minimal connection with a unit volume. Finally, our results can be applied to establish nonexistence of ground state harmonic maps from a manifold of constant positive scalar curvature to a manifold of the same dimension with nonnegative Ricci curvature. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied how variations in $\gamma$ affect parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analyzing these variations, we determined their effect on the measurement error of a specific target, a high-mass brown dwarf, once Gaia's performance is optimized. Additionally, we examined how variations in $\gamma$ affect the measurement error for a range of absolute magnitudes and spectral types. Computational simulations allowed us to verify our analytical predictions and understand how variations in $\gamma$ influence the measurement error in different astronomical contexts. In such a case, understanding how variations in $\gamma$ affect astrometric measurements could become crucial for tackling the challenges posed by gravitational physics in the next decade. We have developed an efficient approach for condensing complex systems into their fundamental behaviors using their primary underlying features. By leveraging observed data, we pinpoint a low-dimensional structure that characterizes the systems' gradual evolution and generate an extremely simple representation of the systems' dynamics within that structure. Building on the SSMLearn algorithm, which applies implicit optimization to fit a system's underlying structure to available data and simplifies the systems' dynamics, we have created two more direct methods that transform the process into explicit problems under specific assumptions. These algorithms demonstrate the ability to create precise and highly simplified models for complex systems on both numerical and real-world datasets, significantly reducing the computational time. Moreover, our results show that our methods can produce systems with stable and predictable behaviors, enabling the generation of valuable knowledge for related systems without explicit data. This knowledge can take the form of systems underlying structures that generalize across multiple conditional statements, providing a foundation for exploring new ideas and identifying new features. Ultimately, our work provides an opportunity to address fundamental questions regarding the learning of simplified complex systems.

This technique is particularly practical in finite-domain settings and significantly simplifies computations in domain divisions, rendering previous, more complicated approaches unnecessary. Our team employed photonic technology to revolutionize the conventional method of spectroscopy, enabling on-device spectral cross-correlation using a template spectrum. This was achieved by designing photonic devices with intricately modulated transmission spectra, thus performing cross-correlation without the need for dispersion. Consequently, our device simplifies the apparatus while reducing its overall cost, enabling precise detection of atomic/molecular substances as well as accurate radial velocity measurements of astrophysical objects.

We outline two innovative design approaches based on distinct photonic platforms, silicon and fibre-based photonics. Silicon-based photonic technology incorporates thermally modulated ring resonators for spectral cross-correlation, whereas fibre-based photonics utilize strain-modulated customized fibre Bragg gratings. Both approaches successfully detected molecular gas in a laboratory setting and are currently undergoing field testing.

Furthermore, our research has far-reaching implications as these photonic devices may pave the way for developing low-cost, custom-built spectrographic instruments capable of simultaneously analyzing multiple objects or providing high-resolution field spectra. This technology has immense potential to contribute to groundbreaking research in stellar radial velocity measurements and exoplanet discoveries. In addition, it has significant potential to deploy spectrographic instruments in developing countries and in real-time monitoring applications in various industries. Lastly, it presents novel opportunities for teaching spectroscopy and astrophysics through hands-on demonstrations using these user-friendly devices. 

In the section on silicon photonic technology, we delved into the detail of designing optimal photonic templates by employing numerical modeling of atomic/molecular absorption lines. This included accounting for hyperfine structures and considering various broadening effects in order to minimize template errors.

In the section on fibre-based photonics, we explored two approaches; the design of customized fibre Bragg gratings and the optimization of transmission spectra in favour of shape factors. This led to successful demonstrations of detecting molecular gas in a laboratory setting and the implementation of a radial velocity measurement system. 

In the final section, we outline and compare our approach with conventional spectrographic techniques and discuss various research and application pathways for these photonic devices. This includes integrating them with laser light and exploring new opportunities with these devices. Lastly, we anticipate that our work will inspire multidisciplinary collaborations among physicists, astronomers and engineers to bring this technology to the forefront of global astronomical research.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This method converges faster and achieves greater model accuracy than alternative approaches, such as local update algorithms alone. Moreover, our results show that the proposed algorithm performs well even with a random server update policy. This is demonstrated through both mathematical analysis and real-world experiments utilizing cancer treatment and election data. The code for this research is available on an open-source platform noted in the paper citation.

Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be dominated by stable geostrophic vortices, has recently been observed to support highly dynamic, downscale energy cascades. In a recent study, researchers employed direct numerical simulations within a triply periodic box, artificially suppressing geostrophic vortices to investigate the properties of turbulent flows. These simulations revealed an inertial wave turbulence that conforms to a specific spectrum first described analytically by Galtier in 2003. Interestingly, it was found that the same underlying mechanisms could either give rise to wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices depending solely on the initial conditions, thus further establishing the concept of bi-stability in rotating turbulent flows. Moreover, the results also indicated that the stability of geostrophic vortices does not impede the occurrence of downscale energy cascades in turbulent flows. In fact, it was observed that the total turbulent kinetic energy is essentially independent of whether the underlying turbulence is characterized by wave turbulence or stable geostrophic vortices. Therefore, it can be inferred that stable geostrophic vortices merely represent an energetically localized manifestation of the broader wave turbulence state. In addition, the simulations revealed that stable geostrophic vortices are capable of emitting weak, forward-slope waves that carry a minor but distinct fraction of the total turbulent energy. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake a major upgrade to the LHC's detector system. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data, courtesy of the Feature EXtractors (FEX) system. Specifically, the jet FEX (jFEX) system aims to enhance jet identification and calculate global variables within an extremely tight latency constraint of under 400 nanoseconds. This will involve six distinct modules, where each module on an ATCA board contains four high-end Xilinx FPGAs to process the data at an astonishing 3.6 terabytes per second rate. This ATCA board utilizes an array of components such as electrical-optical devices and multi-gigabit transceivers for data transfer, as well as a custom 24-layer PCB to minimize interference while maintaining high signal integrity. This project has successfully overcome design hurdles and has demonstrated its performance capabilities with the fully assembled final prototype having achieved up to 2.2 gigabytes per second during in-house and combined ATCA board and jFEX module testing. However, it is essential to note that this rate might be further optimized in future iterations. With the full deployment of 288 jFEX modules across the ATLAS detector by the end of 2021, the jFEX system represents a groundbreaking achievement in high-energy physics with its intricate design and unprecedented processing capabilities. This achievement would not have been possible without the collaborative efforts from a diverse range of companies and research institutions as well as the contributions from numerous researchers and engineers who overcame numerous technical obstacles along the way. This paper provides an in-depth look at the design, technical specifications, performance capabilities, and design evolution of the jFEX system from its initial concept to its final implementation. It also highlights the challenges encountered and how they were overcome with the successful collaboration between industry, university, and CERN research teams. This paper will serve as a reference for any potential future projects that may undertake similar technical endeavors in the future. This paper is targeted at any individual with an interest in understanding the technical aspects and design evolution of the jFEX system. It is particularly relevant to anyone involved in the development of custom high-performance computing projects especially in the field of particle physics and Level 1 trigger systems. This paper will also provide any potential future projects with any valuable lessons learned and any practical design guidelines and technical specifications that can be applied to any future custom computing projects in this field.

The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Experimental results confirm the algorithm's effectiveness across different settings, included comprehensive experiments with real-world applications. A further development of the modified FedBuff targets cross-device federated learning with client retention in mind, with a novel framework awaiting formal convergence rate analysis.
