Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our best outcome with a fine-tuned Czech-only model yielded a 13.5% WER, in comparison to the 16.5% WER achieved by a model trained from scratch on the extended dataset. Our approach also allowed us to achieve better results when using a smaller amount of data, namely 200 hours of data, with a WER of 18.3% as opposed to the 20.4% WER when using a model trained from scratch. All of our models and data are openly accessible on the Hugging Face Model Hub and the related code on GitHub. Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance reported by LHCb in recent times.  Employing a perturbative QCD approach, we calculate the di-kaon distribution amplitudes from LHCb data containing $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance.  Furthermore, we predict branching fractions for $B^{\pm} \to \pi^0 K^{\pm} \pi^{\pm} K^{\mp}$ decays to be $4.5 \times 10^{-5}$ and $5.5 \times 10^{-5}$ for electric and magnetic parity modes respectively.  Moreover, we estimate the contribution from $\rho^0(1450)$ to the $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} \pi^0$ branching fraction to be $8 \times 10^{-6}$.  It is noteworthy that while $\rho^0(1450)$ contributes significantly to $\rho^0\pi^0$ mode, its contribution to $\rho^0 K^S$ mode is minimal due to di-kaon distribution amplitude suppression.  Therefore, verification of $\rho^0(1450)$ through $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} \rho^0$ decay would be highly desirable.  Finally, we suggest that experimenters search for $\rho^0(1450)$ in $B^{\pm} \to \pi^{\mp} K^{\mp} \pi^{\pm}$ decays via kinematical shape analysis for validation purposes.  In addition, we estimate that if $\rho^0(1450)$ contributes significantly to $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} \pi^0$, then it is possible to observe it in decay modes such as $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} J/\psi \pi^0$ and $B^{\pm} \to K^{\pm} D_s^- \pi^0$, given that $D_s^-$ or $J/\psi$ decays do not complicate the analysis. Recent research suggests combining the Swampland program with dark energy's scarcity could predict the presence of an additional dimension with a characteristic scale of a micron. We've investigated how this extra dimension affects the rate of Hawking radiation in black holes and found that their perception of it causes the radiation to slow down. We discuss how this affects the possibility that dark matter consists of primordial black holes and estimate a suitable mass range of 10^14 to 10^21 grams, which expands on the existing four-dimensional theory's scope by three orders of magnitude in the lower mass range. Furthermore, primordial black holes with a mass of approximately 10^12 grams may be responsible for the Galactic 511 keV gamma-ray line, assuming they make up a very small fraction of total dark matter. Conditions are also identified under which they could dominate dark matter, prompting the prediction of a distinct feature in the black hole spectrum when investigating primordial black hole signatures in gravitational waves. Lastly, we explore the implications of extra dimensions on black hole superradiance and find that it could occur more readily, with potential consequences for the direct detection of dark matter through black hole modulation. Overall, our study highlights how the presence of an additional dimension affects the behavior of black holes and primordial black holes within the context of the Swampland program and dark energy's scarcity.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force-controlled system, guiding the achievement of the optimal outcome. This developed algorithm is successfully validated using actual SEA hardware setup for its effectiveness. The outcomes of the experimentation, conducted using different severities of external loads and diverse SEA operating conditions, confirm the capability of the algorithm in delivering superior force control results compared to standard PID controller implementations. Most notably, the results show that the standard deviation of the force error can be reduced by up to 75% when the proposed algorithm is employed. Moreover, the associated force estimation error is also found to be highly mitigable with the developed transmission force observer, leading to acceptable force regulation below 10 N when the system is subjected to up to 50 N of external load. The success of the approach was further confirmed by simulations of SEAs with varying elastic properties and multiple degree-of-freedom force loading conditions. The simplicity and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm make it an appealing solution for the challenging force control problem in series elastic actuators. The associated code is publicly accessible for replication and extension purposes. The algorithm's superior performance paves the way for its adoption in high-precision force-controlled applications of series elastic actuators, such as minimally invasive surgery and delicate handling tasks. The study's findings can also be applied to other nonlinear force-transmitting systems equipped with sensory feedback systems. The publicly available code on GitHub can be utilized as a starting point for further algorithmic innovations aimed at enhancing the force-controlling capabilities of series elastic actuators. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments. This model also helps us understand why, below a certain speed, particles will reassemble quickly enough to prevent cracks from forming, but above this speed, cracks will always appear, no matter how small the strain. We also observe that at very high speeds, the size of clusters increases to the point where it becomes determined by the conditions of our experiment, rather than the raft's dynamics, and we see that by increasing the viscosity of the surrounding fluid, we can slow down the raft's breakdown even further. All of our experiments were conducted using a light microscopy system that allows us to see and measure the movement of individual particles within the raft. By studying the failure of these particle rafts, we hope to be able to apply our understanding to more complex systems. For instance, breakdown in continuous materials is often delayed, and we believe that by recognizing the differences and similarities between continuous and discrete materials, we can gain a deeper understanding of material failure in general. Furthermore, we also think that by changing the properties of the surrounding fluid, such as its viscosity, we may be able to delay the breakdown of materials in various applications. Lastly, we observe that at moderate speeds, the shape of cracks within our particle rafts resembles a bell-shaped curve, often seen in materials that break apart in a different manner, known as ductile failure. Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%. Notably, our method successfully reduced the gap between scores for moderate and severe cases, ultimately ranking second with a Macro F1 Score of 43.11%. Our experiments demonstrated that our initial lesion segmentation component alone achieved the highest score of 51.81% among all competing methods on the test dataset. Nonetheless, our overall approach, while not the top scorer, still secured second place with a score of 51.68%. Moreover, our model's performance was consistently impressive, with a Macro F1 Score ranging from 48.18% to 51.81% in repeated experiments. In summary, our study has made significant contributions to COVID-19 severity detection by introducing an innovative infection-aware 3D classification network and tackling data imbalance issues. Our methods and results have provided valuable insights for future research in this critical area. Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, corresponding to an 'up-up-down' arrangement of the Gd3+ ions. A notable increase in magnetic entropy was also observed in the GdInO3 system, originating from the inherent magnetic frustration within this compound. A model incorporating a classical spin Hamiltonian was employed to develop the theoretical phase diagram, showing a ground state dominated by weak easy-axis anisotropy and closely resembling that of an equilateral triangular-lattice system. This theoretical framework may be a valuable reference point for the interpretation of future experiments utilizing NMR, ESR, or muon-spin relaxation spectroscopy. Notably, the proximity of the 1/3 magnetization plateau to either magnetic instability makes GdInO3 an exciting subject for further study in the field of magnetic materials.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we established that for any mechanism with any number of agents, there will always exist a Nash equilibrium that induces an allocation that is fair up to one good. However, this last result comes with a caveat - there exists a mechanism for three agents whose every Nash equilibrium does not induce an allocation that is fair up to one good. In conclusion, our investigation highlights the mechanisms of Round-Robin and Plaut and Roughgarden as exemplary systems that produce Nash equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, and suggests that such systems may serve as a useful framework for designing fair allocation systems in complex settings. In addition, our investigation is contributing to a better understanding of the interrelation between different notions of fairness and their doability in various scenarios. Lastly, our investigation is opening new research paths for studying fair allocation in complex environments. In particular, our investigation is prompting further inquiry into the global efficiency of systems producing Nash equilibria that are fair allocations, as well as the exploration of systems that always result in pure Nash equilibria producing fair allocations. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines, ultimately resulting in cutting-edge UDA performance on two challenging semantic segmentation evaluation sets. The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the user a choice between efficient yet approximate and comprehensive yet computational methods. The code for our method has been made publicly accessible on GH Reps. Additionally, we introduce an interactive tool, SHAP-ifier, tailored for the feature importance explanation SHAP values. By providing a comprehensive explanation for Random Forest predictions, we hope to facilitate safer adoption of ML in security-sensitive environments. Our research also offers a foundation for explaining other ML models and offers numerous avenues for further investigation. It is our firm belief that data owners possess the most effective perspective for appraising the feature importance of their own data. Consequently, we emphasize the significance of making explainability techniques accessible to non-ML experts who are intimately acquainted with the data at hand. Lastly, we stress the value of interdisciplinary collaboration among computer security specialists, ML researchers, and data owners to push the boundaries of this field. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with varying forecasting lengths. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Our study's outcomes will ultimately contribute to a deeper understanding of how the pion's structure is composed of quarks and their internal dynamics at various quark mass regimes. Moreover, this investigation paves the way for exploring the internal quark dynamics within other hadrons through the analysis of quark current correlations within these particles. Ultimately, this will facilitate a more precise interpretation of lattice correlation functions in terms of partonic interpretation in QCD. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US. The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a comprehensive machine learning pipeline consisting of data preprocessing, feature extraction, and model training. To bridge this gap, a new system, DataScope, has been designed to efficiently compute the Shapley value for training examples within an end-to-end machine learning pipeline, particularly for a type of pipeline referred to as a canonical pipeline, characterized by a positive relational algebra query and a K-nearest neighbor classifier. DataScope's novel approach enables the computation of the Shapley value for a wide range of canonical pipeline subfamilies with near-linear time complexity, outperforming state-of-the-art Monte Carlo-based methods by several orders of magnitude. The system's practical effectiveness is demonstrated through various experiments, including the debugging of machine learning models in real-world settings. The underlying techniques developed in DataScope also form the basis for future research aimed at supporting DataScope's broader goals, which encompass computing the Shapley value for additional machine learning tasks and providing interactive debugging tools. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, with impressive results that outperform baseline methods by a significant margin in accuracy, particularly on difficult datasets. Our implementation and data are freely available for download.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures. The connection between entropy and the phenomenological angle is explored, revealing that the latter has a maximum value of approximately 2.39 times the former. This ratio applies universally across all microcavity lasers, regardless of their structure. Consequently, the entropy can be utilized to estimate the emission angle with satisfactory accuracy. Notably, our analysis also discloses specific conditions under which the emission angle becomes locked to the laser's resonance mode, leading to a nearly uniform emission profile. In contrast, emissions with complex structures arise from another laser mode with different polarization. Our framework is particularly useful for interpreting and designing microcavity lasers exhibiting directional emission. Moreover, it may be applied to any emission system that involves a binary choice between two alternative directions. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has an inaccurate policy while the others are relatively accurate, existing offline methods may skew the learned results in favor of the inferior agent, leading to suboptimal team outcomes. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that prevents one agent's poor performance from negatively impacting the team by limiting the impact of individual trajectories. We demonstrate that high-quality team policies can be achieved through a single offline dataset containing diverse trajectories among the agents, provided that the agents' individual behaviors are reasonably reliable. Moreover, our framework allows us to derive bounds on the optimal team performance when compared to the best possible outcomes achieved through centralized online learning. To realize this goal, we developed an efficient algorithm called SIT-MAVRIK that learns effective team policies directly from the offline dataset without needing intermediate steps. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through various complex scenarios, and the results show that SIT-MAVRIK outperforms existing offline multi-agent methods by a significant margin. Moreover, SIT-MAVRIK exhibits comparable performance to online learning methods in several scenarios. We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Two separate datasets were used to train and test the network. Our 2D experiment utilized the NTIRE 2019 Brain MRI Isotropic Resampling Challenge dataset for both training and testing, whereas our 3D experiment involved the BrainVISA Brain Imaging Database Archive and the Isorta dataset from the NTIRE 2020 Challenge. Both experiments showed significant improvements in target-lesion coverage and planning quality indices compared to conventional methods and the baseline image. Additionally, our 3D experiment revealed a mean distance error of 1.41 mm when tested with new target locations and shapes. Our code is available on GitHub, along with a public demo site. Moreover, we introduced the MV-Deformable-UNET challenge to encourage researchers to contribute their methods and test them on our publicly shared code and data.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment as an analogy to demonstrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, making the phenomenon detectable even when the parties are separated by significant interstellar distances. In this scenario, the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's behavior plays a crucial role in the occurrence of the phenomenon, albeit only when the spreading of the entangled wave function is taken into account. In an effort to mitigate the concerns of an infinitely far separation being unphysical, we introduce a minimum length based on the spreading of the entangled wave function, which serves as an effective range for the phenomenon. In the context of single-particle entanglement, the effective range is vastly more considerable than that based on the spreading of the single-particle wave function itself. In contrast, the effective range for the phenomenon of steering is on the order of the system's original size, as opposed to the vast distances involved in Einstein's thought experiment. As such, we do not consider this to be an instance of'spooky action at a distant star.' Furthermore, we also explore the possibility of observing the phenomenon of steering in laboratory-scale systems. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-based Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-BFL frameworks that meet the unique challenges and requirements of IoVs systems. Furthermore, it provides various problem formulations and relevant mathematical derivations to facilitate comparative analysis in this domain. As the field continues to evolve, it's crucial to address emerging challenges and consider future research avenues to ensure the scalability and security of such frameworks in real-world IoVs environments. This survey is presently available as a non-peer-reviewed manuscript on arXiv, where it has received significant attention and citation.

A proposed precoder codebook and rank adaptation tool utilizes Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to generate codebooks that minimize information rate loss. Initially, a set of fixed precoders and rank-adaptation tools are trained on independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) channel realizations to generate GMMs. These models are then fine-tuned with information about the target channel, enabling the selection of the best-performing codebook entry, precoder, and rank-adaptated layer configuration to minimize the average information rate loss. A proposed algorithm chooses the optimal codebook configuration with minimal computation. This approach outperforms existing techniques such as eigen decomposition (EDE) and minimum mean square error (MMSE)-based methods in simulated scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method exhibits comparable performance to alternative techniques like deep codebook optimization methods while requiring significantly less computational resources. Further research aims to enhance performance over certain channel conditions and expand the method's applicability to other communication systems. This work is relevant to the design of next-generation communication systems by addressing codebook design and optimization challenges. As such, the associated algorithms may be implemented on devices capable of machine learning computations, enabling efficient codebook selection and optimization. As a result, this approach could be an effective solution for codebook design problems in other contexts. The associated code for this study is available online.

One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
Notably, high-performance optimizations do not lead to inaccuracies in the results, guaranteeing the validity of our findings in both healthy and distorted game environments. 
Most notably, we were able to conduct the first-ever experiments involving distributed training of virtual agents. 
Our research also includes the identification of specific bottlenecks hindering further improvement in virtual agents and suggests strategies for future researchers to explore more efficient methods of simulation processing.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by incorporating a sophisticated memory access scheme that minimizes data conflicts and allows for real-time matrix transformations. Experimental results indicate that the compact FDHT-LSTM model and the hardware accelerator it runs on yield outstanding performance, outperforming existing compressed LSTM models and hardware platforms in terms of model size, accuracy, and processing power. Furthermore, when applied to action recognition in video streams, the FDHT-LSTM network demonstrates exceptional energy efficiency and high performance. Experimental evaluations across multiple datasets demonstrate that the compact FDHT-LSTM model exhibits only a 5.57% accuracy drop compared to the baseline LSTM model, which is remarkably minimal. In terms of model size, the FDHT-LSTM structure is approximately 125 times more compact than the baseline LSTM model. In terms of processing performance, the FDHT-LSTM hardware accelerator is capable of processing around 600 frames per second on a single video processing unit (VPU), which is about 25 times faster than the baseline LSTM network. As a result of these advancements, the proposed FDHT-LSTM algorithm and hardware platform offer significant implications for the practical application of LSTMs in video recognition. These achievements lead to substantial model size reductions, tangible accuracy gains, and notable improvements in processing performance, ultimately paving the way for real-time LSTMs in video recognition. Consequently, this research is expected to open up new possibilities for the use of LSTMs in VPU-accelerated video intelligence systems that require low model complexity, high accuracy, and fast processing. As a result, this study is anticipated to yield dividends in various sequence analysis applications across multiple data domains. In video recognition, for instance, these advancements enable LSTMs to tackle more complex tasks such as multiple-action recognition and long-duration video analysis, which were previously out of the model's grasp due to its size. Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways for NLP under low-labeled data settings. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. On the other hand, in theories with a stable vacuum, we've demonstrated that the convexity of a charge under a U(1) symmetry arises naturally from the self-binding energy of a charged particle in those theories, which is in alignment with the framework proposed by Montero and Seifert. To stabilize the ground state estimation in quantum chemistry simulations within a quantum computer's unitary operator circuit, we develop a method using the imaginary time quantum propagation technique. This method involves using the Euler macroscopic substitution (EMS) algorithm to overcome spin contamination common in wavefunction-based calculations. We demonstrate the ground state estimation algorithm's efficacy by applying it to a series of boron chain molecule simulations, one of the challenging chemical platforms involving tunneling effects that are difficult to capture using traditional classical algorithms. The results show that our approach converges to the accurate ground state within 50-100 quantum circuit applications, achieving a unitary cost reduction of almost two orders of magnitude compared to the naive approach and ground state estimation via imaginary time evolution directly from the all-zero initial state. Moreover, our results indicate that the total quantum resource requirements can be minimized through the employment of the Z-X-Z sequence unitary operator and chemical parameter optimization, resulting in a ground state approximation within 1% accuracy within as few as 10 quantum circuit applications for the worst-case scenario examined. Our study provides a crucial step in achieving realistic quantum chemistry simulations on near-term quantum devices.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the equivalence of $F$-rationality to another set of conditions that include the tightness of the tight Hilbert function and the equidimensionality of the ring. We also establish a condition for the equality of two specific polynomials and give it a geometric interpretation. Based on this condition, we are able to conclude that if the ring has a specific dimension, then the tight Hilbert function is 1, which further implies that the ring is $F$-rational. This result generalizes a previously known fact about Lyubeznik's inequality in dimension two. Lastly, we provide a condition for the equality of two sets of integers based on their sums of squares, which leads to a conclusion about the equality of two specific polynomials and thus, for the equality of two set of integers. This generalizes a previously known fact about Hilbert functions in equidimensional excellent local rings. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The proposed modeling approach is applicable to actual case studies, as demonstrated by an exploration of the design issue in the German power market network. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model, along with the design challenges and results explored in this study, is openly accessible on an accompanying repository for reproducibility and further research opportunities. The model offers a versatile platform for conducting in-depth evaluations of complex design issues in the electricity ancillary services and markets. Consequently, this study contributes significantly to the advancement of integrated research into the design of electricity markets and ancillary services. Along with the openly shared code, this study enables Reproducible Research that paves the way for collaborative evaluation of design issues concerning the electricity ancillary services and markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model is now part of the MESA-PyPSA framework, an open-source agent-based power system modeling toolkit, along with other features like modular modeling, integrated data processing, and a graphical user interface. This integrated toolkit is designed to bridge the gap between analytical modeling and policy simulation, making it an ideal platform for collaborative research and development of innovative power system models. The code for this study, including the model extensions, is openly available

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. A combinatorial interpretation of iterated wreath products is also introduced, employing the diagram of the polynomial's composition as a graph. Finally, the connection to the field with one element, particularly in the case of positive characteristic, is touched upon. The paper also includes an appendix regarding the polynomial F's power and its connection to the Galois group's architecture. Moreover, the interplay between the composite polynomial's Galois group and F's architecture is examined when Phi is composed with multiple different polynomials F, resulting in a new set of polynomials with distinct coefficients. In this scenario, the Galois group's structure is identified as an iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) as well. When these composite polynomials have a common base F, the Galois group's structure is a variant of the iterated wreath product, depending on the specific arrangement of the powers of F. The architecture of the Galois group's quotient by its largest abelian normal subgroup is also determined. Lastly, the paper concludes with an exploration of a related graph, particularly in the case where F is a irreducible polynomial over a finite field and Phi is a generic monic polynomial. In this scenario, the structure of the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate is an (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree.

Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a key component of our analysis, we investigate the impact of optimizing cutting strategies for jet properties, such as $k_T$ clustering and thrust minimum, on reducing the background while preserving the signal. We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different new scalar SU(2)L representations. These new scenarios are expected to be probed at a precision of a part in 10^4 by future e+e- colliders due to precise measurements of σ(e+e- → Zh) that complement searches for the Standard Model scalar sector at particle colliders such as the Large Hadron Collider, or a possible future pp collider, or Higgs decay to photons. We also find the sensitivity of σ(e+e- → Zh) and γγ decays of the Higgs boson to have the most notable complementary role in the complex triplet model scenario. A triple system unitarization procedure is adopted to handle the Coleman-Weinberg potential for the Standard Model and its scalar extension scenarios, except for the complex triplet model where the global minimum of the potential remains unknown. In such cases, we employ the decoupling approach to calculate one-loop corrections at low energies. In the complex triplet model scenario, the leading order low-energy effective dimensionless potential is considered for a more qualitative analysis. In all scenarios, except the complex triplet model, we find the shift in the Standard Model value of σ(e+e- → Zh) to be positive when the mass of the additional scalar field is less than 80 GeV, or when the mass of the additional scalar field is greater than 800 GeV, which provides the Standard Model-like scenario in the intermediate mass range. However, in the complex triplet model, a significant shift in σ(e+e- → Zh) can occur for a positive value of the vacuum expectation value of the neutral component of the triplet scalar field, regardless of the value of the additional scalar mass. In the complex triplet model, a positive value of the vacuum expectation value of the neutral component of the triplet scalar field can cause the shift in σ(e+e- → Zh) to an extent that it falls below the SM prediction, or rises above it, depending on the value of the additional scalar mass in the range mentioned above. In the inert doublet and the triplets, quintets, and septets, where the neutral component of the scalar field acquires a zero or negative value, the shift in σ(e+e- → Zh) is always below the SM prediction, or rises above it

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The vortex in the north was also found to be surrounded by enhanced levels of methane. It is possible that the formation of the polar vortex is delayed in the north because the formation of the hexagonal shape causes a level of "friction" in the atmosphere, slowing the formation of the vortex. The fact that the vortex in the north disappears faster than the one in the south may be due to the presence of a prominent storm in the north, which could be interfering with the vortex and causing it to break down. More research is needed to confirm these findings. The study of the polar vortex in Saturn provides valuable insights into the behavior of the planet's atmosphere and offers a framework for comparing it to the atmosphere on Jupiter. In the future, the study of Saturn's polar vortex can be further understood through the analysis of additional data from the Cassini spacecraft and the upcoming Jupiter Polar Orbiter mission. The latter is particularly interested in studying the South Pole of the planet, where the presence of a persistent anticyclone was confirmed through the analysis of data from the Galileo spacecraft. The behavior of the vortex on both Jupiter and Saturn can also be compared to the emerging patterns on the polar atmospheres of the other gas giants and ice giants in the Solar System. The study of the polar vortex in Saturn is significant because it highlights the capability of near-infrared spectroscopy to monitor the formation of complex patterns in planetary atmospheres. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario. This approach also acknowledges the influential contributions of Kapoullis and Panagiotis, as well as Dinh, Dung, and Nguyen in related studies. A global-in-time solution strategy is also presented, relying on an earlier idea by Tsutsumi, and we leverage this method to prove both mass and energy bounds for sub-solutions under these conditions. The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the terminations, the metal-insulator transition may be significantly impeded or totally hindered near the surface due to distinct variations in electron distribution at different layers and altered screening length as compared to the bulk.  A considerable reorganization of spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition has also been observed, with an observable transfer of spectral weight across the entire energy scale from the high-binding energy regime to the low-binding energy regime, in contrast to our findings of unconserved total spectral weight across the metal-insulator transition, which indicates a failure in applying'sum rules of spectral weight',  a hallmark of systems with strong correlations.  Our data suggest that changes in hybridization, charge distribution within unit cells, and lattice parameters within unit cells, along with the charge distribution across unit cells, all play crucial roles in driving the metal-insulator transition in these films.  Lastly, our research offers an initial direct visualization of the change in electron occupancy across the metal-insulator transition, offering new quantitative measures of the degree of charge conduction in V$_2$O$_3$.  Notably, our data also highlight the failure of Drude-Lorentz model in accurately capturing the features of spectral weight across metal-insulator transition in these materials. Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of field operator matrix elements. In the weak-coupling regime, these profiles resemble those of dark solitons. We then precisely examine the interaction between two notches in quantum double dark-soliton states. Observations suggest that quasi-condensation may play a significant role in quantum double dark-soliton dynamics, and that states with high condensate fractions should be well-represented by a quasi-condensation state that follows a mean-field model. Conversely, in cases with low condensate fractions where the quasi-condensation state significantly deviates from the mean-field model, scattering between notch locations may cause a diffusive behavior, and we calculate the diffusion coefficient. Our results also indicate that states with flat regions near notches may exhibit persistent currents when these regions undergo periodic oscillations between two locations. The time scales for these non-equilibrium behaviors are on the order of $n_{1,2}^{-1}$, where $n_{1,2}$ represent the distances between the notch and the edge of the condensate in units of the roton minimum of the one-dimensional Tonks-Girardeau model. Lastly, our findings suggest that weakly-coupled quantum double dark-soliton states may be sensitive to nontthermal excitation by applying a weak perturbation at specific locations. This could be accomplished via optical lattices with adjustable strengths and shapes, or via lattices that selectively influence particular notch locations. This may enable the directed flow of matter waves in these systems. This could potentially lead to the development of precise thermal valve technology in one-dimensional boson gases. The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Moreover, this technique may be extended to different light sources and other dimensions of collected data. As a practical application, we use it to analyze experimental data concerning Eu$^{3+}$ ions doped into a calcium aluminate nanocrystal, and the resulting reconstructed spectra show great agreement with theoretical predictions made by a single-ion model. The algorithm is available upon request.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware. As such, it could play a key role in making quantum technology practical.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics that may arise due to competing isotropic exchanges or an asymmetrical magnetic arrangement. Depending on its anisotropy, the metal can transition between spiral and uniform magnetization orders. A specific type of magnetic arrangement known as the B20 structure further contributes to the device's operation, influencing the long-range pairing of superconducting electrons under intense exchange fields. However, numerical simulations demonstrate that an unusual orientation-dependent effect can be utilized to control the device's behavior at moderately low exchange fields. Consequently, a significant amplification of the device's effect is achieved when specific parameters such as exchange splitting and spiral period are comparable to the superconducting coherence length. A proposed application for this finding includes the design of spiral metal structures using B20 materials with simple London penetration depth to develop controllable magnetic probes of superconducting devices. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This approach to discourse analysis is future-proof as it is devoid of any theoretical presuppositions about language and can be adapted to any new instance of data. For example, predictions made for sentences expressing antagonism could be used in research focused on that specific discourse category. Moreover, this work is the initial step in an enhanced research path that is open to feedback, and the developed framework is provided for the community to contribute to new discourse categories and relationships. The introduced dataset, the discourse relations it is based on, and the associated discourse indicators can be found in the attached code and is ready for further annotation and improvement. The code can be found at the link provided in the paper text. The current version of the dataset encompasses 50 distinct discourse relations and is comprised of 1800 unique sentences from the LSC corpus. Furthermore, 1380 labeled instances from the LSC corpus, spanning 45 distinct discourse relations, are incorporated into a zero-shot discourse classification task. This task leverages 5 fully-supervised semantically annotated datasets that total 2200 instances and 12 distinct discourse relations. The results of this task demonstrate the efficacy of this approach with a score of 58.6% across all relations and 75.8% in the relations found within the LSC corpus. The effectiveness of this method is also compared to a theoretical baseline model that is trained on each instance separately. The comparison shows that the proposed approach has a clear advantage over the baseline model with a significant reduction in error and a notable improvement in accuracy for most discourse relations. The best strategy tested this approach further by conducting a zero-shot classification of the entire LSC corpus

The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Lastly, our findings are substantiated by numerical experiments. Our study offers an initial exploration into the landscape analysis of matrix optimization problems and can serve as a reference for investigating other problems within this broader framework. Our results on the factorized PSD cone geometry may have far-reaching implications, given the increasing popularity of the Burer-Monteiro factorization in solving matrix optimization problems.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms. In contrast, many games failed to reach a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "individual learning" algorithms. Additionally, our results demonstrated that "social learning" significantly outperformed "individual learning" across all game types. In summary, our results clearly showed the superiority of "social learning" over "individual learning" in achieving games' convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. In our analysis of the game types where the NE was not reached, we found that the primary reason was the presence of multiple NE which led to the failure of both learning types to converge to an NE. However, the absence of NE in some games cannot be accounted for by the learning type used. In such cases, both "social" and "individual learning" failed to converge to an NE state. It is also noteworthy that the frequency of games failing to reach an NE state was significantly higher in the context of games with positive spillovers compared to games with negative spillovers. Furthermore, our results indicated a clear tendency for games with complex structures to fail more frequently in reaching an NE state compared to games with simple structures. Lastly, our results showed no significant difference in failure rates among single-player co-ordination games with multiple NE when comparing "social" and "individual learning". In such games, both learning types failed to converge to an NE state the vast majority of the time. In contrast, games with complex structures and multiple NE failed to reach an NE state around 80-90% of the time when played under "social learning" and around 95-99% of the time when played under "individual learning". The Ising model falls within the domain of equilibrium statistical mechanics, in contrast, the voter model represents a system out of equilibrium. Our analysis focuses on an opinion formation model, a hybrid of Ising and voter agents, with concentrations of $p$ and $1-p$. Notably, even though detailed balance is violated for $p<1$, it has been shown that on a fully connected graph the stationary state average magnetization for any $p>0$ follows the same equation as for the pure Ising model ($p=1$). This behavior is further confirmed by numerical simulations; however, the observed equivalence with the pure Ising model is limited to magnetization. While susceptibility diverges at the same temperature as magnetization, its values vary according to the concentration of Ising agents $p$. Simulations conducted on a random graph also reveal that even a minimal proportion of Ising agents can trigger ferromagnetic ordering. These findings highlight the significant impact of the model's dynamical nature on opinion formation. A hybrid approach, combining elements from equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems, may provide valuable insights into understanding real-world social dynamics.

The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling is presented, leveraging Bayesian methodology to cast uncertainties as probability distributions and inform hypernetwork architectures through Bayes optimization. As examples, this approach was applied to two disparate problems: an inverse problem solving a simple model equation and a mapping problem solving the Stokes equations. In both instances, predictions along with their associated uncertainty were generated and compared against ground truth data, confirming the beneficial effects of the proposed framework on uncertainty estimation. Using an exact partition function, we analyze a unitary matrix model based on a single plaquette configuration at a finite $N$ for both the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries. This entails exploring the properties of a specific "dimer" system within the context of the gauge group, and our calculations reveal intriguing results for the chiral phase transition, transition temperatures, and "dimer" formation across various systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the SU($N$) case can be accurately understood through the application of a semi-circle law for Hermitian matrix models, and we also determine that U($N$) systems exhibit behavior closely aligned with their SU($N$) counterparts. However, our studies also uncover distinct effects arising from the presence of phases with a non-trivial topological character in the U($N$) system. A particular "dimer" configuration is found to undergo a transition from being fully enclosed within a single domain to being split across multiple domains as the system's temperature is increased. A thorough theoretical framework, involving both instanton calculations and Kalashnikov-Lashkevich formulas, is employed to visualize these transitions through their energies and height profiles within various systems. Our work provides a foundation for a more comprehensive understanding of the interplay between non-hermitian disorder and topological characteristics in systems governed by the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries. It is also hypothesized that our one-plaquette unitary matrix model may serve as a suitable analogy for describing the behavior of atomic wave functions within optical lattices suffering from loss and drive. Lastly, our research proposes that the SU($N$) case may offer a suitable framework for examining the properties of higher-spin Bose-Einstein condensates in atomic systems. In such scenarios, the number of spin units (angular momentum) is directly proportional to the number of atoms, thereby eliminating the possibility of fully understanding higher-spin systems through the study of single-plaquette models at finite $N$. However, even with this limitation in mind, our one-plaquette unitary matrix model remains a foundational tool for exploring the fundamental characteristics of higher-spin systems in atomic physics. It is also worth noting that our research has the potential to contribute to more comprehensive studies of systems governed by the SU($N$) and U($N$) symmetries, encompassing fractions of a plaquette and multiple-plaquette configurations across various gauge groups. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following our preliminary research, we've conducted an in-depth study into mitigating hardware-induced memory errors affecting CNNs by incorporating activation clipping techniques. Our research evaluates the efficacy of different clipping methods including basic clipping, dynamic, and learned techniques for both artificial and genuine hardware settings. The evaluation reveals that specific activation clipping strategies effectively mitigate hardware errors by preventing malicious memory access and reducing unreliable output. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that certain techniques successfully minimize performance degradation when dealing with hardware errors, which has significant implications for the reliable deployment of CNNs on parallel processing hardware subject to memory faults. We've also observed that instructor-free training methods like cut-softmax outperform others in error-resilient performance by up to 6.3% compared to baseline models and even outperform teacher-free training methods in some cases. Lastly, our research confirms that proper activation clipping techniques can enhance the robustness of CNNs when confronted with hardware-induced memory errors, which has far-reaching implications for the reliable deployment of computer vision systems. The European Central Bank's definition of clearing or netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. Additionally, our investigation into various graph construction methods reveals valuable insights that could guide developers of real-world web-scale clearing systems. Our research is accessible through an interactive online demo, allowing users to input their own graphs and observe the recommended clearing structure. The full-scale implementation of our approach on the Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data is openly available on GitHub. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist. Lastly, we have confirmed that our generalized twist yields a non-trivial algebraic structure in the $r$-symmetrized format. This development originates from our analysis of the quantum YB deformed $so(3)$ Lie algebra, which surprisingly gives rise to the $r$-symmetrized twist. This implies that the true quantum YB deformed $so(3)$ algebra is actually the $r$-symmetrized version. Consequently, we are able to solve the consistency issue related to the $so(3)$ Lie algebra-based monoidal category, achieving a breakthrough in our research. This breakthrough enables us to robustly establish that any 3D rotational symmetric deformed monoidal category can be consistently defined.
